findings.title: migratePlaintextSecretsToEncrypted rewrites every TOTP seed and Discord token at every boot with 0% test coverage, and the codebase already documents that a key rotation makes it destroy them
findings.category: untested data-corruption path that runs unattended at boot
findings.description: I ran the real suite with coverage (356 files, 10158 tests, all passing, 89s). lib/auth/security-migration.ts measures 0% statements / 0% branches / 0% functions (54 statements), and there is no tests/lib/auth/security-migration.test.ts. instrumentation.ts:72-74 dynamically imports it and awaits migratePlaintextSecretsToEncrypted() on every application boot. That function does `SELECT id, totp_secret FROM users WHERE totp_secret IS NOT NULL` (line 84), calls looksEncrypted(v) (line 91), and for anything it judges plaintext runs `UPDATE users SET totp_secret = $1` (line 97) plus the same loop for discord_connections.access_token/refresh_token. looksEncrypted (line 35) decides by calling decryptApiKey(value) inside a try/catch (line 48) and returning false when it throws. The repo's own diagnostic helper spells out the failure mode at scripts/_lib/_lib.2fa-crypto-mirror.mjs:64-72: if API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY is ever rotated, the old ciphertext no longer decrypts under the new key, looksEncrypted returns false, and the boot migration re-encrypts the ciphertext as if it were plaintext. Note the asymmetry: the detector for this corruption IS tested (tests/scripts/_lib.2fa-crypto-mirror.test.ts), the code that causes it is not.
findings.impact: One key rotation, one restore from a backup taken under a different key, or one self-hoster copying an .env between environments, and the next process start silently double-encrypts every stored TOTP seed and every Discord OAuth token. Every 2FA user is locked out at their next login with no way back except backup codes, and the damage is irreversible because the original plaintext is gone. Nothing fails loudly: the loop counts the rows as totpReEncrypted and logs a success line. No test would fail, no CI job would fail.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/auth/security-migration.test.ts driving migratePlaintextSecretsToEncrypted against a fake pool. Assert three cases: (1) a genuine plaintext base32 seed is UPDATEd once, (2) an already-encrypted seed produces zero UPDATE calls, and (3) the key-rotation case, a value that decryptApiKey rejects but that is NOT a valid plaintext seed, produces zero UPDATE calls and increments totpUnreadable. Case 3 fails against the current implementation, which is the point: pair it with a guard in looksEncrypted that treats a non-decryptable, non-plaintext-shaped value as unreadable rather than plaintext.

findings.title: reserveConcurrentScanSlot, the advisory-lock fix for the concurrent-scan TOCTOU, has zero tests; the whole 94-line suite only covers the best-effort pre-check the code's own comment says is not the gate
findings.category: security fix with no regression test
findings.description: lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.ts measures 42.42% statements / 56.25% branches. The file has two exported functions. checkConcurrentScanLimit (line 50) is covered by all seven tests in tests/lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.test.ts, whose single describe block at line 38 is named for it. reserveConcurrentScanSlot (line 91) is not referenced anywhere in tests/ and is entirely unexecuted, which is exactly the 57% shortfall. That function is the fix: its own doc comment at lines 76-90 says checkConcurrentScanLimit 'is check-then-act ... N parallel requests could all pass the count and all insert, overshooting the cap. This closes that race'. The untested body is the whole mechanism: `BEGIN` (line 106), `SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext($1))` keyed per-user (line 110), the in-transaction recount (line 113), the `ROLLBACK` on over-limit (line 120), the insert-then-`COMMIT` (lines 131-132), and the catch-path rollback (line 135). resolveConcurrentLimit's fail-closed guard for a non-finite configured limit (line 43, added because `current >= NaN` silently granted unlimited concurrency) has no test either.
findings.impact: Delete the pg_advisory_xact_lock line, move the count outside the transaction, or return ok:true on the over-limit branch and every test still passes. The cap is a paid-plan differentiator (PlanLimits.concurrentScans) and, because VulnRadar runs every scan in one Node process with no job queue, it is also the only thing bounding how much of that process one account can occupy. A regression is invisible in CI and shows up in production as free accounts running unbounded parallel scans and as latency for everyone else.
findings.recommendation: Extend tests/lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans.test.ts with a describe for reserveConcurrentScanSlot using a fake PoolClient that records the query text in order. Assert: the advisory lock is acquired before the count on every limited path; over-limit issues ROLLBACK and never calls insertRow; under-limit calls insertRow then COMMIT; a throwing insertRow issues ROLLBACK and releases the client; and limit === -1 skips BEGIN entirely. Add one case for resolveConcurrentLimit returning 1 when getUserPlanLimits yields a NaN concurrentScans.

findings.title: canAssignTeamRole, the team role-ceiling privilege control, has no unit test, and two of its three call sites (member removal and role change) sit in the 63% of teams/members that no test executes
findings.category: privilege-escalation control with no regression test
findings.description: `grep -rln canAssignTeamRole tests/` returns nothing. The function at lib/config/constants.ts:608 implements the subset-of-permissions ceiling whose doc comment (lines 596-607) states that without it 'a manager (manage_members, NOT manage_scans) could promote a member to admin and thereby hand out manage_scans, a capability the manager itself lacks (escalation by proxy), or demote/remove an admin that outranks them'. It has exactly three call sites, all in app/api/v3/teams/members/route.ts: line 139 in POST (invite), line 394 in DELETE (remove a member), line 527-528 in PATCH (change a member's role). That route is 570 lines with four handlers and measures 37.16% statements. tests/app/api/v3/teams/members/route.test.ts contains one describe, `POST /api/v3/teams/members`, with seven tests covering notifications, audit logging, seat caps, and rate limiting; grepping it for PATCH, DELETE, or canAssignTeamRole returns nothing. So GET, DELETE, and PATCH are entirely unexecuted, and the only call site that runs at all (POST line 139) runs incidentally with no assertion on its outcome.
findings.impact: The specific escalation the comment describes is undetectable by the suite. A refactor that drops either half of the PATCH check at line 527-528 (the code deliberately validates both the target's CURRENT role and the NEW role) lets a team manager promote a member to admin and grant manage_scans, a permission the manager does not hold. On the DELETE path it lets a manager remove an admin. Both are cross-privilege actions inside a paying customer's team, both leave the audit log looking legitimate, and neither breaks a test, a lint rule, or a typecheck.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/config/canAssignTeamRole.test.ts asserting the partial order directly: owner can act on every role; manager cannot act on admin or on operator (manage_scans); operator cannot act on manager; an unknown role on either side returns false. Then add describes for PATCH and DELETE to tests/app/api/v3/teams/members/route.test.ts asserting 403 for a manager targeting an admin, 403 for a manager assigning admin, 400 for changing your own role, 400 for touching the owner, and success plus the UPDATE for a legal change.

findings.title: Not one of the 10,158 tests bounds execution time or input size, so the entire ReDoS and unbounded-read class that AUDIT-012 found (one critical, four highs) is structurally uncatchable by this suite
findings.category: bug class the suite cannot express
findings.description: Scope: the whole tests/ tree. `performance.now` and `hrtime` appear zero times across all 356 test files. The only three `toBeLessThan(<3+ digits>)` assertions in the suite are about an array index (tests/app/api/v3/account/delete/route.test.ts:203), a string length (tests/lib/ai/scan-summary.test.ts:396), and a check count (tests/lib/scanner/checks-data/_schema.test.ts:238). No test feeds a large or adversarial input into a scanner detector and asserts a wall-clock budget, and no test asserts a body-size cap. That is precisely the shape of AUDIT-012#inj-01 (CRITICAL: maskPlaceholderSecrets runs a quadratic regex over a 1 MB body once per each of 74 detectors, reachable unauthenticated via /api/v3/demo-scan), AUDIT-012#inj-02 (a scanned site's robots.txt drives 9 seconds of backtracking in matchesRobotsRule), AUDIT-012#inj-03 (five detectors still run unbounded quadratic regexes over the full 1 MB body), AUDIT-012#ssrf-01 (safeFetch detaches every abort signal once headers arrive, leaving the body read with no time or size limit), and AUDIT-012#perf-02 (the source-map follow-up fetch has no body-read timeout). Every one of those files has high line coverage: lib/scanner/checks/content.ts and the secrets detectors are exercised in depth, just never with an input large enough or a clock assertion attached. This EXTENDS AUDIT-012#ssrf-09, which noted only that the safe-fetch suite skips the address-range block list; tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts (231 lines, 17 tests) also contains zero occurrences of maxBytes, size, byte, content-length, timeout, deadline, or abort.
findings.impact: A single detector regex edited into a catastrophic-backtracking form, or a body-size guard removed, ships green. Because VulnRadar runs every scan in one Node process, one such input pins the event loop and the whole service stops answering, including for the ~50 paying accounts that had nothing to do with the scan. The suite gives false confidence here: coverage on these files is high, so a reviewer reasonably concludes they are well tested.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/scanner/_perf-budget.test.ts: build a 1 MB pathological body (a long run of word characters, plus a robots.txt with eight `*` wildcards for matchesRobotsRule), run each registered detector bundle and matchesRobotsRule against it, and assert Date.now() elapsed stays under a budget (500 ms per detector is generous and still catches a quadratic blowup). Separately, add cases to tests/lib/scanner/safe-fetch.test.ts that stream a body larger than the configured cap and assert the read aborts, and that a slow body stream is cut off by a deadline, mirroring the shape of AUDIT-012#ssrf-01.

findings.title: No test asserts that a scan path charges the daily quota, which is why all four unmetered scan paths AUDIT-012 found pass the suite cleanly
findings.category: quota accounting never asserted end to end
findings.description: Scope: every scan entry point plus lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts. Eighteen test files reference daily-limits at all, and they are the paths that already charge correctly (scan/route, scan/bulk, scan/crawl, scan/authenticated, schedules, keys, teams, webhooks, browser/sessions). The four paths AUDIT-012 filed as unmetered are exactly the four whose tests never mention it. tests/app/api/v3/scan/discover/route.test.ts mocks six modules (db, auth, rate-limit, api-keys, safe-fetch, dns/promises) and neither of the quota modules, so AUDIT-012#abuse-01 (the two recon endpoints run outside the scan quota, ~200,000 DNS lookups and HTTP probes an hour from one free account) is invisible to it. tests/lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.test.ts mocks nine modules (db, safe-fetch, engine, async-checks, execute-scan, plan-limits, notifications, email, runtime-config) and neither daily-limits nor concurrent-scans, so AUDIT-012#abuse-04 (scheduled scans run with no quota charge, no concurrency slot, and no access-rules check) is invisible to it. Same pattern for AUDIT-012#abuse-02 (API-key crawls skip the quota) and #abuse-03 (the AI chat context path has no token quota). The suite tests that the quota function works; it never tests that a given entry point calls it.
findings.impact: Metering is the product's revenue control and its abuse control, and the suite cannot tell metered from unmetered. Four separate paths shipped free-scan capacity to anyone with an account, and none of them registered as a test failure. Any new scan entry point added tomorrow inherits the same blind spot, so this is a recurring cost, not a one-off.
findings.recommendation: Write one shared table-driven suite, tests/app/api/v3/scan/_metering.test.ts, that enumerates every scan-initiating entry point (scan, scan/bulk, scan/crawl, scan/authenticated, scan/discover, scan/crawl/discover, the scheduled-scans worker, the GitHub review path) and, for each, mocks lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits and lib/rate-limiting/concurrent-scans and asserts checkAndRecordRequest (or the documented equivalent) is called exactly once before any outbound work, and that a denied quota short-circuits with no fetch. Make the table the single list a new entry point must be added to, so an unmetered path is a failing test rather than a future audit finding.

findings.title: The self-update pipeline, which runs release code on the host and deletes files from the live install directory, is at 0% coverage on both the orchestrator and the admin route that triggers it
findings.category: destructive privileged path with no test
findings.description: Measured: lib/updater/apply.ts is 0% statements / 0% branches / 0% functions (134 statements) and app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply/route.ts is 0% (45 statements). Neither has a test file. The primitives around them are well covered (lib/updater/checksum.ts 100%, copy-with-excludes.ts 97.26%, version-compare.ts 100%), so what is untested is precisely the orchestration and the gate. runUpdateJob (line 51) downloads a release, verifies checksum and cosign, then calls copyTreeOverlay over the live app directory (line 260) and pruneExtraneous (line 277), which DELETES destination files, driven by two constant lists declared inline at lines 232-257: PROTECTED_NAMES (node_modules, .git) and PROTECTED_PREFIXES (.next, data, backups, .npm, .cache, logs, uploads), plus STRIP_PREFIXES. Nothing asserts those lists or that they are the ones actually passed to pruneExtraneous. It then runs `npm ci` and `npm run db:migrate` against the production database. The route's POST (line 41) is a five-layer gate: requireAdmin, isSuperAdminRole, isUpdaterSupported, an adminReauth rate limit, a password re-auth against users.password_hash, and a createJob race check. Every other gated admin route in the repo has a route test; this one does not.
findings.impact: Two distinct failures, both silent. Drop 'backups' or 'uploads' from PROTECTED_PREFIXES in a refactor and the next self-update permanently deletes a self-hoster's database backups or uploaded avatars, discovered only after the fact. Drop the isSuperAdminRole check at the route and any admin, not just the super admin, can trigger arbitrary release code execution plus a database migration on the host. Neither change breaks a test, a lint rule, or the typecheck, and this is the flagship self-hosting feature so a regression reaches every self-hosted install.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/updater/apply.test.ts with github-release, checksum, cosign, exec, and copy-with-excludes mocked: assert a checksum mismatch aborts before any copy, a cosign signature mismatch aborts, and that pruneExtraneous is called with exactly the PROTECTED_NAMES/PROTECTED_PREFIXES/STRIP_PREFIXES values (pin the lists in the assertion so removing an entry fails the test). Add tests/app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply/route.test.ts asserting 403 for a non-admin, 403 for a plain admin who is not super_admin, 403 for a wrong password, 429 when rate limited, 409 when a job is active, and 202 plus a createJob call on the happy path.

findings.title: The migration runner, the fresh-install builder, and the restore script total 5,574 untested lines, and scripts/ is excluded from coverage so none of that gap is visible in any report
findings.category: data-loss tooling with no test and no coverage measurement
findings.description: scripts/ holds 13,161 lines across 58 files and vitest.config.ts excludes it twice over: coverage.include is only ["lib/**/*.ts", "app/**/*.ts"] (line 31) and coverage.exclude lists "scripts/**" (line 37). So the 20 test files under tests/scripts/ run but produce no measurable coverage, and the untested remainder is invisible. Mapping tests to sources by hand: scripts/migrate/ is 4,431 lines and tests/scripts/migrate/ contains exactly one file, versions/2.0.0-to-3.0.0.test.ts. That leaves migrate.mjs (577 lines, the entry point), _registry.mjs (637), _planner.mjs (246, decides which steps run and in what order), _runner.mjs (152, executes them), _detect.mjs (84, decides the installed version), _meta.mjs (82), versions/1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs (174), versions/2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs (the deliberate downgrade, 59), _legacy-original.mjs (871), and _snippets.mjs (241) with no test at all. scripts/create-fresh-db/ (1,023 lines plus two schema files) has no test. scripts/restore-db.mjs (120 lines) has no test, although scripts/backup-db.mjs does (tests/scripts/backup-db.test.ts). scripts/db-repair-sequences.mjs has none.
findings.impact: These are the only scripts in the repo that run destructive DDL and DML against a populated production database, and the two least covered are the two that matter most: _planner/_detect decide which migration steps run against a live install (a wrong version detection runs the wrong step, or reruns one), and restore-db.mjs is the recovery path an operator reaches for on their worst day. A broken restore is discovered exactly when it cannot be fixed. The coverage exclusion compounds this: an operator or reviewer running `npm run test:coverage` sees an 81% line figure that says nothing about this 5,574-line surface.
findings.recommendation: Two changes. First, in vitest.config.ts add "scripts/**/*.mjs" to coverage.include and delete "scripts/**" from coverage.exclude so the gap is measurable. Second, add tests using the existing tests/scripts/_pg-mock.ts harness for: _detect.mjs (each version-detection branch and the ambiguous case), _planner.mjs (the step sequence for every from/to pair including the 2.0.0-to-1.0.0 downgrade, and that an unknown version refuses to plan), _runner.mjs (a failing step aborts and does not continue), and restore-db.mjs (refuses a truncated or wrong-schema dump, and does not drop the existing database before the dump validates).

findings.title: The SSRF guard and the access-rule blocklist are stubbed permanently permissive in all three scan-route suites, so deleting both gates from the routes leaves the whole suite green
findings.category: test would pass with the feature removed
findings.description: Three route suites replace the two scan-target security gates with hard-coded always-allow stubs declared inline inside the vi.mock factory, so no test can override them and no test asserts they were even called. tests/app/api/v3/scan/route.test.ts:72 declares `validateScanTarget: vi.fn(async () => ({ safe: true }))` and :76 declares `checkAccessRules: vi.fn(async () => ({ allowed: true }))`. tests/app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.test.ts:68 and :75 do the same. tests/app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.test.ts:57 does it for checkAccessRules. A scripted scan of all 4,494 it/test blocks found zero occurrences of `safe: false` or a checkAccessRules `allowed: false` override in any of those three files, and zero `expect(validateScanTarget).toHaveBeenCalled` style assertions. The gates they stand in for are real: app/api/v3/scan/route.ts:276 calls validateScanTarget and returns 400 on !safe, :285 calls checkAccessRules and returns 403 on !allowed; app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:304 and :310 do the same; app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts:341 does the checkAccessRules half. The exact mutation the suite does not catch: delete lines 275 to 295 of app/api/v3/scan/route.ts, lines 304 to 313 of app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts, and lines 340 to 352 of app/api/v3/scan/crawl/route.ts, and every one of the 697 lines of scan/route.test.ts plus both sibling suites still pass. For contrast, tests/app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.test.ts:179 does drive `mockCheckAccessRules.mockResolvedValue({ allowed: false })`, which is the pattern the three scan routes are missing.
findings.impact: The SSRF gate on the main scan endpoint is the control that stops a user pointing a scan at 169.254.169.254 or an internal 10.x host, and the access-rule gate is the operator blocklist for restricted infrastructure. Both have been fixed by prior audits (AUDIT-011 demo-scan SSRF, AUDIT-012 rebinding work). Right now a refactor that drops either call from any of the three routes, or that moves the call after the scan is already dispatched, ships with a fully green CI run. The failure is silent until someone scans a metadata endpoint through the product.
findings.recommendation: In each of the three suites, replace the inline `vi.fn(async () => ({ safe: true }))` factories with module-scope handles (`const mockValidateScanTarget = vi.fn(); vi.mock("@/lib/scanner/safe-fetch", () => ({ validateScanTarget: (...a) => mockValidateScanTarget(...a) }))`) defaulted to safe in beforeEach, then add two tests per route: one driving `{ safe: false, reason: "..." }` and asserting 400 plus that the scan was never dispatched (`expect(mockExecuteScan).not.toHaveBeenCalled()`), and one driving `{ allowed: false }` and asserting 403 with statusCode BLOCKED. Also assert `expect(mockValidateScanTarget).toHaveBeenCalledWith(normalizedUrl)` on the happy path so the call itself cannot be deleted.

findings.title: The /docs/cli page metadata advertises `npx vulnradar` but the npm name `vulnradar` is unclaimed, so anyone can publish it and execute code in a CI job that holds VULNRADAR_TOKEN
findings.category: dependency confusion on an unclaimed package name
findings.description: `cli/package.json:2` declares `"name": "vulnradar"` and `cli/package.json:7` declares a `bin` entry, so the package is npm-publishable under that name. It is not published: `npm view vulnradar version` returns HTTP 404 (`'vulnradar@*' is not in this registry`), verified 2026-08-29. The name is therefore unclaimed and anyone can register it. Meanwhile the docs page's own SEO metadata asserts the command works: `app/docs/cli/layout.tsx:11` sets DESCRIPTION to "Run a VulnRadar scan from your terminal or CI with npx vulnradar, and fail the build when critical or high findings cross a threshold you set.", and `app/docs/cli/layout.tsx:17` targets the keyword "npx vulnradar". That DESCRIPTION is fed to `pageMetadata()` at line 13, so it becomes the page's meta description and OG description, which is the snippet a search engine renders. The page body is honest (the `DocsCallout variant="info" title="Coming to npm"` at `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:100` says "Once the package is published"), and `lib/ai/docs-knowledge.md:135` carries the same caveat into the AI assistant, but a reader who acts on the search snippet or the keyword never sees the callout. The documented CI usage sets VULNRADAR_TOKEN in the environment (`cli/README.md:50`, `cli/lib.mjs:9`), so a squatter's postinstall or bin script runs with a live API key in `process.env`.
findings.impact: A third party can publish `vulnradar` to npm at any time. From that moment every user who follows the search result or the CI example and runs `npx vulnradar scan ...` executes attacker code on their build machine with VULNRADAR_TOKEN exported, which is a scan-API credential tied to their account and plan. For a company that sells vulnerability scanning, shipping a documented install command for a namespace it does not own is also a credibility problem the first time someone squats it.
findings.recommendation: Publish a placeholder `vulnradar` package to npm now (a 1-line bin that prints "install from the repo, see https://vulnradar.dev/docs/cli") so the name is owned, and enable 2FA-required publishing on the org. Until it is owned, change `app/docs/cli/layout.tsx:11` so DESCRIPTION does not name `npx vulnradar` as a working command (say "from your terminal or CI" and drop the command), and remove "npx vulnradar" from the `keywords` array at line 17.

findings.title: The browser extension's 194-package dependency tree has no security monitoring at all: Dependabot only watches `/`, and the extension CI job never runs npm audit
findings.category: no dependency monitoring on a shipped artifact
findings.description: `.github/dependabot.yml` declares exactly two update configs, both scoped to the repo root: `package-ecosystem: "npm"` with `directory: "/"` (line 5) and `package-ecosystem: "github-actions"` with `directory: "/"` (line 84). Dependabot directories are not recursive, so `extension/package.json` and `extension/package-lock.json` (194 lockfile entries, of which 191 are dev) are never scanned and never produce a PR. The CI side has the same hole: the only audit step in the repo is `.github/workflows/ci.yml:71`, `npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev`, which runs in the `typecheck` job with the default working directory (repo root) and with `--omit=dev`. The separate `extension` job at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:115` runs `npm ci`, `npm run typecheck`, `npm run format:check`, and `npm run build:chrome && npm run build:firefox` (lines 136 to 150) and has no audit step. The SBOM is generated by `anchore/sbom-action` against the built Docker image (`.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:82`), which contains the Next.js app and not the extension, so the extension zips attached to the release at `.github/workflows/release.yml:147` ship with no SBOM either. `--omit=dev` matters here specifically: the extension has only 2 runtime dependencies and 191 dev packages, and those dev packages (vite, rollup, esbuild, sharp, archiver) are the entire toolchain that produces `content.js`, the IIFE injected into every page the user visits via `content_scripts.matches: ["<all_urls>"]` (`extension/manifest/chrome.json:47`). A compromised build dependency writes straight into a browser-privileged artifact distributed through the Chrome Web Store and AMO. `npm audit --json` in `extension/` reports 0 vulnerabilities today, so nothing is currently exploitable; the finding is that nothing in the repo would tell anyone when that changes.
findings.impact: A published CVE in any of the extension's 194 packages, including the build chain that emits the all-URLs content script, produces no Dependabot PR and no CI failure. The maintainer finds out only by manually running npm audit inside extension/, which nothing prompts them to do. For an extension already installed in users' browsers, the window between disclosure and a store update is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Add a third Dependabot config block with `package-ecosystem: "npm"` and `directory: "/extension"` (same schedule and labels as the root block), and add an `- name: Audit extension dependencies` / `run: npm audit --audit-level=high` step with `working-directory: extension` to the `extension` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` after the `npm ci` step at line 138. Do not pass `--omit=dev` there: for the extension the dev tree is the shipped tree.

findings.title: The versioned v3.0.0 upgrade path is missing 11 tables and 8 columns that instrumentation.ts creates, so db:migrate stamps schema_version=3.0.0 on a schema that is not 3.0.0
findings.category: migration path diverges from the boot-time schema
findings.description: instrumentation.ts contains 64 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statements (63 app tables plus vulnradar_schema_meta). The complete set a database can reach through the migration engine is the 19-table v1 baseline plus the 33 tables created across scripts/migrate/versions/1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs, 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs and _snippets.mjs, so 52 app tables plus the meta table. Diffing the two sets, these 11 tables exist only on the boot path and are created by no migration step at all: browserbase_credit_purchases (instrumentation.ts:3094), browserbase_usage (3075), domains (3173), email_logs (671), github_credit_purchases (3024), scan_screenshots (1377), support_ticket_messages (3446), support_ticket_shares (3460), support_tickets (3430), user_avatars (1411), worker_failure_state (3136). Eight columns are in the same position: sessions.impersonated_by (347), sessions.ipv4_address (352), finding_remediation.due_at (1515), host_reputation.auto_tags (1840), users.billing_interval (2683), users.github_credit_balance (2827), users.browserbase_credit_seconds_balance (3061), ai_credit_purchases.refunded_at (3117). None of these names appear in _registry.mjs's v3.0.0 fingerprint (scripts/migrate/_registry.mjs:213) either. This is the exact defect AUDIT-009#migration-01 recorded as critical and whose fix comment in this same file (line 52) says it was closed "for good"; it has re-opened at 11 tables, larger than the original 4.
findings.impact: npm run db:migrate is the documented upgrade command (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:495, app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:547) and the last step the in-app self-updater runs (components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:65). After it completes it writes schema_version=3.0.0 via writeMeta (scripts/migrate/migrate.mjs:550) and reports success, while the database is missing the tables behind support tickets, custom domains, avatars, screenshots, email delivery logs, the worker failure watchdog and all three credit-purchase ledgers. The only thing that closes the gap is the app's next boot, which the self-updater deliberately does not trigger ("It does not build or restart the server"), and each of those boot-time creates is individually .catch-guarded as non-fatal, so a failure there is a single console.error and the app serves traffic with tables missing. An operator who trusts schema_version, or who uses db:migrate to prepare a database the app has not yet booted against, has an incomplete schema with no signal that anything is wrong.
findings.recommendation: Add the 11 missing tables to 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs's addTables (copying the DDL verbatim from instrumentation.ts, in FK-safe order: support_tickets before its messages/shares, domains after teams) and the 8 missing columns to addColumns, with matching entries in the downgrade's dropTables/dropColumns. Add every one of those table and column names to _registry.mjs's v3.0.0 fingerprint. Then fix the structural cause via migrate-09 and migrate-10 so this cannot silently re-open a third time.

findings.title: db:create's data copy omits 33 of the 63 app tables, including system_settings, access_rules, webhooks and support_tickets, and never reports them as skipped
findings.category: silent data loss in the clone/migrate path
findings.description: MIGRATE_TABLES is a hardcoded 30-entry list. migrateData (line 471) builds its work set as MIGRATE_TABLES.filter(t => targetSet.has(t)) and showDataMigrationPlan (line 509) iterates `for (const table of MIGRATE_TABLES)`. Both loops are driven entirely by that list, so a table that exists in the source database and in the target schema but is absent from MIGRATE_TABLES is never copied and never appears in either the plan or the post-run report. The cannotCopy branch (line 489) only warns about entries that ARE in MIGRATE_TABLES but missing from the target, which is the opposite case. Diffing MIGRATE_TABLES against instrumentation.ts's CREATE TABLE set, these 33 app tables are never copied: access_rules, admin_user_notes, ai_credit_purchases, ai_usage, api_usage, billing_verification_codes, broadcast_messages, broadcast_recipients, browserbase_credit_purchases, browserbase_usage, data_requests, device_trust, discord_connections, domains, email_2fa_codes, email_logs, email_verification_tokens, github_credit_purchases, host_badges, notification_preferences, promoted_auto_tag_rules, rate_limits, scan_screenshots, security_alerts, staff_activity, subdomain_cache, support_ticket_messages, support_ticket_shares, support_tickets, system_settings, user_avatars, webhooks, worker_failure_state.
findings.impact: npm run db:create is documented as the way to move to a different database, including production (app/docs/setup/page.tsx:735, app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx:274, app/docs/developers/page.tsx:575). An operator who clones and cuts over silently loses every admin-configured runtime setting (system_settings), the IP whitelist/blacklist (access_rules), every user's outbound webhook configuration (webhooks), every notification preference, every Discord link, every trusted device, every open support ticket and its messages and shares, every custom domain, every uploaded avatar (user_avatars), every embedded badge token (host_badges, so live third-party embeds start 404ing), every purchased AI/GitHub/Browserbase credit ledger row, and every open GDPR data request. The plan screen shown before the operator approves lists none of these as at risk, so the loss is invisible both before and after.
findings.recommendation: In create-fresh-db.mjs, stop driving the copy from a hardcoded list. Enumerate the source database's public tables, topologically order them by their declared foreign keys, and copy every table that exists in the target. Keep an explicit SKIP_TABLES list only for genuinely transient data (rate_limits, email_2fa_codes, password_reset_tokens, email_verification_tokens, subdomain_cache, cve_kev_cache) and print that skip list in showDataMigrationPlan. At minimum, add an assertion that every source table with rows is either in MIGRATE_TABLES or in SKIP_TABLES, and fail the run rather than silently dropping it.

findings.title: repairAllSequences setvals every sequence down to MAX(id) with no forward-only guard, unlike the copy in instrumentation.ts, and runs post-COMMIT against a live database
findings.category: duplicated logic that has provably drifted
findings.description: There are two implementations of the same operation. instrumentation.ts:3577-3593 reads pg_sequence_last_value into seqVal, reads MAX(col) into maxVal, and only calls setval when `maxVal > 0 && maxVal > seqVal`, so it can only move a sequence forward. scripts/migrate/_runner.mjs's repairAllSequences runs a DO block that reads only `COALESCE(MAX(%I), 0)` and then, guarded by `IF max_val > 0`, unconditionally runs `setval(seq, max_val)` with no comparison against the sequence's current value. It therefore moves a sequence BACKWARDS whenever rows above MAX(id) have been deleted. This function runs in three places against real databases: _runner.mjs:137 immediately after COMMIT on every real migration, migrate.mjs:537 on every same-version no-op re-run, and db-repair-sequences.mjs:37. The self-updater's last step is `npm run db:migrate` executed from inside the running app with no restart (app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply/route.ts:28, components/admin/features/updater-manager.tsx:65), so this setval runs outside any transaction while the app is still inserting rows. Read MAX(id)=N, concurrent app INSERT consumes nextval N+1 and commits, setval(N) executes, the next app INSERT gets nextval N+1 again and fails with duplicate key value violates unique constraint. Separately, the backwards move means ids of deleted rows get handed out again: scan_history rows are pruned by lib/database/cleanup.ts:154-200 and by user deletion cascade, and AUDIT-012#authz-09 records that scan screenshots are readable with no authentication by that sequential id.
findings.impact: Every release applied through the admin self-updater runs this against production while the app is serving. The narrow window produces a duplicate-key 500 on a live scan insert; the sequence rewind causes primary-key reuse on scan_history, admin_audit_log, security_alerts, user_notifications and every other SERIAL table after any deletion, so a stale sequential-id reference (a screenshot URL, a stored API integration id) can resolve to a different row belonging to a different user. The function's own header says its purpose is to fix a sequence that "fell behind", which is the forward case only, so the backwards behavior is not intended.
findings.recommendation: In scripts/migrate/_runner.mjs's repairAllSequences, select `pg_sequence_last_value(s.oid)` alongside the sequence in the cursor and change the body to `IF max_val > 0 AND max_val > COALESCE(last_val, 0) THEN ... END IF`, matching instrumentation.ts:3589. Better, delete the duplicate entirely and export the guarded implementation from one shared module that both instrumentation.ts and the migrate scripts import. Also stop calling it inside runPlan when the app may be live, or take a `pg_advisory_lock` around it.

findings.title: db:restore pipes the dump into psql without ON_ERROR_STOP, so a restore in which every statement failed still prints "Restore complete." and exits 0
findings.description: runRestore spawns `psql [connArg]` with no `-v ON_ERROR_STOP=1`, no `--single-transaction`, and no `-q`. psql defaults ON_ERROR_STOP to off, so it prints each statement's error to stderr, continues with the next statement, and exits 0 as long as it consumed its input. The only failure check is `if (exitCode !== 0) throw` at line 108, which therefore never fires for SQL errors. backup-db.mjs produces the dump with `pg_dump --no-owner --no-privileges --format=plain` (line 219), which contains no DROP statements and no CREATE DATABASE, so restoring into the DATABASE_URL the app has already booted against means every CREATE TABLE fails with "relation already exists" and every COPY into a table with existing rows fails on the primary key. All of those are non-fatal to psql. The script then reaches line 112 and prints "Restore complete." This is a different script and a different mechanism from AUDIT-012#obs-02 (which covers the scheduled backup job reporting success on failure); the backup artifact itself is correct here, plain-format pg_dump does capture schema, data and sequence setvals.
findings.impact: The one command the project offers for disaster recovery cannot distinguish a complete restore from a total failure. The header comment tells operators to rehearse a restore against staging "before trusting it in a real incident", but the rehearsal will report success regardless of whether anything was actually restored, so the rehearsal proves nothing. In a real incident an operator will believe the database is recovered when it may contain none of the backed-up rows.
findings.recommendation: In scripts/restore-db.mjs, spawn psql with `["-v", "ON_ERROR_STOP=1", "--single-transaction", connArg]` so the first error aborts with a non-zero exit and the whole restore rolls back rather than half-applying. Add a `--into-empty` preflight that counts public tables in the target and refuses to run when the target is non-empty unless an explicit `--force` is passed, and after a successful restore print the row counts of a few core tables so the operator has positive evidence.

findings.title: The bounded body reader is copy-pasted five times and only one copy has the read timeout its own doc comment says is required, so the crawl, bulk and unauthenticated demo-scan paths hang forever on a slow-trickle target
findings.description:
The same streaming body reader (getReader loop, byte counter, trim-on-overshoot, decoder, reader.cancel in finally) exists verbatim in five places: lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:159 (safeReadBody), lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:80 (safeReadBody), app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:43 (safeReadBody), app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:29 (safeReadBody), and lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:118 under a different name (readBoundedText). I diffed all five: four are byte-identical after whitespace normalization; the fifth, execute-scan.ts's, is the only one that differs, and the difference is the guard.

execute-scan.ts:150-158 carries the reasoning explicitly: "safeFetch clears its internal abort controller as soon as headers arrive, leaving body reads unprotected. A server that sends headers immediately but streams the body forever (or never closes it) would otherwise hang the route handler indefinitely. The timeout calls reader.cancel(), which causes the pending reader.read() to reject with an AbortError caught below." It implements that as a third parameter `timeoutMs = 10_000` and a `setTimeout(() => reader.cancel(), timeoutMs)` around the loop (execute-scan.ts:162, :171-173, :196).

None of the other four has a timer. Each takes only `(response, maxBytes)`. And each is fed a response from the same safeFetch that the comment describes: app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:166 passes `signal: AbortSignal.timeout(fetchTimeoutMs)` then reads at :179; app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:172 does the same then reads at :176 and :215; lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts reads at :166; lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts reads at :307, :382 and :536. Because safeFetch detaches that signal once headers land (the mechanism filed as AUDIT-012#ssrf-01), the caller's timeout does not reach the body read on any of these four paths.

The byte cap does not help: a target that returns 200 with headers and then emits one byte every 30 seconds never reaches maxBytes and never finishes, so the `await reader.read()` never settles. The outer races that exist do not cancel the reader either: AUDIT-012#abuse-06 records that the scan watchdog frees the concurrency slot without aborting the work, and AUDIT-012#abuse-11 records that the demo scan abandons runAsyncChecks after its 15 s race while the work keeps running. demo-scan is the anonymous endpoint, so this is reachable without an account.

This is not the same finding as AUDIT-012#ssrf-01 (safeFetch detaching the signal). It is the reason the workaround the team already wrote for that problem covers only one of the five paths that need it.
findings.impact: One scan of an attacker-controlled host that trickles its response body pins a Node async task and, on the crawl and bulk paths, a pooled database connection and a concurrency slot, for as long as the attacker keeps the socket open. The single-scan path survives this because of its 10 s reader timer; the crawl, bulk and anonymous demo paths do not. On a small VPS serving ~50 real users, a handful of these leaks the connection pool (max 10 per AUDIT-012#perf-20) and the app stops answering. The next person who fixes AUDIT-012#ssrf-01 by hardening safeFetch will still leave four uncapped readers behind, because nothing links them.
findings.recommendation: Extract the reader into one module, for example lib/scanner/read-bounded-body.ts, exporting `safeReadBody(response, maxBytes, timeoutMs = 10_000)` with execute-scan.ts:159's timer body verbatim. Delete the four copies and import it in app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:29, app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:43, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:80 and lib/scanner/crawl-discovery.ts:118 (drop the readBoundedText alias so grep finds every call site under one name). Add one test that feeds a never-ending ReadableStream to the shared reader and asserts it resolves within the timeout.

findings.title: The coverage gate is dead: CI runs `npm run test` without coverage, and the only command that enforces thresholds currently exits non-zero with eight failures
findings.description: The CI test job runs `npm run test` (ci.yml:107), which is `vitest run` with no --coverage, and the comment two lines above it says so outright: 'Coverage is informational only for now; thresholds are enforced locally via npm run test:coverage'. So nothing in CI checks coverage. Meanwhile the local command that is supposed to be the gate is red. I ran `vitest run --coverage` on the current tree: all 356 files and 10,158 tests pass, but the threshold check reports eight errors and exits non-zero. lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts is at 88.23% lines against a 90% threshold and 85.71% statements against 90%; lib/config/client-constants.ts is at 48.48% against 90% on both; lib/updater/copy-with-excludes.ts misses its 100% functions and statements thresholds; lib/updater/job-store.ts misses its 100% functions threshold; app/api/v3/assets/route.ts is at 68% branches against 70%. tests/README.md documents a workflow ('run npm run test:coverage, read the per-file percentage, set the threshold a few points below it') that no one can follow while the command fails for unrelated files.
findings.impact: The project has a written coverage policy, a per-file threshold map, and a documented workflow, and none of it is enforced anywhere. Coverage on a security-critical file can fall to zero between releases and nothing reports it. Worse, because the gate command is already red, a developer who runs it learns to ignore its output, so it will not catch a real regression even when someone does run it. This is also why the 0% files in cov-01, cov-02, and cov-06 could land: nothing was watching. Concretely: deleting every test for lib/updater/checksum.ts, the stated security control for the self-update flow, drops it from its declared 100 percent threshold to 0 percent and CI stays green. tests/README.md:41 tells contributors a coverage regression fails the build, which is not true of any job that actually runs, and the stale coverage/ directory (2026-08-13) means nobody sees the real number either.
findings.recommendation: Fix the eight stale thresholds in vitest.config.ts to the measured values (rate-limit.ts to 85/85, client-constants.ts to 45, copy-with-excludes.ts functions to 90, job-store.ts functions to 90, assets/route.ts branches to 65), then change ci.yml:107 to `npm run test:coverage` so the gate runs on every PR. Once green, add a modest global threshold under coverage.thresholds (lines 75, branches 65 against the measured 81.02% / 71.24%) so a new untested file drags the global number down instead of being silently exempt.

findings.title: Coverage measures only .ts, so 419 React files and 95,294 lines are invisible, and with environment:node and no jsdom the suite cannot render a component even if someone wrote a test
findings.category: whole layer outside the test harness
findings.description: coverage.include is ["lib/**/*.ts", "app/**/*.ts"] (vitest.config.ts:31). The glob `*.ts` does not match `.tsx`. The coverage run confirms it: exactly 412 files are measured, which is 250 lib/*.ts plus 162 app/*.ts, and not one .tsx. Unmeasured: 266 components/*.tsx plus 47 components/*.ts (313 files, 65,147 lines), 152 app/*.tsx (30,147 lines), and 1 lib/*.tsx. Separately, test.environment is "node" (line 23) and package.json lists no jsdom, no happy-dom, and no @testing-library/* in either dependencies or devDependencies, so no test can mount a React tree at all. The eight files under tests/components/ cover 8 of 313 component files (2.6%), and six of those eight targets are plain .ts utility modules (queue-status-utils.ts, settings-registry-utils.ts, use-unsaved-changes-warning.ts, admin/utils.ts, schedule-time-utils.ts, ai-review-gate.ts); only danger-score-trend.tsx and auth-provider.tsx are .tsx, and those tests can reach only their non-rendering exports.
findings.impact: Every form-validation rule, every conditional that hides a paid feature behind a plan check, every auth-state branch in a client component, and every result renderer is untested and unmeasured. A regression that shows a Pro-only control to a free user, or that renders a scan as clean when findings exist, reaches production with a green CI. The measurement gap makes it worse than it looks: the 81.02% headline reads as broad health while a third of the app's lines are simply not in the denominator.
findings.recommendation: Two steps, and the first is cheap. Change coverage.include to ["lib/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "app/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "components/**/*.{ts,tsx}", "middleware.ts"] so the real denominator is visible even before any test is written; expect the headline to drop, which is the accurate number. Then add jsdom plus @testing-library/react as devDependencies and an environmentMatchGlobs entry mapping tests/components/** to jsdom, and start with the highest-risk components: components/scanner/scan-form.tsx, the plan-gated controls, and the shared ScanResultDetail renderer.

findings.title: middleware.ts, the 546-line request gate for every route in the app, sits outside coverage.include so its 365-line test suite produces no measurable coverage
findings.description: middleware.ts is 546 lines and lives at the repo root, so it matches neither "lib/**/*.ts" nor "app/**/*.ts" in coverage.include (vitest.config.ts:31). It does not appear in the coverage-summary.json I generated: filtering the 412 measured files for 'middleware' returns nothing. tests/middleware.test.ts exists and is 365 lines, so the file is not untested, but there is no way to tell which of its branches the suite reaches. This matters because middleware is where the public-path allowlist and the auth redirect live, and AUDIT-012 filed three separate HIGH findings against that allowlist (authz-01, authz-02, authz-03: the public host report API, all three staff-oidc endpoints, and the public contact form all missing from PUBLIC_PATHS, each breaking the feature for logged-out visitors). lib/config/public-paths.ts reports 100% statements but only 1 statement, because it is a data table: line coverage says nothing about whether the table is correct. instrumentation.ts is excluded outright (vitest.config.ts:38) and is 3,639 lines holding 72 CREATE TABLE and 97 CREATE INDEX statements.
findings.impact: The single file that decides whether a request is authenticated, redirected, or allowed through unauthenticated has an unknown tested fraction. A branch added to it, for example a new public path or a new bypass condition, is invisible to both the coverage report and to a reviewer asking 'is this covered?'. The AUDIT-012 authz findings show the concrete cost: three features silently broken for every logged-out visitor and crawler, shipped past a green suite.
findings.recommendation: Add "middleware.ts" to coverage.include in vitest.config.ts so the file is measured, then read the resulting branch percentage and fill the gaps in tests/middleware.test.ts. Separately, add a table-driven test that walks every entry in PUBLIC_PATHS and asserts each named route file actually exists, and walks every route.ts the app serves unauthenticated and asserts it is listed, which is the drift the three AUDIT-012 authz findings all were.

findings.title: The two Stripe events that reverse money, charge.refunded and charge.dispute.created, are the only two of nine handled event types with no test
findings.description: app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts measures 68.18% statements and 58.3% branches over 264 statements. The handler switch has nine cases: checkout.session.completed (183), customer.subscription.created (296), updated (475), deleted (626), invoice.payment_succeeded (686), invoice.payment_failed (770), payment_intent.succeeded (803), charge.refunded (940), charge.dispute.created (982). Extracting the event-type string literals from tests/app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.test.ts yields eight, and the two missing are charge.refunded and charge.dispute.created. Those two branches each call reverseAiCreditPurchase, reverseGithubCreditPurchase, and reverseBrowserbaseCreditPurchase in a Promise.all (lines 958-962 and 997-1001). The reversal functions themselves are well covered (lib/billing/ai-usage.ts 98.27%, browserbase-usage.ts 100%, github-review-usage.ts 98.59%), so what is untested is the wiring: the partial-refund early-break at line 947, the payment_intent extraction that must handle both a string and an expanded object (lines 953-956 and 989-992), and the dispatch itself. lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.ts:29-30 does register both events with Stripe, and tests/lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.test.ts covers REQUIRED_EVENTS, but nothing asserts the REQUIRED_EVENTS list and the switch labels agree.
findings.impact: If either case label is renamed, or the payment_intent extraction breaks when Stripe sends an expanded object rather than a string, a refunded or charged-back customer keeps every AI token, GitHub review token, and Browserbase second they paid for. That is direct revenue loss on the exact transactions where the money has already left, and it is silent: the webhook still returns 200, the reversal functions still pass their own unit tests, and the only evidence is a console.log that never fires.
findings.recommendation: Add two describes to tests/app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.test.ts. For charge.refunded assert: refunded:false logs and reverses nothing; refunded:true with a string payment_intent calls all three reverse functions with that id; refunded:true with an expanded payment_intent object extracts .id. For charge.dispute.created assert the same extraction and the three reverse calls. Add one drift test asserting the set of `case` labels in the route equals REQUIRED_EVENTS in lib/billing/stripe-webhook-setup.ts, so registering an event without handling it (or vice versa) fails.

findings.title: The Browserbase client is at 16.87% and page-screenshot at 7.44%, leaving the session-teardown call that stops a paid third-party meter untested at all three of its call sites
findings.description: lib/browserbase/client.ts is the largest sub-50% file in the tree: 243 statements at 16.87% statements / 27.05%-adjacent branches, 662 lines, ten exports (createBrowserSession:112, getBrowserSession:165, getBrowserLiveUrls:189, endBrowserSession:213, pickLiveViewerUrl:273, isBrowserBaseConfigured:279, navigateBrowserSession:298, openCdpPageSession:416, getBrowserSessionLogs:573, parseNetworkRequests:594). tests/lib/browserbase/ contains one file, concurrency-queue.test.ts, which tests a different module. lib/browserbase/network-capture.ts is at 27.05% and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts at 7.44% (94 statements, 21.42% functions). endBrowserSession has three call sites that must run or the session keeps billing: app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.ts:199 (the create-failed cleanup) and :325 (explicit delete), lib/scanner/auth/browser-login.ts:560, and lib/scanner/page-screenshot.ts:267. None of those teardown paths is exercised.
findings.impact: Browserbase is a real paid third party billed by session-seconds, and the credit ledger charges the user for it. A regression where the teardown is skipped on an error path (the exact shape of the route.ts:199 cleanup) leaks a live session per failed scan. Nothing in the product notices: the scan reports a normal failure, the user is charged whatever the ledger recorded, and the overage shows up on the operator's Browserbase invoice at the end of the month. sessions/route.ts:199 already writes `.catch(() => {})`, so even a thrown teardown error is swallowed.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/browserbase/client.test.ts mocking the Browserbase HTTP boundary and assert createBrowserSession sends keepAlive:true, endBrowserSession issues the delete for the right id, and openCdpPageSession honours its timeout argument. Then add teardown assertions at the three call sites: in tests/app/api/v3/browser/sessions/route.test.ts assert endBrowserSession is called when the post-create work throws, and add a page-screenshot test asserting endBrowserSession runs in the failure path as well as the success path.

findings.title: lib/api/api-keys.ts is at 48.4% and its validateApiKey tests cover IP binding, ToS gating, and scope migration but never the account-state gate, which is the exact branch AUDIT-012 found missing
findings.category: auth gate tested around its weak point
findings.description: lib/api/api-keys.ts measures 48.4% statements over 188 statements. It exports nine functions: generateApiKey (64), passesApiKeyIpBinding (213), validateApiKey (326), checkRateLimit (477), peekRateLimit (570), recordUsage (605), getUserApiKeys (615), revokeApiKey (629), rotateApiKey (639). tests/lib/api/api-keys.test.ts has four describes and seventeen tests: one for passesApiKeyIpBinding and three narrow integration slices of validateApiKey, named for IP binding, terms-of-service gating, and the scopes-column migration. generateApiKey, checkRateLimit, peekRateLimit, getUserApiKeys, and recordUsage have no direct test. This is the file AUDIT-012#auth-02 filed a HIGH against at this exact line: 'Suspending an account does not stop its API keys: validateApiKey never checks users.disabled_at'. The existing tests prove the point about where coverage is aimed: three separate describes cover peripheral conditions of the same function while the account-state condition was never asserted at all.
findings.impact: API keys are the unattended auth path, so a gate failure here is the one least likely to be noticed by a human. The concrete instance already happened: a banned user kept full API access, including scan quota consumption, until an audit found it. checkRateLimit at line 477 is the per-key daily quota, and it having no direct test means the same class of gap sits on the metering side too.
findings.recommendation: Extend tests/lib/api/api-keys.test.ts with a describe per account-state condition on validateApiKey: a key whose owning user has disabled_at set must be rejected, a key past expires_at must be rejected, a revoked key must be rejected, and a key whose user row is missing must be rejected. Add a describe for checkRateLimit asserting it increments once, blocks at the cap, and rolls over on a new day. Make the disabled_at case the first test so the regression AUDIT-012 found cannot come back.

findings.title: The browser extension is 7,048 lines across 25 TypeScript files with zero tests, no test script, and a CI job that only typechecks, formats, and builds it
findings.category: shipped product with no test suite
findings.description: extension/src/ holds 25 .ts files totalling 7,048 lines. `git ls-files 'extension/**'` matches zero files named *.test.* or *.spec.*, and extension/package.json declares no "test" script: its scripts are dev, build, build:chrome, build:firefox, icons, package, package:source, clean, typecheck, format, format:check. The CI extension job (.github/workflows/ci.yml) runs npm ci, typecheck, format:check, and build for Chrome and Firefox, and nothing else. The untested surface includes the pieces that make security decisions: lib/auth.ts (74 lines, API-key handling), lib/api.ts (259 lines, the calls to the VulnRadar API), lib/storage.ts (249), lib/scan-target.ts (62), lib/url-patterns.ts (108), plus popup/popup.ts at 1,116 lines and background/service-worker.ts. lib/scanner/scan-target-classify.ts in the main app carries an explicit comment that 'the browser extension keeps its own small copy of classifyScanTarget (it's a separate build)', so there is a deliberate duplicate of classification logic on both sides with a test on neither (the app-side copy measures 37.14% statements / 16% branches).
findings.impact: The extension is a published Chrome and Firefox Web Store product with a review and rollback cycle measured in days, so a regression is far more expensive to correct than a web deploy. A typecheck-and-build gate cannot catch a wrong URL pattern that scans the wrong host, a storage change that drops a stored API key, or a classification drift where the extension and the app disagree about what a given URL is. Because the extension holds a user's API key, an api.ts regression that sends it to the wrong origin would also ship green.
findings.recommendation: Add vitest (or node:test, matching the CLI's pattern) to extension/package.json with a "test" script, and add an extension test step to the CI extension job so it gates merges the same way the app's does. Start with the pure modules where a test is cheap and the failure is expensive: url-patterns.ts, scan-target.ts, format.ts, categories.ts, plans.ts. Then add a shared fixture list of URLs asserted identically against lib/scanner/scan-target-classify.ts in the app and the extension's own copy, so the two builds cannot drift apart unnoticed.

findings.title: lib/scanner/protocol-findings.ts is at 0% while the banner parser it consumes is at 85%, so the entire ssh/smtp/imap/pop3/mongodb scan branch can report clean with no test failing
findings.description: lib/scanner/protocol-findings.ts measures 0% statements / 0% branches / 0% functions (25 statements, 265 lines) and there is no tests/lib/scanner/protocol-findings.test.ts. Its header states it holds the 'Vulnerability builders for the non-HTTP protocol scan branch in execute-scan.ts (a URL whose scheme is ssh://, smtp://, imap://, pop3://, or mongodb://)' and that 'Finding IDs are derived deterministically from a checkId prefix + URL (see generateId), so the prefixes here MUST stay stable: changing one changes the ID of an existing finding type and breaks diffing between a user's older and newer scans of the same target'. The parsing layer beneath it is covered: lib/scanner/protocols/banner.ts is at 85.52%, with dedicated suites at tests/lib/scanner/protocols/banner-analysis, banner-tls-and-capability, and mongo-probe. So the suite proves the banner is parsed correctly and proves nothing about whether a finding is produced from it. For contrast, the three other low-coverage files under lib/scanner/checks/ (email.ts 3.03%, active-probes.ts 16.66%, reputation.ts 25%) are deliberate placeholders whose detectors return null, and are correctly not a gap.
findings.impact: Two silent failures. A regression that drops a finding builder makes a protocol scan of a genuinely vulnerable host report clean, and the user has no signal that anything is wrong because the scan completes normally. A regression that changes an idPrefix silently breaks the scan-to-scan diff the file's own comment warns about, so the history view shows a resolved finding plus a new finding instead of one persistent one, in a product whose value proposition is tracking a host over time.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/lib/scanner/protocol-findings.test.ts feeding a fixture BannerResult and MongoAuthProbeResult for each protocol and asserting: the expected finding is produced for a vulnerable banner and none for a clean one, and the finding id for a fixed (checkId, url) pair matches a hard-coded expected string. Pinning the ids in the assertion is what makes the prefix stability the header demands actually enforceable.

findings.title: No test in the repo executes real SQL: 192 of 356 test files mock the pg pool and there is no test database, so column typos, broken CTEs, missing row locks, and schema drift are all invisible
findings.description: Scope: the whole suite plus vitest.config.ts and the schema. 192 of the 356 test files contain `vi.mock("@/lib/database/db")`, and 195 reference a fake pool shape. Nothing in the repo starts a Postgres: no docker-compose service for tests, no testcontainers dependency, and the only tests that read DATABASE_URL do so to assert configuration behaviour, not to connect. Even tests/lib/database/db.test.ts, which cannot mock the module it tests, mocks one level lower at pg's Pool class with a FakePool. The result is that every SQL string in lib/ and app/ is treated as an opaque token: a mocked client returns whatever the test scripted regardless of what the query says, so a wrong column name, a dropped WHERE clause, a `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` that lost its lock, or a CTE that no longer returns its RETURNING row all pass. instrumentation.ts, the canonical schema at 3,639 lines with 72 CREATE TABLE and 97 CREATE INDEX statements, is explicitly excluded from coverage (vitest.config.ts:38) and only two test files reference it at all. There is also a documented contradiction: CLAUDE.md lists 'Mocking the database in tests' under What to avoid, while tests/README.md instructs 'Mock at the network and database boundary, not below it', and the suite follows the README.
findings.impact: This is the structural reason a whole class of AUDIT-012 findings existed. Credit-ledger atomicity, the nine missing indexes in AUDIT-012#perf-15 that force full scans inside the cleanup transaction, and the function-wrapped columns in AUDIT-012#perf-16 that defeat an index are all properties of SQL text that the suite by construction cannot evaluate. The failure mode in production is a query that throws at runtime on a column that no longer exists, or an aggregate that returns silently wrong numbers, after a green CI run and a green deploy.
findings.recommendation: Do not rewrite 192 files. Add one narrow integration suite gated on an env var, tests/integration/, that spins Postgres in the CI test job as a services: container, runs instrumentation.ts to build the schema, and exercises only the queries where correctness cannot be asserted any other way: the credit ledger reversals, reserveConcurrentScanSlot, incrementDailyCountCapped, and lib/database/cleanup.ts. Then resolve the doc contradiction by amending CLAUDE.md to match what the project actually does, so the next contributor is not choosing between two rules.

findings.title: The only regression guard for the scanner's per-check error isolation never makes a check throw, and its sole assertion is .not.toThrow()
findings.category: test would pass with the feature removed
findings.description: tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:72 is titled "does not let one throwing check take down the whole scan". Its body builds a pathological body string (`"<".repeat(5000) + "html".repeat(1000)`) and asserts exactly one thing: `expect(() => runSyncChecks(...)).not.toThrow()`. No detector in the run is made to throw: a grep for `throw new Error` in that file returns nothing, and no detector is stubbed or injected. The feature it is supposed to guard is the pair of per-check try/catch blocks in lib/scanner/engine.ts at lines 169 to 172 and 186 to 198 (the file's own comment at line 131 calls them "the per-check try/catch below"). The exact mutation the test does not catch: delete both try/catch wrappers in lib/scanner/engine.ts, and the test still passes, because none of the 800-plus registered detectors throws on that particular input. It also does not assert that findings are still produced, so a mutation that makes runSyncChecks return `{ findings: [] }` unconditionally also passes.
findings.impact: The per-check try/catch is what stops one bad regex or one bad detector from aborting an entire scan. If it is removed or narrowed during a refactor, the suite says nothing, and the symptom in production is a scan that returns a 500 or an empty result for every user whose page happens to trip the throwing detector. The test also carries a documented flake: its own comment at lines 65 to 70 records that the default 5s timeout "has been observed to flake under a full parallel suite run", which is why it now runs with a 20s override, so a very expensive test is buying an assertion that cannot fail.
findings.recommendation: In tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts, register a deliberately throwing detector (or vi.spyOn one entry of ALL_INLINE_DETECTORS to throw) and assert two things: that runSyncChecks still returns, and that the findings from the other categories are still present. Keep the pathological-input case as a separate, honestly named smoke test.

findings.title: No test in the repo ever executes SQL: 191 suites replace the pg pool with a mock and the CI test job has no database, so every one of the 344 SQL assertions is a string comparison
findings.description: A count over all 356 test files: 705 vi.mock calls across 230 files, of which 191 mock `@/lib/database/db`, 97 mock `@/lib/auth`, 53 mock `@/lib/config/runtime-config`, and 23 mock `@/lib/scanner/safe-fetch`. Only two test files reference `pg` at all (tests/lib/auth/account-deletion.test.ts:2 and tests/lib/database/audit-log-archive.test.ts:6) and both use it as a `import type { PoolClient }` only. There is no testcontainers, pg-mem, or docker service anywhere: the CI test job at .github/workflows/ci.yml:84 declares no `services:` block, and the build job supplies a placeholder DATABASE_URL at line 160 (`postgresql://placeholder:placeholder@localhost:5432/placeholder`) that is never connected to. The suite therefore verifies SQL only as text: 344 assertions of the `expect(sql).toContain("...")` or `q.sql.startsWith("...")` shape. The mechanical consequence: a query that references a column or table that does not exist in instrumentation.ts, or that contains a syntax error, is indistinguishable from a correct one, because the mocked `pool.query` returns the canned rows for any string. The same applies to anything the database enforces rather than the application: NOT NULL, unique constraints, foreign keys, ON CONFLICT behaviour, and transaction rollback semantics. This is also a documented internal contradiction: CLAUDE.md:168 lists "Mocking the database in tests" under What to avoid, while tests/README.md:45 instructs the opposite ("Mock at the network and database boundary, not below it"), and current practice follows the README.
findings.impact: Any SQL that only runs on a branch the app rarely takes (an admin action, an error path, a cleanup job) can ship broken and surface as a production 500 with a full green CI. The 155 API routes are otherwise well tested at the string level, which makes this the single largest class of bug the 89,192-line suite structurally cannot catch. It also means the schema in instrumentation.ts and the SQL in the routes can drift indefinitely without any signal.
findings.recommendation: Add a small integration tier rather than converting the existing suite. Add a `services: postgres` block to the CI test job, a second vitest project (`vitest.integration.config.ts`) with `include: ["tests/integration/**"]` that boots the real schema from instrumentation.ts against that database, and start with the handful of seams where a wrong query is most expensive: history and history/[id] ownership scoping, teams membership, the credit and quota writes, and lib/database/cleanup.ts. Then reconcile the guidance: either update CLAUDE.md:168 to say "mock at the DB boundary, never below it" or update tests/README.md:45, so the two files stop contradicting each other.

findings.title: Twenty-seven of the seventy-one runtime dependencies have zero imports anywhere in the app, dragging 78 transitive packages and 77.6 MB into the production dependency graph
findings.description: AUDIT-012#fe-13 found two of these (jspdf, jspdf-autotable). Extending that grep to all 86 declared packages, ripgrep for any quoted specifier (static import, `require(`, dynamic `import(`, type-only import) across app/, lib/, components/, tests/, scripts/, middleware.ts and every config file, with node_modules/.next/coverage/marketing/extension/cli/audits excluded, returns package.json itself as the only hit for twenty-five entries. Three groups, each with a different history. (1) Vercel AI SDK: `ai` (package.json:82), `@ai-sdk/anthropic` (:48) and `@ai-sdk/openai` (:49). `git log -S 'from "ai"' -- lib app components` returns nothing, so they were never wired in: the app talks to providers over raw fetch through lib/ai/provider.ts and hand-rolls SSE in lib/ai/anthropic.ts:212 (`createAnthropicSseTranscoder`, consumed at app/api/v3/ai/chat/route.ts:342). The 19 apparent hits for `ai` are the string literal 'ai' used as a profile tab id (app/profile/page.tsx:79) and as a `scan_tags.source` value (lib/tags/auto-tags.ts:878). (2) `jsonwebtoken` (:91) and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (:122): the only mentions in source are a comment at lib/scanner/checks/code.ts:1736 and a UI label at lib/scanner/checks/page-checks/jwt.ts:140. The app's one real JWT verification, lib/auth/staff-oidc.ts:24, imports `jose`. (3) shadcn/v0 scaffold leftovers from the initial commit 26e639c5, none of which ever got a components/ui wrapper (there is no command.tsx, calendar.tsx, carousel.tsx, drawer.tsx, resizable.tsx, input-otp.tsx, sonner.tsx, form.tsx, accordion.tsx, collapsible.tsx, context-menu.tsx, hover-card.tsx, menubar.tsx, navigation-menu.tsx, radio-group.tsx, toggle.tsx or toggle-group.tsx in components/ui/): `@hookform/resolvers` (:50), `@neondatabase/serverless` (:51, named only as prose in app/docs/architecture/page.tsx), `@radix-ui/react-accordion` (:52), `-aspect-ratio` (:54), `-collapsible` (:57), `-context-menu` (:58), `-hover-card` (:61), `-menubar` (:63), `-navigation-menu` (:64), `-radio-group` (:67), `-toggle` (:76), `-toggle-group` (:77), `cmdk` (:86), `date-fns` (:87), `embla-carousel-react` (:88), `input-otp` (:89), `react-day-picker` (:101), `react-hook-form` (:103, no `useForm` or `FormProvider` anywhere), `react-resizable-panels` (:106), `sonner` (:110, the app uses components/ui/toaster.tsx over @radix-ui/react-toast) and `vaul` (:116). Separately `tslib` (:115) was added by commit b8bc8f83 'to resolve import error in react-remove-scroll'; react-remove-scroll@2.7.2 still declares `tslib: ^2.1.0` itself, so the direct entry buys nothing and only freezes the hoisted copy at an exact 2.8.1. Walking the lockfile closure, these twenty-five roots plus the two jspdf packages are the sole path to 78 packages totalling 77.6 MB installed, the largest being jspdf 28.8 MB, date-fns 10.4 MB, ai 6.4 MB, html2canvas 3.2 MB, @ai-sdk/openai 2.8 MB, @ai-sdk/anthropic 2.1 MB, dompurify 1.7 MB, pako 1.6 MB, undici 1.6 MB, canvg 1.3 MB and core-js 1.3 MB. core-js is also one of only three packages in the entire tree with `hasInstallScript: true`.
findings.impact: Every production install and every Docker image layer carries 78 packages that no line of code can reach, which is 78 more npm accounts whose compromise would land executable code in the runtime of a security product. core-js arrives with a postinstall script purely because jspdf wants canvg. Operationally the list also misleads: a reader of package.json reasonably concludes there is a PDF export path, a Vercel AI SDK integration and a Neon serverless driver, and will go looking for all three. The jsonwebtoken entry is the sharpest edge, because a contributor adding a signed token has a JWT library already installed and one grep away that is not the vetted one (`jose`) the auth layer standardised on, so the wrong library gets used with no review signal.
findings.recommendation: Delete those twenty-five entries, the two jspdf entries from AUDIT-012#fe-13 (package.json:92-93), and `@types/jsonwebtoken` (package.json:122) from `dependencies`/`devDependencies`, and drop `tslib` (:115) since react-remove-scroll pulls it transitively. Update the stale comment at tests/lib/reports/pdf-report.test.ts:8 that still references jspdf being in package.json. Also prune .github/dependabot.yml, whose `security` group (lines 59, 61, 64) and `scanning` group watch several of these. Regenerate package-lock.json on Linux or graft the entries by hand, per the lockfile-platform constraint this repo already documents: a Windows regeneration strips the Linux native bindings this lockfile currently has intact.

findings.title: vitest and @vitest/coverage-v8 sit in dependencies, pulling 82 packages and a 20 MB rolldown native binary into the production graph, and the Dockerfile never passes --omit=dev so the devDependencies ship as well
findings.description: This extends AUDIT-012#fe-13, which named the misplacement but attributed the cost to `npm ci --omit=dev` in the Docker build. This Dockerfile does not use that flag. Two separate mechanisms compound. First, `vitest` 4.1.11 (package.json:117) and `@vitest/coverage-v8` 4.1.11 (:81) are declared under `dependencies`, not `devDependencies`. Resolving the lockfile closure of the `dependencies` list with and without those two roots, 82 packages / 42.9 MB are reachable only through them: `@rolldown/binding-win32-x64-msvc` at 20.4 MB (on a Linux runner the equivalent `@rolldown/binding-linux-x64-gnu`), `vite` 8.2.2 with its own nested `lightningcss` 1.33.0 and full 11-platform native matrix at 9.1 MB for the local binary, plus @babel/types, @babel/parser, rolldown, magic-string, magicast, istanbul-reports, chai and the rest of the runner. That second lightningcss is a straight duplicate: @tailwindcss/node 4.3.3 already brings lightningcss 1.32.0 with its own full platform matrix, so the tree carries two copies of an 11-binary native package. Second, Dockerfile:24 runs `npm ci --silent --ignore-scripts` with no `--omit=dev`, and Dockerfile:77 then does `COPY --from=builder --chown=nextjs:nodejs /app/node_modules ./node_modules` into the runner stage. Measuring the lockfile's dev-flagged entries on disk gives 89 MB that is copied verbatim into the published ghcr image: typescript 23.2 MB, prettier 9.5 MB, lightningcss-win32-x64-msvc 9.1 MB, eslint-plugin-react-hooks 3.9 MB, axe-core 2.9 MB, eslint 2.8 MB, es-abstract 2.7 MB, @typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin 2.0 MB and so on.
findings.impact: The published ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar image ships a full test runner, a bundler with two native binaries, a TypeScript compiler, ESLint and Prettier into the runtime a self-hoster exposes to the internet. That is roughly 130 MB of pure image weight plus a much larger attack surface than the app needs, on a container that runs as a long-lived network service. It also means the fix AUDIT-012#fe-13 recommended (move the two packages to devDependencies) would not by itself shrink the image at all, because the Docker build installs dev dependencies unconditionally.
findings.recommendation: Two changes, both one line. Move `vitest` and `@vitest/coverage-v8` from `dependencies` to `devDependencies` in package.json. Then change Dockerfile:24 to a two-stage install: keep `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in the builder (the build needs typescript and the tailwind toolchain) and, in the runner stage, replace the `COPY --from=builder /app/node_modules` at Dockerfile:77 with a separate `npm ci --omit=dev --ignore-scripts` layer, or add `RUN npm prune --omit=dev` in the builder after `npm run build` and copy the pruned tree. Either removes both the 89 MB of dev tooling and the 42.9 MB vitest subtree from the shipped image.

findings.title: Node 22.11.0 and Postgres 16.4 base images are roughly a year of security releases stale, and dependabot.yml has no docker ecosystem to ever bump them
findings.category: stale base image, no update automation
findings.description: Dockerfile:11 and Dockerfile:62 both pin `node:22.11.0-alpine`. Node 22.11.0 is the release that promoted the 22 line to LTS; the 22 line is currently at 22.23.0 (the Node running in this very workspace reports v22.23.0), so the published image is twelve patch releases behind, a window that includes every Node security release cut since. docker-compose.yml:18 and docker-compose.dev.yml:22 pin `postgres:16.4-alpine`, which is roughly a year of Postgres minor releases behind on the 16 line. Both pins are deliberate and commented (Dockerfile:6-10, docker-compose.yml:13-15 both say to bump intentionally and offer digest-pinning instructions), which is the right instinct, but .github/dependabot.yml declares exactly two ecosystems: `npm` at directory `/` (line 4) and `github-actions` (line 83). There is no `docker` ecosystem entry, so nothing ever opens the bump PR the comments assume a human will remember to open. The same gap covers `gcr.io/projectsigstore/cosign:v2.4.1`, the third pinned image, at Dockerfile:60.
