findings.impact: The container a self-hoster pulls from ghcr, and the one this SaaS itself deploys, runs a Node runtime and an Alpine userland with a year of published, unpatched CVEs, on a product whose whole pitch is finding unpatched software on other people's sites. The scanner's own `software-inventory` check would flag this stack on a customer's site. Because the pin is manual and unautomated, the drift only grows: it has already gone from 'pinned last release' to 'twelve patches behind' with nobody noticing.
findings.recommendation: Add a third block to .github/dependabot.yml: `- package-ecosystem: "docker"` with `directory: "/"` (which covers Dockerfile) and a second entry for the compose files, on the same weekly schedule and with the same labels as the npm block. Then take the first PR it opens to move Dockerfile:11 and :62 to the current node:22.x-alpine patch and docker-compose.yml:18 / docker-compose.dev.yml:22 to the current postgres:16.x-alpine.

findings.title: The overrides block forces ESLint 10 into three eslint-config-next plugins whose peer ranges stop at ESLint 9, and eslint.config.mjs already documents one total lint crash this caused
findings.category: peer conflict papered over by an override
findings.description: package.json:130 declares `eslint: ^10.9.0`. eslint-config-next 16.3.2 (package.json:131) declares `peerDependencies: { eslint: ">=9.0.0" }`, which ESLint 10 satisfies, but its own hard dependencies do not: the lockfile shows `node_modules/eslint-config-next/node_modules/eslint-plugin-import` 2.32.0 with `peerDependencies.eslint: "^2 || ^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7.2.0 || ^8 || ^9"`, `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` 6.10.2 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9"`, and `eslint-plugin-react` 7.37.5 with `"^3 || ^4 || ^5 || ^6 || ^7 || ^8 || ^9.7"`. ESLint 10 is outside all three. The `overrides` block at package.json:146-154 forces it in anyway with three nested `{ "eslint": "$eslint" }` entries, which is what makes `npm ci` resolve instead of throwing ERESOLVE. That override is not cosmetic: eslint.config.mjs:47-55 documents the first thing it broke, in the repo's own words, 'eslint-config-next sets settings.react.version to "detect", which makes eslint-plugin-react probe the filesystem via context.getFilename(). ESLint 10 removed that legacy context method, so detection crashes the whole run', worked around by hardcoding `react: { version: "19.2.8" }` at eslint.config.mjs:55. Two more unguarded uses of removed ESLint 10 context APIs remain in the installed plugin (eslint-plugin-react/lib/rules/forward-ref-uses-ref.js:60 `context.getSourceCode()`, jsx-filename-extension.js:64 `context.getFilename()`); those two rules are off in core-web-vitals today, so they are latent rather than live. Running `npx eslint .` in the current working tree reproduces the failure class end to end: `TypeError: scopeManager.addGlobals is not a function at addDeclaredGlobals (node_modules/eslint/lib/languages/js/source-code/source-code.js:221)`, zero files linted, whole run aborted. To be precise about what that proves: this workspace's node_modules has drifted to eslint 10.8.1 while the lockfile pins 10.9.0, and CI on main is green, so this exact crash is not what CI runs. What it demonstrates is that the plugin set has no floor under it, because ESLint 10 patch releases are free to keep removing legacy APIs that three unsupported plugins still call.
findings.impact: `npm run lint` is a required, merge-blocking CI job (.github/workflows/ci.yml, the `lint` job), and it depends on three plugins that upstream does not claim to support on this ESLint major. When one of them next touches a removed API, lint does not report findings, it aborts with a TypeError and zero files checked. The failure mode is the bad one: a crash that reports no problems reads, to anyone skimming, a lot like a clean run, and the repo has already had to hand-patch one instance of it inside eslint.config.mjs.
findings.recommendation: Pick one of two. Either drop `eslint` back to `^9` in package.json:130 (which is what eslint-config-next 16.3.2's whole plugin set is tested against) and delete the three nested overrides at package.json:146-154, or keep ESLint 10 and stop depending on the unsupported plugins: replace `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` in eslint.config.mjs:13 with `@next/eslint-plugin-next`'s recommended rules plus `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` 7.1.1 (which is the one plugin in the set that already declares `^10.0.0` support) and configure jsx-a11y/import rules explicitly or not at all. Whichever is chosen, add a comment to the overrides block naming why it exists, since an override that silences a real peer conflict is invisible once ERESOLVE stops firing.

findings.title: The extension exposes popup.html, options.html and welcome.html as web_accessible_resources to <all_urls> although none of the three is ever opened from a web page, letting any site fingerprint the extension and iframe the API-key settings page
findings.description: `extension/manifest/chrome.json:55` (and the identical `extension/manifest/firefox.json:65`) declares `"web_accessible_resources": [{ "resources": ["popup.html", "options.html", "welcome.html"], "matches": ["<all_urls>"] }]`. web_accessible_resources governs access from web pages and other extensions only; the extension's own contexts can always load its own pages. Every actual open path in the source is an extension context: popup.html is the `action.default_popup` (line 12) and is re-opened as a tab by the popup itself at `extension/src/popup/popup.ts:789` via `browser.runtime.getURL("popup.html")` plus `browser.tabs.create`; options.html is the `options_ui.page` (line 51) and is opened via `browser.runtime.openOptionsPage()` at `extension/src/onboarding/welcome.ts:98` and `extension/src/popup/popup.ts:781`; welcome.html is opened by the service worker at `extension/src/background/service-worker.ts:91` with `browser.tabs.create({ url: browser.runtime.getURL("welcome.html") })`. No web page ever loads any of the three, so all three WAR entries are unnecessary. The cost of leaving them is concrete. In Chrome the extension ID is fixed once published, so any site can probe `chrome-extension://<id>/popup.html` and reliably fingerprint installed users, and any site can frame those pages. options.html is the credential surface: `extension/src/options/options.ts:395` renders the `api-key-input` field, line 318 renders the stored key prefix, and line 422 renders a "Clear the stored API key" control, all backed by `pasteKey()` and `clear()` in `extension/src/lib/auth.ts:23` and `:34`. A framed, overlay-covered options page is a clickjacking target for wiping or replacing the user's stored `vr_live_` key. There is no `use_dynamic_url: true` on the WAR entry, which is the MV3 mitigation for the fingerprinting half.
findings.impact: Any website a user visits can detect that VulnRadar is installed (which for a security-tool extension is itself a targeting signal), and can iframe the extension's own API-key settings page to bait a click that clears or overwrites the stored scan credential. Neither capability is needed by any code path in the extension.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `web_accessible_resources` block from both `extension/manifest/chrome.json` (lines 55 to 60) and `extension/manifest/firefox.json` (lines 65 to 70), then rebuild and confirm the popup, the options page, and the first-run welcome tab still open. If a future feature genuinely needs a page reachable from a content script, add back only that one resource with `"use_dynamic_url": true` and a narrow `matches` list.

findings.title: @types/chrome and @types/firefox-webext-browser are unused devDependencies whose ambient globals let a file that forgets the webextension-polyfill import type-check clean and then die with ReferenceError in Chrome
findings.category: unused dependency that weakens the typecheck
findings.description: `extension/package.json:29` and `:30` declare `@types/chrome: ^0.0.287` and `@types/firefox-webext-browser: ^120.0.4`, and `extension/tsconfig.json:7` force-loads both with `"types": ["chrome", "firefox-webext-browser", "node"]`. Neither is used. A grep of `extension/src` for the global `chrome.` namespace finds two hits and both are inside comments (`src/background/service-worker.ts:789`, `src/lib/scan.ts:127`). Every browser API call in the extension goes through `import browser from "webextension-polyfill"`, present in 9 of the 10 source files that reference `browser.`; the tenth, `src/lib/constants.ts`, only mentions `browser.tabs.sendMessage` in a comment on line 58. The types for that import come from `@types/webextension-polyfill` (`extension/package.json:32`), which is the one that is actually needed. The two unused packages are not inert. `node_modules/@types/firefox-webext-browser/index.d.ts` declares the whole API as ambient globals (`declare namespace browser.alarms` at line 837, `declare namespace browser._manifest` at line 8, and so on), so a source file that writes `browser.tabs.query(...)` while forgetting `import browser from "webextension-polyfill"` satisfies the compiler through the global and `npm run typecheck` passes. At runtime Chrome MV3 defines no global `browser`, so that file throws `ReferenceError: browser is not defined` on load. For `content.js` and `background.js`, which `extension/scripts/build.mjs:57` builds as single-entry IIFE bundles, a load-time throw kills the entire script, which is exactly the silent-whole-script-death failure the comment in `extension/vite.config.ts:9` documents having already hit this project once on Firefox. Both packages are also badly stale on top of being unused: `npm outdated --json` in extension/ shows @types/chrome at 0.0.287 against latest 0.2.7 and @types/firefox-webext-browser at 120.0.5 against latest 143.0.0, while `extension/manifest/firefox.json:19` sets `strict_min_version: "140.0"` and uses the Firefox 140+ `data_collection_permissions` key.
findings.impact: CI's `npm run typecheck` is the only gate on the extension (there is no test suite and no linter of its own), and these two packages punch a hole in it: a forgotten polyfill import compiles clean, ships, and then bricks the background service worker or the all-URLs content script in Chrome with no error surfaced to the user beyond the extension silently doing nothing. It also carries 1.2 MB of type definitions describing a Chrome and Firefox API surface roughly a year behind the browser versions the manifest actually targets.
findings.recommendation: Remove `@types/chrome` and `@types/firefox-webext-browser` from `extension/package.json` devDependencies and drop `"chrome"` and `"firefox-webext-browser"` from the `types` array in `extension/tsconfig.json:7`, leaving `["node"]`. Run `npm run typecheck` in extension/ to confirm nothing depended on the ambient globals. If a future feature needs a Chrome-only API such as `chrome.offscreen` (already noted as wanted at `src/background/service-worker.ts:789`), add `@types/chrome` back at a current version and reference it from just that file.

findings.title: The root package.json `overrides` block that pins postcss, sharp and brace-expansion does not apply to extension/ or marketing/, so a security pin added at the root silently leaves the shipped extension unpatched
findings.description: `package.json:137` declares an `overrides` block that pins `postcss: "8.5.26"`, `sharp: "^0.35.0"`, `brace-expansion@1: "1.1.18"`, `brace-expansion@2: "2.1.4"`, and the four @typescript-eslint packages. npm `overrides` are scoped to the manifest that declares them and to that install tree only. `extension/` and `marketing/` are not npm workspaces (the root manifest has no `workspaces` field) and each has its own independent `package-lock.json`, so none of those pins reaches them. The divergence is already visible in the resolved trees: postcss is 8.5.26 in the root lock (the pinned value) and 8.5.23 in `extension/package-lock.json`, even though the extension still runs postcss on every build (`extension/vite.config.ts:39` sets `css.postcss.plugins: []`, which selects an empty plugin list, not a bypass of the postcss pipeline). brace-expansion resolves to 1.1.18 plus 5.0.9 at the root, 2.1.4 in extension, and 1.1.18 plus 2.1.4 in marketing. esbuild is 0.25.12 in extension and 0.28.1 in marketing. All of those specific versions happen to be past their known advisories today, so nothing is exploitable right now; the finding is the mechanism. The root overrides exist precisely because someone reacted to an advisory by pinning a transitive package, and that reflex will not protect the artifact that ships to users' browsers.
findings.impact: The next time a transitive advisory is handled by adding an entry to the root `overrides` block, the browser extension keeps the vulnerable version and nothing reports it (see subdeps-02: the extension tree is not audited or watched at all). The operator will reasonably believe the pin covered the repo.
findings.recommendation: Either convert `extension` into an npm workspace of the root manifest so one lockfile and one `overrides` block govern both trees, or, if the separate lockfile is deliberate (CI caches `extension/package-lock.json` separately at `.github/workflows/ci.yml:129`), add an `overrides` block to `extension/package.json` and add a short note to the root `overrides` block at `package.json:137` saying that every entry added there must be mirrored into `extension/package.json`.

findings.title: The extension builds with Vite 6.4.3, two majors behind the supported window (latest 8.2.2, previous 7.3.6), and that toolchain emits the IIFE injected into every page the user visits
findings.category: unsupported major on the build toolchain
findings.description: `extension/package.json:37` declares `"vite": "^6.4.3"`, resolved to 6.4.3 in `extension/package-lock.json`. `npm view vite dist-tags` returns `latest: 8.2.2` and `previous: 7.3.6`, so Vite 6 is neither the current nor the previous major and is outside the line that receives backported fixes. The same tree carries esbuild 0.25.12 (marketing's independent tree already resolves 0.28.1) and archiver 7.0.1 against latest 8.0.0 per `npm outdated --json`. This is not an ordinary application dependency: `extension/scripts/build.mjs:44` and `:59` call Vite's programmatic `build()` twice, once for the three HTML pages and once per entry for `background/service-worker.ts` and `content/detector.ts`, and those two IIFE bundles are what the manifest injects as the MV3 service worker and as a `content_scripts` entry matching `<all_urls>` (`extension/manifest/chrome.json:47`). The same `build.mjs` output is what `extension/scripts/package.mjs` zips and what `.github/workflows/release.yml:147` builds and attaches to the GitHub release for Chrome Web Store and AMO upload. Because the root's own Vite (8.2.2, pulled in transitively by vitest 4.1.11) is a completely separate install tree, the repo already proves Vite 8 works here for the rest of the codebase; only the extension is stuck. Combined with subdeps-02 (no Dependabot and no audit on this manifest), nothing will ever nudge this forward.
findings.impact: The one toolchain that generates browser-privileged code for real users is on a major that will not get security fixes, and no automation watches it. A build-chain compromise or a Rollup/esbuild output bug lands directly in an extension with all-URLs content-script access, and the upgrade path only gets longer the further behind it drifts (a 6 to 8 jump is two sets of breaking changes at once).
findings.recommendation: Bump `extension/package.json:37` to `"vite": "^8.2.2"` and `"archiver": "^8.0.0"` at line 33, run `npm install` inside `extension/` only (its lockfile is separate from the root's, so this does not touch the root package-lock), then verify `npm run build:chrome && npm run build:firefox` still emits classic-script `background.js` and `content.js` with no top-level imports, which is the invariant documented in `extension/vite.config.ts:9`. Load both unpacked builds once before releasing.

findings.title: marketing/ is entirely gitignored, so 401 packages, a 270 MB downloaded Chromium and a local .env full of credentials sit inside the repo tree with zero supply-chain visibility
findings.category: untracked dependency tree inside the repo
findings.description: First, the question that sets the severity of everything else here: marketing/ is NOT built or deployed as part of the product. `.gitignore:74` ignores the whole `marketing/` directory, `git ls-files marketing` returns 0 files, and no workflow, `next.config`, `vercel.json`, `tsconfig.json` or root script references it (grep for "marketing" across `.github`, `next.config.*`, `vercel.json`, `package.json`, `tsconfig.json` returns nothing). It is a standalone Remotion asset-generation project run manually on the maintainer's machine. Its dependencies therefore carry no production risk. What they do carry is a blind spot. Because `marketing/package.json` and `marketing/package-lock.json` are untracked, Dependabot cannot see them (it needs a committed manifest), `npm audit` at the root never walks into them, and the CycloneDX SBOM built from the Docker image (`.github/workflows/docker-publish.yml:82`) excludes them. Measured on disk: `marketing/node_modules` is 648 MB across 401 lockfile entries, of which `node_modules/.remotion/chrome-headless-shell/win64/` is 270 MB, a Chromium headless-shell binary that @remotion/renderer downloads over the network on first render rather than at install, and `@remotion/compositor-win32-x64-msvc` is another 29 MB of native binary including a bundled `ffmpeg.exe`. That tree executes on a machine where `marketing/.env` (365 bytes, present on disk, correctly ignored) holds credentials, and `marketing/package.json:31` wires `npm run audio` to `node scripts/make-audio.mjs`, which is what consumes them. The tree is also drifting on its own: React 19.2.3 against the root's 19.2.8, @types/react 19.2.7 against 19.2.18, prettier 3.8.1 against 3.9.6, eslint 9.19.0 against the root's 10.9.0.
findings.impact: Nobody is watching 401 packages plus two downloaded native binaries that run with full user privileges on the maintainer's workstation next to a credentials file. A malicious postinstall or a compromised Remotion transitive release would execute there and nothing in the repo's security automation would notice, because from git's point of view the directory does not exist. Separately, the project is unreproducible: no other contributor can restore the exact tree that rendered the shipped videos, since the lockfile is not in git.
findings.recommendation: Decide which of the two this is. If marketing/ should stay private, move it out of the repo working tree entirely (a sibling directory or its own repo) so it is not silently inside a scanned checkout, and keep a lockfile under version control wherever it lands. If it should stay in place, narrow `.gitignore:74` from `marketing/` to `marketing/node_modules/`, `marketing/out/`, `marketing/.env`, and `marketing/public/` so that `marketing/package.json` and `marketing/package-lock.json` become tracked, then add a `directory: "/marketing"` block to `.github/dependabot.yml`. Either way, document that the 270 MB chrome-headless-shell arrives on first `remotion render`, not on `npm install`.

findings.title: The schema-version marker is written in a third separate transaction after the DDL commit, so an interruption between them leaves a fully migrated database the app refuses to boot on
findings.category: version marker not atomic with the change it records
findings.description: A migration reaches durability in three independent commits. First runPlan (scripts/migrate/_runner.mjs:83) opens one transaction, runs every plan step, and COMMITs at line 134. Second, still inside runPlan at line 137, `await repairAllSequences(client)` runs as its own autocommit statement with no try/catch. Third, control returns to migrate.mjs, which only reaches `await writeMeta(livePool, {...})` at line 550 if runPlan returned normally. So an exception from repairAllSequences, a killed process, or a dropped connection anywhere after the COMMIT leaves the schema fully upgraded while vulnradar_schema_meta still holds the old version. instrumentation.ts:148-190 then compares that stale version against MIN_SCHEMA_VERSION ("3.0.0", lib/config/config-values.ts:28) and calls process.exit(1) with a SCHEMA VERSION MISMATCH box. This extends AUDIT-009#migration-03, which reported the unguarded repairAllSequences call as a confusing false failure message; that call is still unguarded at _runner.mjs:137 and at migrate.mjs:537. What is new here is the structural point the false message is a symptom of: writeMeta is not in the same transaction as the DDL it records, and the consequence is not a confusing log line but a hard boot refusal.
findings.impact: The app will not start at all, on a database that is actually correct, until someone re-runs db:migrate. Because the self-updater runs db:migrate as its last step from inside the running app, the operator's next restart is the moment this surfaces, with the misleading message that the database schema is older than the app requires. Re-running db:migrate does recover (every step is idempotent), but only if the operator ignores the message telling them the schema is behind.
findings.recommendation: Move the writeMeta INSERT into runPlan's transaction: pass the target version and app version into runPlan and issue the vulnradar_schema_meta upsert as the last statement before COMMIT, so schema and version marker commit or roll back together. Move repairAllSequences after that COMMIT and wrap it in its own try/catch that warns without failing the run.

findings.title: Two indexes are UNIQUE on the boot path and non-unique on the migration path, and CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS means whichever runs first wins
findings.category: index definition drift between the two schema sources
findings.description: The upgrade's addIndexes entry at 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:999-1003 is expanded by scripts/migrate/_planner.mjs:140 into `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_github_connections_github_user_id ON "github_connections"(github_user_id)`, a plain non-unique index. instrumentation.ts:1933 creates an index with the identical NAME as `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_github_connections_github_user_id ON github_connections(github_user_id)`. IF NOT EXISTS matches on the index name only, not its definition, so whichever path runs first permanently decides whether the constraint exists, and the other silently no-ops. db:migrate is documented and scripted to run before the app boots, so on any migrated database the index is non-unique. The same shape applies to idx_host_badges_token_hash: non-unique and partial at 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:1019-1024 (`WHERE badge_token_hash IS NOT NULL`) versus `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` with no predicate at instrumentation.ts:3387.
findings.impact: github_connections has no other constraint on github_user_id (the table's only UNIQUE is on user_id, see 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:333, and lib/github/github-connections.ts:103 upserts on ON CONFLICT (user_id)). On a fresh-boot database, a second VulnRadar account connecting the same GitHub identity fails with a unique violation; on a migrated database it succeeds. Two accounts can then both hold an encrypted access token for one GitHub user and both consume that user's review quota, and behavior differs between two installs that both report schema_version=3.0.0. For host_badges the practical exposure is smaller because badge_token is already NOT NULL UNIQUE, but the index shape still differs between installs.
findings.recommendation: Add a `unique: true` flag to the addIndexes step shape in scripts/migrate/_planner.mjs's expandPlan (line 139) and emit CREATE UNIQUE INDEX when set, then mark both entries in 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs unique and drop the WHERE predicate on idx_host_badges_token_hash so it matches instrumentation.ts exactly. Add a test that every `addIndexes` name in a version file resolves to an index in instrumentation.ts with the same uniqueness and predicate.

findings.title: Both "frozen" schema snapshots are wrong: the v2.0.0 file was edited twice despite its DO NOT EDIT header, and the v1.0.0 file ships a v3-era table with a different column shape
findings.description: scripts/create-fresh-db/schemas/instrumentation-v2.ts:2-4 says "Frozen at v2.0.0" and "DO NOT EDIT". It contains 37 CREATE TABLE statements. The registry's v2.0.0 fingerprint (scripts/migrate/_registry.mjs:114-151) is 34 tables. The three extras are support_tickets (instrumentation-v2.ts:567), support_ticket_messages and support_ticket_shares, added by commits db113cfb "feat(support): in-app support ticket backend" and eae5e781 "feat(support): share a ticket with specific teammates", both v3.7-era work. Separately, scripts/create-fresh-db/schemas/instrumentation-v1.ts:389 creates processed_stripe_events, which the registry lists as a v3.0.0 addition and which the v1.0.0 fingerprint (_registry.mjs:53-73, 19 tables) does not contain, and it creates it with a DIFFERENT shape than every other path: `event_id TEXT, event_type TEXT, received_at TIMESTAMP` versus instrumentation.ts:548's `event_id VARCHAR(255), event_type VARCHAR(100), processed_at TIMESTAMP`. Because both later paths use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS (instrumentation.ts:547, 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:395), neither can ever repair the column name.
findings.impact: AUDIT-009 proved its migration-01 fix by "building a true v2.0.0-shaped scratch DB from the frozen instrumentation-v2.ts snapshot" and diffing the migrated result against instrumentation.ts. That baseline is no longer v2.0.0, so any repeat of that verification silently excuses drift on the support-ticket tables, which is part of why migrate-01 re-opened. For the v1 path, `npm run db:create` at 1.0.0 followed by `npm run db:migrate` produces a database where processed_stripe_events has received_at instead of processed_at: instrumentation.ts's `CREATE INDEX idx_processed_stripe_events_processed_at` then errors on every boot (logged non-fatally at line 555), and app/api/v3/admin/billing-overview/route.ts:131 and :140 both select processed_at and fall into their .catch fallbacks, so the admin billing overview permanently reports zero failed payments.
findings.recommendation: Revert the three support-ticket table blocks out of scripts/create-fresh-db/schemas/instrumentation-v2.ts and remove processed_stripe_events from instrumentation-v1.ts, restoring both to the 34-table and 19-table shapes the registry fingerprints declare. Add a test that asserts the CREATE TABLE set parsed from each snapshot equals its version's fingerprint tables exactly, so an edit to a frozen file fails CI rather than passing silently.

findings.title: fingerprintDetect counts missing columns but never lets them disqualify a version, so a half-migrated database is detected as complete and then bricks the app at boot
findings.category: version detection accepts an incomplete schema
findings.description: fingerprintDetect rejects a version only when a fingerprint TABLE is missing (line 33, `if (missingTables.length > 0) continue`). Column checks at lines 38-45 accumulate a missingColumns count that is used for exactly one thing: downgrading `confidence` from "high" to "medium" at line 73. The match is still returned as the detected version. So a database with all 34 v2 tables but missing v2 columns on users (the exact state a partial or interrupted 1.0.0 to 2.0.0 run leaves) is reported as "2.0.0 (confidence: medium)". migrate.mjs:365 accepts that value with no threshold check, buildPlan("2.0.0", "3.0.0") is composed, and the 1.0.0 to 2.0.0 addColumns entries that would have supplied users.plan, stripe_customer_id, subscription_status, beta_access and daily_scan_limit (scripts/migrate/versions/1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs:62-119) are never run. writeMeta then stamps 3.0.0. instrumentation.ts never re-adds those columns either: they exist only inside the inline CREATE TABLE users at line 280, and there is no `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS plan` anywhere in the file.
findings.impact: On the next boot, `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_plan ON users(plan)` at instrumentation.ts:325 raises column does not exist. That statement is inside the pool.query block starting at line 279, one of the 41 blocks with no .catch, so it reaches the outer handler at line 3618 and calls process.exit(1). The app is permanently unbootable, the operator is told schema creation failed partway through, and re-running db:migrate does not help because the meta row now says 3.0.0 so the detector never revisits the v1 to v2 columns. Recovery requires hand-editing vulnradar_schema_meta. This is precisely the case the meta table's own header (scripts/migrate/_meta.mjs:11) claims to prevent.
findings.recommendation: In scripts/migrate/_detect.mjs, treat a non-zero missingColumns as disqualifying: `continue` past that version the same way a missing table does, so detection falls back to the highest version that is genuinely complete. Keep the medium-confidence path only for columns explicitly marked optional in the fingerprint. In migrate.mjs, refuse to proceed on a low-confidence or ambiguous detection when running non-interactively.

findings.title: Nothing verifies the schema against the target fingerprint after a migration, even though the registry's own header says that is what fingerprints are for
findings.description: scripts/migrate/_registry.mjs:5-8 states the migrator uses fingerprints "both for: Detecting the current version when no meta table exists [and] Verifying a target version was reached after a migration." The second half does not exist. Grepping the whole scripts/ tree, fingerprintDetect is imported and called in exactly one place, scripts/migrate/migrate.mjs:354, inside step 1 (detect current version), and only when the meta row is absent or names an unknown version. After runPlan returns, migrate.mjs goes straight from the failure check at line 543 to writeMeta at line 550 with no re-read of the live schema and no comparison against getVersion(target).fingerprint. getActualSchema is likewise only called at line 353.
findings.impact: There is no gate between "every SQL statement executed without error" and "the schema now matches version X". That is the structural reason migrate-01 could regress by 11 tables while db:migrate kept reporting success, and it is why the same class of defect has now shipped twice (AUDIT-009#migration-01, then again). It also means a version file that is simply incomplete, or a step whose IF NOT EXISTS silently no-ops against a pre-existing object of the same name (see migrate-06), produces an identical success message.
findings.recommendation: Add a verification step to migrate.mjs between runPlan and writeMeta: re-run getActualSchema, compare against getVersion(target).fingerprint's tables and columns, and refuse to write the meta row (exit non-zero, naming every missing table and column) if anything is absent. Combined with migrate-10's parity test, that gives one guard at author time and one at run time.

findings.title: The only migration test suite asserts against hardcoded name lists with arrayContaining, so it structurally cannot detect drift from instrumentation.ts
findings.category: test cannot fail for the defect it appears to guard
findings.description: tests/scripts/migrate/versions/2.0.0-to-3.0.0.test.ts is the only test that touches scripts/migrate/versions/. Its central assertion, "upgrade adds every table that survives to the final v3.0.0 shape" (line 30), is `expect(names).toEqual(expect.arrayContaining([...literal list...]))`. arrayContaining is a subset check, and the literal list is maintained by hand in the test file, so the test passes as long as the migration contains the names someone remembered to type. It never reads instrumentation.ts, never enumerates its CREATE TABLE statements, and never compares the two sets in either direction. The sibling assertions at lines 139, 175, 187, 195, 233, 279, 306 and the fingerprint assertions at 370-476 all have the same shape. The list at line 30 even carries a comment naming the four tables AUDIT-009#migration-01 caught, which is a record of the defect but not a guard against it.
findings.impact: Every one of the 11 tables and 8 columns in migrate-01 was added to instrumentation.ts while this suite stayed green. The project has now had the same drift twice, and the test that exists specifically because of the first occurrence cannot fail for the second. Because scripts/** is excluded from coverage in vitest.config.ts, coverage reporting also does not surface the gap.
findings.recommendation: Add one parity test that parses instrumentation.ts for `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS <name>` and `ALTER TABLE <t> ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS <c>` (the same regex scripts/create-fresh-db/create-fresh-db.mjs:227 already uses to extract those blocks), builds the same set from the v1 baseline plus every version file's addTables/addColumns, and asserts set equality with toEqual, not arrayContaining. Assert the fingerprint in _registry.mjs equals the same set. An explicit allowlist constant can carry any deliberate exception, so adding one is a conscious edit rather than a silent omission.

findings.title: Boot-time schema application takes no advisory lock, so two instances starting together race on CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS and one exits 1
findings.description: register() issues its schema statements as 94 separate pool.query calls with no BEGIN, no COMMIT and no lock of any kind; grepping instrumentation.ts for pg_advisory_lock, BEGIN or CONCURRENTLY returns nothing. PostgreSQL's IF NOT EXISTS is a catalog existence check followed by an insert, not an atomic operation, so two backends running the same CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS concurrently can both pass the check and one gets `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "pg_type_typname_nsp_index"` (23505) or `relation already exists` (42P07); the same race on CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS raises 23505 on pg_class, and concurrent ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS raises `tuple concurrently updated`. 41 of those pool.query calls carry no .catch, including the entire core-table run from line 279 (users) through line 1167 (subdomain_cache). An error in any of them unwinds to the outer catch at line 3618, which sends a critical admin alert and calls process.exit(1).
findings.impact: Any deployment that starts more than one Node process against the same database (a scale-up, a rolling restart, docker compose with a replica, or a supervisor restarting a crashed process while the old one is still initializing) can lose one instance to a schema race on startup. The failure is transient (the next attempt sees the object already present) but it presents as a critical boot_schema_creation_failed alert and a crash-looping container, which is indistinguishable from a genuine schema problem. The 53 blocks that do have a .catch degrade differently and worse: they log non-fatally and let the app serve traffic on a schema whose creation actually failed.
findings.recommendation: Wrap the whole schema block in a session-level `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(<constant>)` taken on a dedicated client before the first CREATE TABLE and released in a finally, so a second booting instance blocks until the first finishes and then finds every object present. Take the lock on a single pool.connect() client, not on the pool, so it is held for the duration.

findings.title: The pre-migration backup passes the database password in pg_dump's argv and writes an unencrypted, never-pruned dump, both of which backup-db.mjs was explicitly fixed to avoid
findings.category: two backup implementations with different security properties
findings.description: backupDatabase, called from scripts/migrate/migrate.mjs:519 before any DDL runs, spawns `pg_dump [connectionString]` with the full DATABASE_URL as argv[1]. scripts/backup-db.mjs:214-221 does the opposite and documents why: "Keep the DB password out of pg_dump's argv (visible via ps on a shared host); libpq reads it from PGPASSWORD in the child env instead", using splitDbUrlForEnv from scripts/_lib/_lib.db-url.mjs. The migration-time copy imports neither. The same file writes the dump to databases/v{major}/{version}/vulnradar_backup_{ts}.sql (line 59) as plaintext SQL with no encryption, while backup-db.mjs:194-197 encrypts with AES-256-GCM by default and falls back to API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY specifically so backups are "encrypted by default rather than silently written in plaintext". There is also no retention pruning on this path, unlike backup-db.mjs's selectExpiredBackups.
findings.impact: db:migrate is run on the production host, including automatically as the self-updater's last step, so on any shared or multi-tenant host the production database password is briefly readable in the process list by every local user. The dump it writes contains every password hash, every encrypted API key and token, every Stripe customer and subscription id, and the full scan history, sitting unencrypted under the app directory and accumulating one file per migration forever. On the self-hosted panel deployments the docs target, that directory is typically browsable through the panel's file manager.
findings.recommendation: In scripts/_lib/_lib.backup.mjs, import splitDbUrlForEnv from ./_lib.db-url.mjs and spawn pg_dump with `[connArg]` plus the returned env, exactly as scripts/backup-db.mjs:216 does. Then reuse backup-db.mjs's createBackupCipher and selectExpiredBackups here rather than maintaining a second, weaker dump path, or have backupDatabase simply invoke runBackup with a version-scoped --dir.

findings.title: Every index is built without CONCURRENTLY and the migration rewrites scan_history twice inside one transaction, while the self-updater runs it against a still-serving app
findings.description: runPlan wraps the entire plan in a single BEGIN/COMMIT (line 95 to line 134) because "half-migrated schemas are the worst-case outcome", and the file header notes CONCURRENTLY is deliberately avoided since it cannot run in a transaction. The 2.0.0 to 3.0.0 plan contains 18 CREATE TABLE, 48 ADD COLUMN, 17 CREATE INDEX and 18 dataUpdates, all under that one transaction. Two of the ADD COLUMNs force a full rewrite of scan_history and hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on it for the whole remaining transaction: `share_token_hash TEXT GENERATED ALWAYS AS (...) STORED` (2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:608-615) and `public_id TEXT DEFAULT (replace(gen_random_uuid()::text, '-', ''))` (line 879-883), whose volatile default is evaluated once per existing row. A third, `UPDATE scan_history SET public_id = ... WHERE public_id IS NULL` (line 1059), is an unbounded UPDATE over the same table. The boot path has the same property without the transaction: all 103 CREATE INDEX / CREATE UNIQUE INDEX statements in instrumentation.ts are plain, taking a SHARE lock that blocks writes for the build, and the same two scan_history rewrites appear at instrumentation.ts:1284 and 2613. The self-updater runs db:migrate from inside the running app and explicitly does not restart it (app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply/route.ts:28), so the app is serving throughout.
findings.impact: At the current production size (roughly 50 users) this is seconds, not minutes, so the practical cost today is a short stall rather than an outage. But every request that reads or writes scan_history or users blocks for the full duration of the migration transaction, with no timeout and no warning anywhere in the UI: the updater dialog tells the operator only that the server is not restarted, implying it keeps serving normally. The cost scales linearly with scan_history, which is the fastest-growing table in the product, so the same release flow gets worse every month with no signal until it is a real outage.
findings.recommendation: Split the plan into a transactional DDL phase and a post-commit index phase, and run the CREATE INDEX steps outside the transaction with CONCURRENTLY (which requires per-statement error handling and a re-run path for INVALID indexes). Set `SET LOCAL lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` at the start of the migration transaction so a blocked ACCESS EXCLUSIVE acquisition fails fast instead of queuing every request behind it. Add a warning to the updater dialog that db:migrate briefly locks the database.

findings.title: access_rules.created_by carries two conflicting foreign keys because the self-healing migration adds ON DELETE SET NULL but never drops the original inline NO ACTION constraint
findings.description: The CREATE TABLE for access_rules declares `created_by INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id)` (instrumentation.ts:1014, and identically in scripts/migrate/versions/_snippets.mjs:27). An inline REFERENCES with no ON DELETE clause creates a real, named constraint, `access_rules_created_by_fkey`, with ON DELETE NO ACTION. The self-healing block at instrumentation.ts:1033-1062 then checks only for a constraint named `fk_access_rules_created_by`; when absent it runs `ALTER TABLE access_rules ALTER COLUMN created_by DROP NOT NULL` (:1044) followed by `ADD CONSTRAINT fk_access_rules_created_by FOREIGN KEY (created_by) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` (:1047). It never drops `access_rules_created_by_fkey`, so the column ends up with two foreign keys to the same parent with contradictory delete actions. Compare the sibling fix 1,840 lines later for the identical bug class on broadcast_messages.created_by, which explicitly runs `DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS broadcast_messages_created_by_fkey` (instrumentation.ts:2895) before adding the SET NULL version, and the admin_audit_log.target_user_id fix at :592-622, which sidesteps the problem by declaring the column as plain `INTEGER` with no inline REFERENCES (:571). access_rules is the only one of the three that leaves the original constraint in place. On top of that, lib/auth/account-deletion.ts explicitly nulls the four other plain-FK columns it knows about (security_alerts.resolved_by :155, system_settings.updated_by :159, broadcast_messages.sent_by :167, sessions.impersonated_by :174) and does not null access_rules.created_by, because it assumes the schema-level SET NULL handles it. On `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1` (account-deletion.ts:180) Postgres queues one after-row RI trigger per constraint and fires them in trigger-name order, which for internal RI triggers is constraint-OID order, so the older NO ACTION check on `access_rules_created_by_fkey` runs before the newer SET NULL action and sees the still-referencing row. Note that the existing account-deletion test suite cannot catch this: tests/lib/auth/account-deletion.test.ts drives the function with a fake client, so no real constraint is ever evaluated.
findings.impact: Any staff account that ever created an IP or URL access rule from the admin panel cannot be deleted. Both delete paths (POST /api/v3/account/delete and the admin delete_account action at app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:2000) wrap deleteUserAccountData in one transaction, so the foreign-key violation rolls the whole thing back and the user gets a 500 on a GDPR erasure request. This is exactly the failure AUDIT-001#db-01 reported for admin_audit_log and this block was written to prevent. Even in the benign ordering where the delete succeeds, every INSERT and UPDATE on access_rules pays two identical RI checks instead of one, and any future reader of the schema sees two constraints disagreeing about what a user deletion means.
findings.recommendation: In instrumentation.ts's access_rules self-healing block (around line 1041), add `ALTER TABLE access_rules DROP CONSTRAINT IF EXISTS access_rules_created_by_fkey;` before the ADD CONSTRAINT, matching the broadcast_messages fix at :2895. Also drop the inline `REFERENCES users(id)` from the CREATE TABLE at :1014 and from scripts/migrate/versions/_snippets.mjs:27 so a fresh install never creates the NO ACTION constraint in the first place. To confirm the current state on a live database: `SELECT conname, confdeltype FROM pg_constraint WHERE conrelid = 'access_rules'::regclass AND contype = 'f';` should return one row, not two.

findings.title: Two tables exist only as lazy runtime DDL: staff_invites and admin_audit_log_archive are in no schema file, no migration, and no required-table check, and staff_invites re-runs its CREATE TABLE on every admin request
findings.description: instrumentation.ts is documented as the canonical schema and contains 64 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statements. Two more tables exist that it never creates. (1) `staff_invites` is created by `ensureStaffInvitesTable()` (lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:33-48), whose own doc comment at :22-31 says it is "intentionally NOT called from instrumentation.ts directly" and instructs whoever wires the schema change to add the import there. That was never done: a repo-wide grep for `ensureStaffInvitesTable` finds it called only from the three handlers in app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts (:75, :177, :216), never at boot. (2) `admin_audit_log_archive` is created by `ensureAuditLogArchiveTable()` (lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:43-57), whose doc comment at :37-41 gives the same never-executed wiring instruction; the only real call site is inside `archiveAdminAuditLogBeforePurge` at :77, which runs it against the transactional client of the nightly cleanup pass (lib/database/cleanup.ts:308), so DDL executes inside the long cleanup transaction on every run. Neither table appears anywhere in scripts/create-fresh-db/ or scripts/migrate/ (grep for both names in those directories returns nothing), and neither is in lib/database/required-tables.ts, so the boot-time verification at instrumentation.ts:3515-3543 and GET /api/v3/health both report a healthy schema on a database that is missing them. The public accept endpoint app/api/v3/auth/staff-invite/[token]/route.ts queries `staff_invites` at :57, :104 and :208 without ever calling ensureStaffInvitesTable first.
findings.impact: `npm run db:create` and `npm run db:migrate` both produce a database that is missing these two tables, and nothing reports it. The staff-invite feature only works because its admin route happens to create the table as a side effect of the first request. That side effect also means every GET, POST and DELETE on /api/v3/admin/staff-invites executes one CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus two CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS against the system catalogs before doing any work, which is the same per-request DDL antipattern AUDIT-003#misc-01 reported for ai/conversations and that was fixed there. Anyone reading instrumentation.ts to understand the schema, or diffing it against a production database, gets a wrong answer for two tables.
findings.recommendation: Move both CREATE TABLE statements into instrumentation.ts's boot block, as each module's own doc comment already asks: put staff_invites next to team_invites (after line 917) and admin_audit_log_archive next to admin_audit_log (after line 579). Keep the ensure* functions but call them once at boot and delete the calls from app/api/v3/admin/staff-invites/route.ts:75, :177 and :216 and from lib/database/audit-log-archive.ts:77 so no DDL runs on a request path or inside the cleanup transaction. Add both names to lib/database/required-tables.ts, and add the DDL to scripts/create-fresh-db and the current migration version so a fresh install and a migrated install agree.

findings.title: Twenty-six foreign-key child columns have no index, so every user deletion and every scan retention pass sequentially scans the child tables once per deleted parent row
findings.description: Extends AUDIT-012#perf-15, which named nine missing indexes chosen from application WHERE/ORDER BY clauses. This is the orthogonal set: Postgres does not index a foreign-key child column automatically, and for every FK constraint it fires one referential-integrity query per deleted parent row (`DELETE FROM child WHERE fk = $1` for CASCADE, `UPDATE child SET fk = NULL WHERE fk = $1` for SET NULL). Cross-checking all 84 REFERENCES clauses in instrumentation.ts against all 97 CREATE INDEX statements leaves 26 FK columns with no index at all. Two of them hang off scan_history and are the worst: `scan_finding_feedback.scan_history_id` (instrumentation.ts:1460, ON DELETE SET NULL) and `auto_tag_dismissals.scan_id` (:2505, ON DELETE CASCADE). auto_tag_dismissals' only index is on `tag` (:2511) and scan_finding_feedback's three indexes are on (user_id, finding_id, finding_url), (finding_id, verdict) and (user_id, created_at) (:1467-1472), none of which lead with the scan column. Both fire on the four per-plan retention DELETEs in lib/database/cleanup.ts:152-195, which run inside the single 350-line cleanup transaction, and on `DELETE FROM scan_history WHERE user_id = $1` in lib/auth/account-deletion.ts:79. The scan_history sibling FKs are fine: scan_tags.scan_id is indexed (:446), scan_screenshots.scan_id is the primary key (:1378), and host_reputation.source_scan_id has a partial index whose predicate an equality lookup satisfies (:1723). Twenty-three more unindexed FK columns point at users(id) and each adds one sequential scan to `DELETE FROM users WHERE id = $1` (account-deletion.ts:180): sessions.impersonated_by (:347), user_badges.awarded_by (:510), admin_user_notes.admin_id (:698), password_reset_tokens.user_id (:753), email_verification_tokens.user_id (:763), teams.owner_id (:890), team_invites.invited_by (:911), gifted_subscriptions.gifted_by (:948) and .revoked_by (:953), admin_notifications.created_by (:985), access_rules.created_by (:1014), security_alerts.resolved_by (:1103), system_settings.updated_by (:1122), broadcast_messages.created_by (:1139) and .sent_by (:1330), auto_tag_dismissals.dismissed_by_user_id (:2507), promoted_auto_tag_rules.created_by (:2947), ai_credit_purchases.user_id (:2994), github_credit_purchases.user_id (:3026), browserbase_credit_purchases.user_id (:3096), support_ticket_messages.author_user_id (:3449), support_ticket_shares.shared_by_user_id (:3463), and staff_invites.invited_by (lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:40). The last of those, user_badges.badge_id (:508), points at badges. password_reset_tokens.user_id and email_verification_tokens.user_id are also hit outside deletion, by the explicit `DELETE FROM ... WHERE user_id = $1` that precedes every token issue (app/api/v3/auth/forgot-password/route.ts:81, app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:186, lib/auth/email-verification.ts:37, app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:787). Note that scripts/create-fresh-db/schemas/instrumentation-v1.ts:258 does create `idx_prt_user_id ON password_reset_tokens(user_id)`, so a database built from that older path has an index the current canonical schema never creates.
findings.impact: Deleting one user runs about 23 sequential scans of unrelated tables, several of which (sessions, support_ticket_messages, gifted_subscriptions) grow without bound. More seriously, a nightly retention pass that deletes N free-plan scans performs N sequential scans of scan_finding_feedback and N of auto_tag_dismissals, all inside the single transaction AUDIT-012#perf-22 already flagged for holding a pooled connection for its whole duration. At today's row counts this is invisible; it degrades quadratically with scan volume, and the failure mode is the cleanup transaction holding locks for minutes and eventually timing out, which stops every retention rule at once because the whole pass is one transaction.
findings.recommendation: Add the two scan_history child indexes first, since they are the ones that scale with scan volume: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_sff_scan_history_id ON scan_finding_feedback(scan_history_id) WHERE scan_history_id IS NOT NULL;` and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_auto_tag_dismissals_scan_id ON auto_tag_dismissals(scan_id);` in the performance-index block at instrumentation.ts:1584. Then add plain indexes for password_reset_tokens(user_id), email_verification_tokens(user_id), sessions(impersonated_by), support_ticket_messages(author_user_id) and teams(owner_id). For the remaining low-traffic bookkeeping columns (created_by, revoked_by, updated_by, awarded_by, sent_by, dismissed_by_user_id) use partial indexes `WHERE col IS NOT NULL` so they stay small. Adding these is also the cheapest way to bound the cost of the transaction in lib/database/cleanup.ts.

findings.title: Account deletion leaves the user's free-text feedback notes, the URLs they scanned, and their raw email address behind in two tables the deletion path never touches
findings.description: lib/auth/account-deletion.ts's docstring (:3-15) calls the function "the single, exhaustive list of DELETEs that make up 'permanently erase this account's data'" and it is the only definition both delete paths use (app/api/v3/account/delete/route.ts:91 and app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:2000). Two tables holding that user's data are not in it. (1) `scan_finding_feedback`: user_id is `REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE SET NULL` (instrumentation.ts:1459), so a deletion nulls the owner and leaves the row, which still carries `finding_url` (the exact URL the user scanned, frequently their own domain) and `notes`, free text the user typed in the feedback dialog (written at app/api/v3/scan/feedback/route.ts:56-70). The rows persist until CLEANUP_SCAN_FINDING_FEEDBACK_RETENTION_DAYS expires, which defaults to 90 (lib/config/config-values.ts:1348) counted from the feedback's own created_at, not from the deletion. The same file already recognised this exact shape for ai_conversations and added an explicit DELETE for it with a comment saying "A GDPR erasure must remove it now" (account-deletion.ts:117-124), and did not apply the same reasoning here. (2) `email_logs.recipient VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL` (instrumentation.ts:673) stores every recipient address in clear, written by lib/email/email.ts's sendEmail on every send. It has no user_id and no FK, so nothing links it to the deleted account and nothing purges it; it survives for CLEANUP_EMAIL_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS, default 30 (config-values.ts:1347). Contrast admin_audit_log, where the same risk was handled properly: target_user_id is de-identified at account-deletion.ts:139 and any email embedded in `details` is masked at write time by redactEmailsInDetails (lib/auth/authorization.ts:221-226).
findings.impact: After a user exercises their right to erasure, up to 90 days of their free-text notes and the list of hostnames they scanned remain queryable, and up to 30 days of their email address remains in email_logs, readable by any staff member through Admin > System > Email Logs. The privacy policy and the deletion confirmation email both present deletion as complete. The scan_finding_feedback rows are also no longer reachable through any user-facing path, so a later data-subject request cannot even find them to confirm.
findings.recommendation: In lib/auth/account-deletion.ts, add `DELETE FROM scan_finding_feedback WHERE user_id = $1` next to the ai_conversations delete at :122, using the same reasoning its comment already states. If the aggregate learning signal must survive, keep the row but null the identifying payload instead: `UPDATE scan_finding_feedback SET notes = NULL, finding_url = '' WHERE user_id = $1` before the FK nulls user_id, so only (finding_id, verdict) is retained, which is all lib/scanner/regression-alert.ts and the engine-feedback admin panel actually aggregate. For email_logs, add `DELETE FROM email_logs WHERE recipient = $1` using the email captured before the purge (app/api/v3/account/delete/route.ts:76 already captures it for the notification), or store a hash of the recipient rather than the address.

findings.title: components/admin/config.ts is a graveyard of superseded copies: its tab table lists 5 of the panel's 13 tabs and its action-label map is a stale subset of one inlined in app/admin/page.tsx
findings.category: superseded dead code that still looks authoritative
findings.description: Four of the eight exports in components/admin/config.ts are dead, and each has a live replacement that was inlined into app/admin/page.tsx instead of being edited here. (1) ADMIN_TABS (declared line 7, block 6-17) declares five tabs: users, teams, notifications, admins, audit. The live tab set is built at app/admin/page.tsx:861 as ALL_ADMIN_TABS by flattening NAV_GROUPS, and it drives every render path: the nav at :1004 and :1077, the header at :1036, the role-fallback redirect at :889-892, and the per-tab render switch at :1182-1187, which alone names access-rules, blocked-data, content, security-alerts, settings and broadcast. (2) ACTION_LABELS (declared line 262, block 261-288) maps 25 admin action names to success-toast text. app/admin/page.tsx:530-561 declares a local const labels with the same 25 entries verbatim plus six more (notify_account_changes, toggle_ai_ban, verify_email, unverify_email, send_notification, send_email) and uses it at :566 via showToast(labels[action] || 'Action completed.'). The exported copy is a stale subset. (3) DEFAULT_AUDIT_PAGE_SIZE and DEFAULT_STAFF_PAGE_SIZE (lines 330-331), replaced by the inline literal in useState(10) at app/admin/page.tsx:210. DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE on line 329 is also unreferenced but shares a name with the live CONFIG_PAGINATION_DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE, so I left it out of the count. The four names occur nowhere in the repo but their own declarations; config.ts is imported four times and only for ACTION_META and PASSWORD_GATED_ACTIONS. The same pattern appears one file over: parseAdminHash and buildAdminHash at components/admin/utils.ts:234-269 parse and build '#users/user-12' hashes for a hash-routing scheme the panel abandoned; state now goes to query params through updateUrlWithUser at app/admin/page.tsx:255-274, which calls setQueryParam/setQueryParams. Neither helper has a caller anywhere, including tests, and parseAdminHash:246 hardcodes the same stale five-tab whitelist. Total: 42 lines in config.ts (6-17, 261-288, 330-331) plus 36 lines in utils.ts (234-269), 78 lines.
findings.impact: A developer adding an admin tab or a new admin action reaches for components/admin/config.ts, the file literally named 'Admin panel configuration - tabs, action metadata, filters', edits ADMIN_TABS or ACTION_LABELS, and nothing happens: the real copies are inline in app/admin/page.tsx. Adding a label to ACTION_LABELS is the likeliest version of this, because a new admin action needs one and the map here looks like the place. The result is a new action that silently falls back to the generic 'Action completed.' toast. The same trap catches anyone adding a deep link, who will find and extend parseAdminHash rather than updateUrlWithUser. This is dead code that is actively misleading, not merely unused.
findings.recommendation: Pick one direction and apply it to the whole file. Preferred: move the live copies down into components/admin/config.ts, that is, replace the local labels const at app/admin/page.tsx:530-561 with an import of ACTION_LABELS after adding its six missing entries, and move ALL_ADMIN_TABS/NAV_GROUPS out of app/admin/page.tsx:861 into ADMIN_TABS with the full 13-tab set. Otherwise delete ADMIN_TABS (6-17) with its now-unused lucide-react and AdminTab imports on lines 3-4, ACTION_LABELS (261-288), and lines 330-331. Separately delete parseAdminHash and buildAdminHash (components/admin/utils.ts:234-269) either way, since query-param routing has no use for them.

findings.title: Severity ordering is redeclared in nine private tables under three mutually incompatible numeric conventions, two of which share the identifier SEVERITY_RANK, and the info label already differs between the app and the ~750 public /checks pages
findings.description:
There is a canonical severity ordering: SEVERITY_PRIORITY at lib/config/constants.ts:628 (critical 5, high 4, medium 3, low 2, info 1), consumed with a `b - a` comparator by components/scanner/results-list.tsx:335, app/api/v3/demo-scan/route.ts:236, app/api/v3/scan/bulk/route.ts:252 and app/api/v3/scan/authenticated/route.ts:427. Eight further private tables encode the same idea:

Convention A, critical is 5 down to info is 1 (same as canonical): lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:18 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:37 `SEVERITY_RANK`.
Convention B, critical is 0 up to info is 4 (inverted): lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:47 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:136 `SEVERITY_RANK`, lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:78 `SEVERITY_ORDER`, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 `SEVERITY_ORDER`.
Convention C, info is 0 up to critical is 4 (a third numbering): lib/scanner/software-inventory.ts:715 `SEVERITY_RANK`.

So the identifier `SEVERITY_RANK` means three different things in five files, and the comparator direction flips with it: compliance-report.ts:150 sorts `severityRank(b) - severityRank(a)` while scan-summary.ts:77 and auto-tag-suggest.ts:166 sort `severityRank(a) - severityRank(b)`, and both are correct only for their own table. Lifting either constant into a shared module, or copying a comparator between these files, silently reverses the ordering with no type error, because every table is `Record<Severity, number>`.

The name `SEVERITY_ORDER` is separately overloaded: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:12 exports it as `readonly Severity[]` (consumed by six other components: results-list.tsx:345, dashboard.tsx:428, ai-choice-modal.tsx:154, ai-verify-result-modal.tsx:60, repos/page.tsx:49 and github-scan-result-modal.tsx:59), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:23 declares another `Severity[]`, and execute-scan.ts:78 / execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 declare it as a numeric Record.

The label layer has already drifted user-visibly. components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx:71 (SEVERITY_TONE), lib/reports/markdown-report.ts:31 and lib/reports/compliance-report.ts:29 all label the lowest level "Info". lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:25 labels it "Informational", and that is the SeverityPill rendered on app/checks/[id]/page.tsx and app/tools/api-scanner/page.tsx, which is the ~750-page public SEO surface. There are also two different components exported as `SeverityPill` (components/history/severity-pill.tsx:11, which delegates to severityTone(), and lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:41, which inlines its own hsl alphas of 0.1/0.25 against SEVERITY_TONE's /15 and /40), plus four colour maps: components/scanner/severity-badge.tsx SEVERITY_TONE, components/docs/docs-types.ts:75 SEVERITY_COLORS, lib/reports/pdf-report.ts:18 SEVERITY_COLORS as RGB tuples, and lib/config/client-constants.ts:304 SEVERITY_COLORS, which has zero consumers.
findings.impact: Today: the same info-severity finding reads "Info" in the product and "Informational" on the public check pages, and the same severity pill has two different tints depending on which surface renders it. Tomorrow: a developer who consolidates `SEVERITY_RANK` (a natural cleanup, since the name is already shared) or copies a working comparator between two of these files inverts a sort with no compile error, and findings list least-severe-first in a report, an AI summary, or the dedupe winner selection. lib/scanner/dedupe.ts:175 uses its rank to pick which duplicate finding survives, so an inversion there would keep the info-level copy and discard the critical one.
findings.recommendation: Put one table in lib/config/client-constants.ts next to SEVERITY_LEVELS: keep SEVERITY_PRIORITY's convention (critical highest) and export both it and the ordered array. Delete the seven private tables and rewrite each comparator to `PRIORITY[b.severity] - PRIORITY[a.severity]`, checking each one's direction as you go (lib/ai/scan-summary.ts:77, lib/ai/auto-tag-suggest.ts:166, lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:712, lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:220 and :585 all currently sort ascending against an inverted table). Rename lib/scanner/execute-scan.ts:78 and lib/scanner/execute-crawl-scan.ts:73 out of the way first so `SEVERITY_ORDER` unambiguously means the array. Move SEVERITY_TONE's labels to that same module and have lib/seo/seo-ui.tsx:25 read them so "Info" is one string, and delete the unconsumed lib/config/client-constants.ts:304 SEVERITY_COLORS.

findings.title: Two auth crypto primitives are copy-pasted rather than shared: generateBackupCodes exists verbatim in both 2FA routes with its security rationale already diverged, and the HMAC signed-token sign/verify pair is duplicated across pending-2fa and ipv4-echo-token with two different freshness contracts
findings.description:
generateBackupCodes is defined identically in app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:22 and app/api/v3/auth/2fa/backup-codes/route.ts:11: same `count = 8`, same `crypto.randomBytes(10)`, same hex/uppercase, same XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX-XXXXX split. Both carry a copy of the comment recording a prior hardening ("10 bytes (80 bits) per code. The previous `randomBytes(4)` (32 bits) is below NIST 800-63B guidance for backup verification codes"), and the comment itself has already drifted: the setup.ts copy adds "The 2FA verify endpoint rate-limits to 5 attempts per 5 minutes per user+IP, so 32-bit codes were computationally in scope" and the backup-codes.ts copy does not. Nothing links the two, so a future change to code length, alphabet, or count applies to enrolment or to regeneration but not both, and the two paths would then mint differently shaped codes into the same column.

Separately, lib/auth/pending-2fa.ts and lib/auth/ipv4-echo-token.ts each implement the whole signed-token primitive: signingKey() reading and length-checking API_KEY_ENCRYPTION_KEY (pending-2fa.ts:24, ipv4-echo-token.ts:24), computeTag() as HMAC-SHA256 over `${HMAC_DOMAIN}.${payloadB64}` with the same codeql suppression comment (pending-2fa.ts:34, ipv4-echo-token.ts:34), and a verify half that splits on the last dot, length-checks, timingSafeEquals the tag and base64url-JSON-decodes the payload (pending-2fa.ts:59-77, ipv4-echo-token.ts:66-92). ipv4-echo-token.ts:17 states the relationship outright: "Format mirrors lib/auth/pending-2fa.ts: base64url(json).base64url(hmac)." Only the domain string differs, and the two have already diverged on their security contract: verifyIpv4Token enforces max-age and a clock-skew floor inline (ipv4-echo-token.ts:88-90), while verifyPendingToken enforces no freshness at all and delegates it to callers (pending-2fa.ts:57).
findings.impact: A fix to either primitive is applied to one site and silently missed on the other. For generateBackupCodes that means one of the two 2FA paths keeps weaker codes after the next hardening. For the token pair it means a padding, canonicalization, or replay fix to one signed-token format leaves the other exposed, and the split freshness contract is exactly the kind of asymmetry that produces a replay window: any new caller of verifyPendingToken that forgets its own `ts` check gets an eternally valid token, while the identically shaped ipv4 token cannot be replayed past 120 seconds.
findings.recommendation: Move generateBackupCodes into lib/auth/ (next to the existing 2FA helpers) and import it in both app/api/v3/auth/2fa/setup/route.ts:22 and app/api/v3/auth/2fa/backup-codes/route.ts:11. Extract the signed-token primitive into one module, for example lib/auth/signed-token.ts exporting `sign(domain, payload)` and `verify(domain, token, { maxAgeMs })`, and rewrite lib/auth/pending-2fa.ts and lib/auth/ipv4-echo-token.ts as thin domain-specific wrappers over it; make maxAgeMs required so a new caller cannot accidentally get the no-freshness behaviour.

findings.title: The documented 1 MiB request-body cap lives inside parseBody, which only 19 of the 73 body-reading routes use; the other 54 call request.json() directly and there is no global limit behind them
findings.category: guard applied to a subset of siblings
findings.description:
lib/api/api-utils.ts:170-176 documents the cap as a deliberate fix: "L-10: Hard cap on JSON request bodies. Without this, a client can send a multi-GB JSON body that the server will buffer before rejecting. 1 MiB is more than enough for our route shapes." It is enforced only inside parseBody (lib/api/api-utils.ts:181-228), which checks content-length against MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES at :188-196 before calling request.json().

I split every route.ts under app/api by which one it uses. 19 files call parseBody, 54 call `request.json()` or `req.json()` directly, and the two sets do not overlap at all. The 19 are almost entirely under app/api/v3/auth/, app/api/v3/account/, plus keys, browser/sessions, admin/staff-invites and admin/updater/apply, which is the shape of a fix applied by directory and never extended. The 54 include the whole scan surface (app/api/v3/scan/route.ts, scan/bulk, scan/crawl, scan/verify-batch, scan/import-spec, scan/remediation/bulk), the whole teams and support-ticket surface, app/api/v3/admin/route.ts, app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts, app/api/v3/domains/route.ts, and the two contact forms.

There is no backstop underneath them: I checked next.config.mjs and middleware.ts and neither sets a body size limit, and Next.js App Router route handlers have no default one (the Pages Router's 1 MB bodyParser limit does not apply). app/api/v3/account/unsubscribe/route.ts is in PUBLIC_PATHS (lib/config/public-paths.ts:178) and reads its body raw, so at least one uncapped route is reachable with no session.
findings.impact: Any signed-in account (signup is open) can POST an arbitrarily large JSON body to app/api/v3/scan/route.ts or any of the other 53 routes and the server buffers it in memory before any validation runs. On a deployment sized for ~50 users, a few concurrent multi-hundred-megabyte bodies are enough to OOM the process. The narrower and more likely cost is maintenance: the cap is written down as a security requirement in one helper that 74% of the body-reading routes do not go through, so the requirement is not actually a property of the API.
findings.recommendation: Do not try to convert 54 handlers. Add the content-length check to middleware.ts for any request to /api/ with a method that carries a body, using the same MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES value exported from lib/api/api-utils.ts, and return 413 there. Then parseBody's own check becomes a redundant second line rather than the only one, and a new route cannot opt out by forgetting to call it.

findings.title: The relative-time consolidation missed three call sites, and two of them reintroduce verbatim the exact two defects the shared module's own doc comment says it was written to fix
findings.description:
lib/ui/relative-time.ts:22-31 documents a completed consolidation and names the defects it removed: "The single source for this format: previously ~10 near-identical copies had drifted (some read '0m ago' instead of 'just now', one never fell back to a date and read '92d ago' forever, and the date fallback varied between 'Aug 12' and '8/12/2026')." formatRelativeTime (:32-52) is the survivor, re-exported through components/admin/utils.ts:123 and components/assets/assets-types.ts:25 with "Canonical relative-time formatter" comments.

Three files still hand-roll it, and two of them are the two named defects:

1. components/admin/features/support-inbox.tsx:68 `timeAgo` ends at `return \`${Math.round(hrs / 24)}d ago\`` with no date fallback. That is the "read '92d ago' forever" bug, restored.
2. components/contact/support-tickets.tsx:65 `timeAgo` falls back at 30 days to `new Date(iso).toLocaleDateString()`, which renders "8/12/2026". That is the "varied between 'Aug 12' and '8/12/2026'" bug, restored; the canonical formatter falls back at 7 days to `toLocaleDateString("en-US", { month: "short", day: "numeric" })`, i.e. "Aug 12".

These two render the same objects. support-inbox.tsx is the staff view of a support ticket and support-tickets.tsx is the user's view of the same ticket, so one ticket's "last activity" reads "412d ago" to staff and "8/12/2026" to the user. The same pair also duplicates STATUS_STYLES and StatusBadge (support-inbox.tsx:79, support-tickets.tsx:89, identical bodies).

3. components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:92 defines a private `formatAge` even though lib/ui/relative-time.ts:8 exports one, and lib/ui/relative-time.ts:2-4 names this very component as its consumer: "shared by the result panels that show freshness (subdomain discovery, DNS records, port sweep). Matches the wording SubdomainDiscovery introduced." The two sibling panels do import it (components/scanner/port-scan-panel.tsx:22, components/scanner/dns-records-panel.tsx:24), and subdomain-discovery.tsx:22 imports formatRefreshAvailability from that same module in the same statement while shadowing formatAge. The bodies are currently identical, so this one is a live divergence risk rather than a current bug. A third, unrelated `formatAge(ageMs: number | null)` exists at components/admin/features/queue-status-utils.ts:41, so the name means two things.
findings.impact: Staff triaging the support inbox see ages like "412d ago" that are unreadable as dates, on the one screen where knowing when a ticket last moved matters. The same ticket shows the user a different format. Beyond that, the consolidation is not actually done: the module presents itself as the single source and is not, so the next timestamp change is applied once and misses three screens, exactly as it did the last time.
findings.recommendation: Delete components/admin/features/support-inbox.tsx:68 and components/contact/support-tickets.tsx:65 and import formatRelativeTime from @/lib/ui/relative-time in both. Delete components/scanner/subdomain-discovery.tsx:92 and use the exported formatAge already imported alongside formatRefreshAvailability at :22. Rename components/admin/features/queue-status-utils.ts:41 to formatAgeMs so the name is unambiguous. Hoist the shared StatusBadge and STATUS_STYLES out of the two support components into components/contact/ or a shared module.

findings.title: Three credit-checkout components and three checkout pages are functionally identical except for the server-action names, roughly 1,900 duplicated lines, and a focus-ring fix has already landed on only one of the three pages
findings.category: N components doing the same job
findings.description:
components/billing/ai-credit-checkout.tsx (391 lines), components/billing/github-credit-checkout.tsx (378) and components/billing/browserbase-credit-checkout.tsx (380) are the same component three times. Stripping comments and normalising the product word, ai vs github diffs in 40 lines and every one of them is a rename: createAiCreditPaymentIntent vs createCreditPaymentIntent, confirmAiCreditPurchase vs confirmCreditPurchase, AiCreditTier vs CreditTier, useConfirmAiCreditPurchase vs useConfirmCreditPurchase, AiCreditCheckout vs CreditCheckout. There is no behavioural difference at all. ai vs browserbase diffs in 85 lines, again all renames plus the unit pair (tokens/balance vs minutes/balanceSeconds). Four sub-components are exact duplicates across the set: PaymentFormSkeleton in all four billing checkouts including stripe-checkout.tsx:23, PendingStatus in the three credit ones, ConfirmingStatus and VerifiedStatus in two each.

The files say so themselves. ai-credit-checkout.tsx:24-29: "Copied verbatim from components/billing/stripe-checkout.tsx's own PaymentFormSkeleton ... Kept as its own copy instead of an import so this file never has to touch the subscription checkout flow it's deliberately not modifying." github-credit-checkout.tsx:24-26 then copies that comment and points at ai-credit-checkout instead, so the chain of copies is three deep.

The pages are the same story: app/checkout/credits/page.tsx (254), app/checkout/github-credits/page.tsx (253) and app/checkout/browser-credits/page.tsx (256) diff in 60 lines, nearly all the tier catalog name and the redirect path. Drift has already started: the "Back to Billing" link on app/checkout/github-credits/page.tsx:124 carries `focus-visible:ring-inset` and the byte-identical link on app/checkout/credits/page.tsx:122 and app/checkout/browser-credits/page.tsx:126 does not, so the same control has a different focus ring depending on which credit you are buying. All three files apply that same class correctly on their tier buttons (credits:167, github-credits:166, browser-credits:169), which is what makes the back link the one that was missed.
findings.impact: Every change to the payment flow has to be made three times in the components and three times in the pages, and the focus-ring divergence shows that in practice it is made once. This is the money path: a retry-schedule change, a Stripe API bump, an error-message fix, or a PCI-relevant change to how card details are validated before a PaymentIntent is created will ship to one credit product and not the other two, and there is no test or type that would catch it. It is also roughly 1,900 lines of the 65,147-line components tree carrying no distinct behaviour.
findings.recommendation: Collapse the three components into one `CreditCheckout` in components/billing/ that takes the two server actions and the tier type as props or a small config object (`{ createIntent, confirmPurchase, unitLabel, formatBalance }`), and keep the three thin wrappers only if the call sites need distinct names. Hoist PaymentFormSkeleton, ConfirmingStatus, PendingStatus and VerifiedStatus into components/billing/checkout-parts.tsx and have stripe-checkout.tsx use them too. Do the same for the three pages with a shared `CreditCheckoutPage` that takes the tier catalog and the route slug. Start with the four sub-components, which are pure and carry no product-specific logic at all.

findings.title: Sixteen modal overlays are hand-rolled instead of using components/ui/dialog, and the accessibility behaviour Radix would give free is present on only three of them, including two hand-rolled modals in the same admin directory as dialog-based ones
findings.category: two primitives doing the same job
findings.description:
components/ui/dialog.tsx wraps Radix Dialog and is imported by 18 files (components/scanner/share-modal.tsx, components/repos/github-repo-picker-modal.tsx, components/modals/premium-upgrade-modal.tsx, components/admin/features/mass-email-manager.tsx, components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx and so on). components/ui/alert-dialog.tsx adds 10 more. Radix supplies focus trap, focus restore on close, Escape-to-close, aria-modal + role=dialog, a portal, and body scroll lock.

Sixteen other components build the overlay by hand with a `fixed inset-0` div and no import from the dialog family. I checked each for the four behaviours Radix would have provided:

  components/admin/features/engine-feedback-manager.tsx:838   role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/admin/features/ip-rules-manager.tsx:273          role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/admin/staff/staff-list.tsx:290 and :634          role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/admin/teams/teams-list.tsx:168                   role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/admin/users/gift-subscription-modal.tsx:66       role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx:1534        role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/scanner/crawl-url-selector.tsx:98                role no, aria-modal no, Escape no, scroll lock no
  components/modals/tos-modal.tsx:231                         role no, aria-modal no, Escape no (deliberate, see :163), scroll lock no
  components/scanner/ai-choice-modal.tsx:36                   role yes, aria-modal yes, Escape no, scroll lock no
