  components/admin/shared/admin-mobile-toc.tsx                role yes, aria-modal yes, Escape yes, scroll lock no
  components/docs/docs-mobile-nav.tsx                         role yes, aria-modal yes, Escape yes, scroll lock no

Not one of the sixteen locks body scroll. The split runs straight through single directories: components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx uses Dialog while components/admin/users/gift-subscription-modal.tsx next to it hand-rolls one, and components/admin/features/mass-email-manager.tsx uses Dialog while components/admin/features/ip-rules-manager.tsx does not.
findings.impact: Seven admin and billing modals cannot be dismissed with Escape, do not announce themselves as dialogs to a screen reader, and let keyboard focus tab out into the page behind them, including the gift-subscription modal and the staff-invite modal, which are destructive admin actions. Every one of them also scrolls the page underneath on mobile because no overlay locks the body. Because the behaviour depends on which of the two primitives a component happened to pick, an accessibility fix applied to ui/dialog reaches 28 call sites and misses 16, and each of the 16 has to be fixed by hand.
findings.recommendation: Migrate the nine true modal dialogs (engine-feedback-manager, ip-rules-manager, staff-list x2, teams-list, gift-subscription-modal, profile-billing-tab, crawl-url-selector, ai-choice-modal) onto components/ui/dialog.tsx. Start with components/admin/users/gift-subscription-modal.tsx, which sits beside a Dialog-based sibling and is the smallest. Leave admin-mobile-toc, docs-mobile-nav, chat-widget, tos-gate, notification-center, site-notifications and onboarding-tour, which are drawers, banners and coach marks rather than modal dialogs, but add the body scroll lock to the drawers.

findings.title: Extends AUDIT-012#obs-09 with the success-shape half: GET responses use four different envelopes, three routes return a bare array, one paginated route names its count totalTeams while its three siblings use total, and lib/api/client.ts is imported by 2 files while 94 call fetch directly
findings.description:
AUDIT-012#obs-09 inventoried the ERROR shapes (five of them, 117 of 155 routes bypassing ApiResponse/withErrorHandling). It did not cover the success side or the client side. I extracted the last success return from every GET handler in app/api (56 of them) and grouped them.

Envelopes in use:
  1. Named-key object, the majority: `{ shares }`, `{ teams }`, `{ tickets }`, `{ notifications }`, `{ feedback }`, `{ teammates }`, `{ invitations }`, `{ remediation }`, `{ summaries }`, `{ repos }`.
  2. Bare array, no envelope: app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:60 (`result.rows`), app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:42 (`result.rows`), app/api/v3/badge/scans/route.ts (`scans`). A client cannot add a sibling field to these without a breaking change.
  3. `{ success: true, data: {...} }`: app/api/v3/checkout/verify-subscription/route.ts. Nothing else uses it, and app/api/v3/finding-types/route.ts uses `{ success: false, error }` for its failure but a bare object for its success, so `success` is not a reliable discriminator anywhere.
  4. Flat top-level fields with no envelope at all: app/api/v3/billing/route.ts, app/api/v3/config/client/route.ts, app/api/version/route.ts, app/api/v3/health/route.ts.

Pagination envelope keys diverge on one route: app/api/v3/admin/content/route.ts, app/api/v3/admin/email-logs/route.ts and app/api/v3/admin/error-logs/route.ts all return `{ <items>, page, totalPages, total }`, and app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:71 returns `totalTeams` instead of `total` for the identical concept. components/admin/features/content-manager.tsx:107 reads `data.total || 0` to drive its "N total" footer; that pattern silently renders 0 against the teams endpoint, which is why components/admin/teams/teams-list.tsx:646 only consumes totalPages and drops the count. app/api/v3/admin/route.ts returns `total` with no page/totalPages at all.

The query-parameter side is, for the record, consistent: all seven paginated routes take `page` and `limit`, no route uses offset or cursor, so there is nothing to fix there.

On the client, lib/api/client.ts:44-49 is the shared reader that normalises `errorData.error` and falls back to the literal `API error: <status>`. It is imported by exactly 2 files under app/ and components/, while 94 files call `fetch(` directly and each re-implements its own `data.error || "Something went wrong"` handling. So the normalisation obs-09 recommends adopting has no adoption to build on.
findings.impact: Every new client call site has to discover, per endpoint, whether the payload is the array itself, a named key, `data`, or flat fields, and whether the count is `total` or `totalTeams`. That is why the teams list drops its result count and why 94 files each carry their own error-unwrapping block. The three bare-array endpoints (schedules, webhooks, badge/scans) cannot gain pagination or a count without breaking their callers. Documented in app/docs/api, these inconsistencies are also the public API surface, so third-party integrators hit them too.
findings.recommendation: Pick the named-key envelope as canonical, since it is already the majority, and write it down in app/docs/api. Fix the three cheap deviants first: wrap app/api/v3/schedules/route.ts:60 and app/api/v3/webhooks/route.ts:42 as `{ schedules }` / `{ webhooks }` (both have exactly one client each, in components/profile/tabs/developer/), rename app/api/v3/admin/teams/route.ts:71 `totalTeams` to `total`, and convert app/api/v3/checkout/verify-subscription/route.ts off the lone `{ success, data }` shape. Then extend lib/api/client.ts to return the unwrapped payload and migrate call sites by directory, starting with components/profile/ where nine of them already duplicate the same error block.

findings.title: app/actions/stripe.ts, the 220-statement checkout and credit-purchase server-action surface, is at 56.36% statements and 53.79% branches
findings.description: Measured: app/actions/stripe.ts is 56.36% statements, 53.79% branches, 53.33% functions over 220 statements, the largest under-60% file in the billing area. It imports from lib/billing/browserbase-usage (line 21) and is the entry point users hit to start a checkout and to buy AI, GitHub-review, and Browserbase credit packs. The lower-level catalogs and usage modules around it are all at or near 100% (catalog.ts 100%, ai-credit-catalog.ts 100%, browserbase-credit-catalog.ts 100%, github-credit-catalog.ts 100%, stripe-catalog.ts 100%, plan-limits.ts 100%), so as with the updater in cov-06 the pattern is well-tested primitives with an untested orchestrator. Nearly half the branches are the error, already-subscribed, wrong-plan, and mismatched-currency arms that decide what the user is actually charged for.
findings.impact: Roughly half the decision points on the path that creates a Stripe checkout session are unexercised. A regression in a branch that picks the price id or the quantity charges the wrong amount, and the failure is only visible once a customer complains or the operator reconciles Stripe by hand.
findings.recommendation: Add tests/app/actions/stripe.test.ts with the Stripe SDK mocked, asserting one case per branch that selects a price or quantity: each credit pack maps to its catalog price id, a user already on the target plan is rejected rather than double-charged, an unknown pack id is rejected, and a Stripe API error surfaces as a handled error rather than a thrown server action.

findings.title: lib/scanner/checks/host-validation.ts is at 42.98% branches and lib/scanner/checks/dns.ts at 34.14% functions, the two weakest branch numbers among real (non-placeholder) scanner checks
findings.description: Measured across the 101 files in lib/scanner: the scanner is the best-covered part of the codebase overall, and only two real check modules fall meaningfully short. lib/scanner/checks/host-validation.ts is 62.77% statements / 42.98% branches / 88.88% functions over 180 statements, meaning most functions are entered but well over half their conditional arms never run. lib/scanner/checks/dns.ts is 65.51% statements / 86.04% branches / 34.14% functions, the inverse shape: two thirds of its functions are never called at all. Neighbouring modules for comparison sit in the high 80s and 90s. lib/scanner/host-reputation.ts (47.82%) and lib/scanner/scan-target-classify.ts (37.14% statements / 16% branches) are also low; the latter is imported directly by components/scanner/scan-form.tsx:50 and is the module the extension keeps a duplicate copy of.
findings.impact: Branches in a detection module are the conditions under which a finding is or is not emitted. An unexercised arm that stops emitting is the worst failure this product has, because the user sees a completed scan with fewer findings and no error, and reasonably concludes the host is clean. host-validation in particular decides which hosts a scan is allowed to touch, so its unexercised arms also carry an access-control component.
findings.recommendation: Work from the branch report rather than the statement report: run npm run test:coverage and open the HTML report for these two files, then add a case per uncovered arm to tests/lib/scanner/checks/host-validation.test.ts and dns.test.ts. Prioritise arms that decide whether a finding is emitted over arms that only shape a message. For scan-target-classify.ts, add a shared URL fixture table (search-engine hosts, query-param variants, redirect cases) asserted against both the app copy and the extension copy, which also closes the drift risk noted in cov-14.

findings.title: Fifteen API routes have no test file at all, including both LLM discovery endpoints, the admin content route, and three routes that stream binary screenshots
findings.description: Mapping all 157 route.ts files against tests/app/ shows 142 with a corresponding test and 15 without: app/api/security-txt, app/api/v3/admin/content (61 statements, 0% coverage), app/api/v3/admin/updater/apply (covered separately in cov-06), app/api/v3/admin/updater/status, app/api/v3/ai/conversations (50 statements, 0%), app/api/v3/ai/info, app/api/v3/config/client, app/api/v3/finding-types, app/api/v3/openapi.json, app/api/v3/scan/discover/progress/[requestId], app/api/v3/scan/screenshot/[id] (16 statements, 0%), app/api/v3/shared/[token]/screenshot (14 statements, 0%), app/api/version, app/llms.txt (62 statements, 0%), and app/llms-full.txt (31 statements, 0%). Coverage confirms every one of them at 0%. Two are worth separating from the rest: app/api/v3/admin/content is a 61-statement admin mutation surface with no gate test, and the two screenshot routes serve stored scan artefacts addressed by a scan id and a share token respectively, which is the shape prior audits repeatedly found cross-tenant IDOR in (AUDIT-010 and the AUDIT-2 remediation both fixed one).
findings.impact: For the two screenshot routes the concrete risk is an ownership check that regresses and lets one user fetch another user's scan screenshot by id, exactly the class of bug two prior audits already fixed elsewhere in this codebase. For admin/content it is an admin gate with no test. For llms.txt and llms-full.txt it is lower stakes, but the memory notes AI crawlers already have trouble discovering this project, so a route that silently starts 500ing is a real if quiet loss.
findings.recommendation: Add route tests in priority order. First the two screenshot routes: assert 401 unauthenticated, 403 or 404 for a scan belonging to another user, 404 for an unknown share token, and 200 with the right content type for the owner. Then app/api/v3/admin/content: assert 403 for a non-admin on every exported method. Then a single smoke test covering llms.txt, llms-full.txt, openapi.json, api/version, security-txt, config/client, ai/info, and finding-types that asserts each returns 200 with the expected content type, which is cheap and catches a route that stops rendering.

findings.title: CLI has one 81-line test for 254 lines of source, and marketing/ has none, leaving the two smaller packages effectively unverified
findings.description: cli/ is a standalone dependency-free Node package excluded from the app's tsc, eslint, and vitest, with its own `node --test` suite that CI does run (.github/workflows/ci.yml, 'Run CLI unit tests'). The suite is one file, cli/vulnradar.test.mjs at 81 lines, against cli/lib.mjs (136 lines) plus cli/vulnradar.mjs (118 lines). No coverage is collected for it, so the tested fraction is unknown, but 81 lines of test against 254 lines of source that includes argument parsing, API-key handling, and output formatting is thin. marketing/ is a separate Remotion project with its own package.json and node_modules and no test setup or CI job at all; that is defensible for a video project and is noted for completeness rather than as an action item.
findings.impact: The CLI is a published entry point that carries a user's API key. A regression in argument parsing or in how the key is read and sent is caught only if it happens to break the single existing suite. The blast radius is smaller than the extension's (cov-14) because a CLI fix ships immediately with no store review.
findings.recommendation: Add `--experimental-test-coverage` to the CLI's test script so the number is at least visible, then extend cli/vulnradar.test.mjs to cover each subcommand's argument parsing, the missing-API-key path, a non-200 API response, and the JSON versus human output formats. Leave marketing/ as is.

findings.title: vitest collects only .test.ts, so a .test.tsx file is silently never run, and with no DOM environment or testing-library dependency no component can be rendered in a test at all
findings.description: vitest.config.ts:24 sets `include: ["tests/**/*.test.ts", "tests/**/*.spec.ts"]` and line 23 sets `environment: "node"`. Neither `.test.tsx` nor `.spec.tsx` is collected, and package.json declares no jsdom, happy-dom, @testing-library/react, or @testing-library/dom dependency (grep returns nothing for all four). Counted: tests/ holds 356 `.test.ts` files, 0 `.spec.ts`, and 0 `.test.tsx`. The 8 files under tests/components/ test only extracted pure helpers (queue-status-utils, settings-registry-utils, utils, danger-score-trend), not components. The mechanical failure: a contributor adds `tests/components/scanner/scan-form.test.tsx`, runs `npm test`, gets a normal green run with no warning that their file was not collected (vitest reports nothing about files outside `include`), and ships. Even a `.test.ts` file that imported a component would fail, since `environment: "node"` supplies no document.
findings.impact: Two effects. First, a contributor can believe they have shipped a test that has never run once, which is worse than no test. Second, none of the 266 .tsx files under components/ has any behavioural test, so hook state, conditional rendering, and event handlers are covered only by the typechecker. Given the AUDIT-011 critical finding was a UI regression (admin row actions invisible but still hit-testable on touch), that gap is the one most likely to recur.
findings.recommendation: Add `"tests/**/*.test.tsx"` and `"tests/**/*.spec.tsx"` to `include` in vitest.config.ts:24 so a .tsx suite cannot be silently skipped. If component tests are wanted, add jsdom plus @testing-library/react as devDependencies and set `environment` per file via the `// @vitest-environment jsdom` docblock rather than switching the whole suite off node.

findings.title: Fourteen tests assert only .not.toThrow(), and two of them name a behavioural contract the assertion never checks
findings.description:
A scripted pass over all 4,494 it/test blocks found 14 whose every expect matcher is `not.toThrow`. Most are honest ("does not throw on truncated markup"), but two claim a behaviour they do not verify. tests/lib/scanner/safety-rating.test.ts:215 is titled "falls back to a default weight for an unrecognized severity string" and its whole body is `expect(() => getDangerScore([{ severity: "unknown", title: "Something Odd" }])).not.toThrow()`. The fallback it names is lib/scanner/safety-rating.ts:327, `const baseWeight = SEVERITY_WEIGHTS[sev] ?? 0.1`. Exact mutation not caught: change `?? 0.1` to `?? 10` and the test passes, while every scan containing one finding with an unrecognised severity string jumps to the top of the danger scale and the site is reported unsafe. tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:103 is titled "does not create an element for an end tag with no matching start" and asserts only `expect(() => toElements(tokenize("

ok

"))).not.toThrow()`. Exact mutation not caught: make toElements emit an element for the stray ``, and the test passes while every page check that counts or walks elements sees a phantom node. The other 12 are: tests/lib/api/playground.test.ts:67, tests/lib/api/request-utils.test.ts:93, tests/lib/auth/password-hash.test.ts:45, tests/lib/backup/job-store.test.ts:53 and :57, tests/lib/database/error-log-capture.test.ts:87, tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:72 (filed separately as tq-03), tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:68, tests/lib/scanner/page-context.test.ts:144, tests/lib/scanner/scan-jobs.test.ts:155, tests/lib/ui/url-state.test.ts:66, tests/lib/updater/job-store.test.ts:52.
findings.impact: Two named contracts, the danger-score fallback weight and the tokenizer's stray-end-tag handling, have a test that reads as covering them in a coverage review but cannot fail on a wrong answer, only on a crash. The danger score is the number shown to users as the site's safety rating, so a wrong fallback weight is directly user visible.
findings.recommendation:
In tests/lib/scanner/safety-rating.test.ts:215, assert the score itself: compare `getDangerScore([{ severity: "unknown", ... }])` against the value implied by the 0.1 weight, and add a sibling case proving an unknown severity scores strictly below an info finding. In tests/lib/scanner/html/tokenizer.test.ts:103, assert `toElements(tokenize("

ok

")).map(e => e.tag)` equals `["p"]`. Leave the other 12 as they are; their titles match what they assert.

findings.title: Thirteen tests assert only that a value exists (toBeDefined / toBeTruthy / not.toBeNull) where the contract they name is the value's content
findings.description: Scripted over all 4,494 blocks: 13 have no assertion stronger than a positive-existence matcher. The ones where the content is the actual contract: tests/lib/scanner/checks-data/_schema.test.ts:77 "every entry has required fields" loops the required list (id, title, category, severity, description, evidence, fixSteps, codeExamples) and asserts `expect(entry[field]).toBeDefined()` at lines 90 to 93, so an entry shipped with `description: ""`, `fixSteps: []`, or `codeExamples: []` passes the only required-fields guard the whole 750-plus check catalogue has. tests/lib/scanner/auth/logout-guard.test.ts:63 "returns a non-secret reason for a destructive URL" asserts only `expect(reason).toBeTruthy()`, so a reason that does leak a credential or query string passes, even though the sibling test at :55 to :60 does run a `not.toMatch(/password|cookie=|token=/i)` check for a different URL. tests/lib/scanner/registry.test.ts:119 is titled "etag-inode uses the real headers.ts detector, not configuration.ts's disabled stub" but asserts the fired finding is defined rather than asserting its identity, the way the sibling tests at :107 and :128 do. Three worker suites (tests/lib/backup/scheduled-backup-worker.test.ts:102, tests/lib/domains/reverify-worker.test.ts:167, tests/lib/notifications/posture-digest.test.ts:331) each assert `toBeDefined` on "registers a timer and cleanly cancels it" without asserting the interval passed to setInterval or that cancel actually clears the same handle. The remaining cases are weaker in form than in substance: tests/lib/auth/password-strength.test.ts:355 and :363 end in `toBeDefined` but pin the text inside the preceding `.find(w => w.includes(...))`, and the four in tests/lib/auth/authorization.test.ts (:128, :146, :159, :228) use `not.toBeNull` as an allow/deny signal that the `it.each` at :95 already backs with an exact object comparison.
findings.impact: Each of these reads as covering a named behaviour but only fails if the code returns nothing at all. The _schema.test.ts:77 case is the widest: it is the single guard over the whole JSON check catalogue and it accepts empty strings and empty arrays for every required field, so a check shipped with a blank description or no fix steps reaches the ~750 public /checks SEO pages and the scan result UI with nothing to render.
findings.recommendation: Tighten the content assertions: in _schema.test.ts:77 replace `toBeDefined` with a non-empty check per field (a string field must be a non-empty string, fixSteps and codeExamples must be non-empty arrays); in logout-guard.test.ts:63 apply the same `not.toMatch(/password|cookie=|token=/i)` assertion the sibling test at :60 already uses; in registry.test.ts:119 assert the detector's identity the way :107 and :128 do; in the three worker suites assert the interval argument passed to setInterval and that clearInterval was called with the same handle.

findings.title: Sixty-five suites index mockQuery.mock.calls positionally while the real 30-second module-level settings cache decides whether a settings query lands in that list, so running a single test with -t can fail a test that passes in a full run
findings.description: lib/config/runtime-config.ts:64 caches the whole system_settings snapshot at module scope for TTL_MS = 30_000. Because vitest isolates per file but not per test, the first it() in a file that reaches a settings read issues a `SELECT key, value FROM system_settings` through the mocked pool and warms the snapshot; every later it() in the same file does not. Any test that then reads `mockQuery.mock.calls[0]` or `[1]` is reading a different call depending on which test ran first. Three suites document the hazard in their own comments and defend against it: tests/app/api/v3/shared/[token]/route.test.ts:30-38 ("whichever test first reaches the Promise.all in the route would warm it and silently change how many pool.query calls, and in what order, every later test makes"), tests/lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.test.ts:33-36, and tests/app/api/v3/history/route.test.ts:17-28, which intercepts the settings SQL inside the mock instead. 36 files call invalidateSettingsCache(). Counted: 65 files mock @/lib/database/db, do not mock @/lib/config/runtime-config, never call invalidateSettingsCache, never intercept the system_settings query, and do index mock.calls positionally. vitest.config.ts declares no setupFiles, so every suite has to remember this by hand.
findings.impact: Deterministic today only because vitest runs a file's tests in declaration order. The moment a developer narrows a run with `npx vitest run <file> -t "..."`, a different test warms the cache and the positional index points at the wrong query, producing a failure that does not reproduce in a full run. The same breaks if anyone enables sequence.shuffle or reorders tests during a refactor. The debugging cost is high because the failure looks like a real assertion failure about SQL.
findings.recommendation: Add `setupFiles: ["tests/_setup.ts"]` to the test block in vitest.config.ts and have that file call `invalidateSettingsCache()` in a global beforeEach, so the snapshot is cold for every test in every suite. That removes the hazard for all 191 DB-mocking suites at once and lets the three hand-written guards be deleted.

findings.title: Eight tests create concurrency overlap with real wall-clock sleeps instead of fake timers, in a runner the repo already documents as stalling under parallel load
findings.description: Only 12 of 356 test files use vi.useFakeTimers, and 7 use setSystemTime. Eight tests instead sleep on the real clock to let a concurrent operation interleave: tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts:63, :85, :87 (10ms each), tests/lib/scanner/scheduled-scans-worker.test.ts:465, :565 (5ms) and :494 (1ms), tests/lib/ai/verify-findings.test.ts:100 (5ms), tests/lib/scanner/protocols/banner-tls-and-capability.test.ts:328, :330 (10ms). The one with a real failure window is tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts:80, "admits a priority (paid-plan) waiter before a non-priority one queued earlier": it configures BROWSERBASE_QUEUE_MAX_WAIT_MS to 2000, parks two waiters behind two 10ms sleeps, then releases one slot and asserts `paidResult.acquired` is true. If the worker process stalls for more than two seconds anywhere between line 82 and line 89, both waiters time out and the assertion fails with a message about queue priority rather than about scheduling. That stall is not hypothetical here: tests/lib/scanner/engine.test.ts:65-70 records that the default 5s timeout "has been observed to flake under a full parallel suite run (267 files, heavy CPU contention across workers)", and vitest.config.ts:6-9 exists specifically because worker startup was failing intermittently under memory pressure. The suite has since grown from 267 to 356 files.
findings.impact: An intermittent red CI on a test whose failure message points at browserbase queue priority, not at the runner. That is the kind of failure that gets re-run rather than diagnosed, and repeated re-runs erode trust in the suite.
findings.recommendation: Convert tests/lib/browserbase/concurrency-queue.test.ts to vi.useFakeTimers with vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync, so the 2000ms wait window is simulated rather than raced. Where a real sleep is only draining microtasks (the setTimeout(resolve, 0) calls in tests/app/api/v3/scan/route.test.ts:433, tests/lib/scanner/execute-scan.test.ts:529 and friends), leave them: those are deterministic because pending microtasks always drain before a macrotask.

findings.title: The Dockerfile and package.json both document an npm allow-scripts whitelist that does not exist: .npmrc has no such setting and npm has no allowScripts field
findings.description: Dockerfile:19-24 says: '--ignore-scripts prevents transitive postinstall scripts from running during image build. Native deps (sharp, esbuild, unrs-resolver, core-js) are whitelisted in .npmrc so they DO run via npm's `allow-scripts` mechanism.' Three parts of that are wrong. (1) The whole of .npmrc is three lines, `audit-level=high`, `fund=false`, `update-notifier=false`. There is no whitelist in it. (2) npm has no `allow-scripts` mechanism; the `allowScripts` object at package.json:156-160 is not a field npm reads (it is the key `@lavamoat/allow-scripts` uses under a `lavamoat` parent, and pnpm's equivalent is `pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies`), so npm silently ignores it. (3) Two of the four packages named do not match the tree: `esbuild` is not installed at all (`npm ls esbuild` returns empty), and `sharp` 0.35.3 has `hasInstallScript: false` in the lockfile because 0.35 ships prebuilt binaries as @img/* optional dependencies rather than building at install time. Scanning every lockfile entry for `hasInstallScript`, the tree has exactly three: core-js 3.49.0 (a donation banner, reachable only through the unused jspdf, see deps-01), fsevents 2.3.3 (macOS-only, optional) and unrs-resolver 1.12.2 (dev-only, used by eslint-import-resolver-typescript, and the Docker build never lints). So `--ignore-scripts` is currently harmless, but for the opposite reason to the one the comment gives.
findings.impact: Nothing breaks today. The hazard is the next native dependency. A maintainer who adds one, hits a broken image, and follows the comment will add a name to the `allowScripts` block at package.json:156, get no error from npm, and still ship a broken image, with the config change looking like it should have worked. The comment also misstates the security posture in the other direction: it reads as 'we ran a curated set of install scripts on purpose' when in fact none ran.
findings.recommendation: Delete the `allowScripts` block at package.json:156-160 and rewrite the Dockerfile:19-24 comment to say what actually happens: `--ignore-scripts` is on, no install script runs during the image build, and none is needed because sharp 0.35 and the Next SWC binaries ship prebuilt. If a future dependency genuinely needs its install script, the correct fix is a targeted `npm rebuild <pkg>` line after `npm ci`, not a whitelist field.

findings.title: docker-compose.yml pins the app image at 3.0.0 while the repo is on 3.7.2, so a self-hoster following the shipped compose file gets a two-month-old build with every audit fix since missing
findings.description: docker-compose.yml:53 is `image: ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar:3.0.0`. package.json:3 is version 3.7.2. `git log -L 53,53:docker-compose.yml` shows the tag was last touched on 2026-06-28 by commit cbc7652e ('fix(security): close 1 critical, 8 high, 11 medium findings from audit'), so the pin has not moved across seven minor releases. The pin itself is deliberate and well commented (docker-compose.yml:46-52 explains why a fixed tag beats `:latest` and how to move to a digest), but nothing in the release pipeline updates it: .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml pushes `$IMAGE:${VERSION}` and `$IMAGE:latest` on a tag push (lines 53-54) and never writes back to the compose file, and there is no docker ecosystem in dependabot.yml to notice (see deps-03).
findings.impact: The compose file is the documented self-hosting path. Anyone who clones the repo today and runs `docker compose up` gets release 3.0.0, which predates every security and correctness fix shipped in 3.1 through 3.7.2, including the remediations from AUDIT-010 through AUDIT-012. They will also be running a schema that instrumentation.ts in the checked-out repo no longer matches, since the app image carries its own copy.
findings.recommendation: Add a step to .github/workflows/docker-publish.yml that rewrites the tag in docker-compose.yml:53 to the released version and commits it, or change the line to `ghcr.io/vulnradar/vulnradar:${VULNRADAR_VERSION:-3.7.2}` so the default tracks the repo version and a self-hoster can still pin. Either way bump it to 3.7.2 now.

findings.title: No packageManager field or engine-strict in any manifest, so nothing mechanically prevents the pnpm and Windows-lockfile failures this repo has already suffered
findings.description: package.json:7-9 declares only `engines: { node: ">=22.0.0" }`. There is no `packageManager` field in the root manifest or in cli/, extension/ or marketing/, and .npmrc (three lines: audit-level, fund, update-notifier) does not set `engine-strict`. The only statement of policy anywhere is the prose `npm install` in CONTRIBUTING.md:8 and README.md:127. This repo has two documented, repeatedly painful failures that a `packageManager` pin is exactly the mechanism for: a pnpm install breaks node_modules and loses lucide-react types, and a package-lock.json regenerated on Windows strips the Linux native bindings (@next/swc-linux-*, @img/sharp-linux-*, @tailwindcss/oxide-linux-*, lightningcss-linux-*) and breaks CI and deploy. Both are one wrong command away with nothing in the tree to stop it. The `engines` range is also open-ended upward while everything that actually runs the code is pinned to 22: .nvmrc and .node-version both say `22`, all five CI jobs pass `node-version: "22"`, and Dockerfile:11 and :62 use node:22.11.0-alpine.
findings.impact: A new contributor, or an agent working in this repo, runs `pnpm install` or `yarn`, gets a plausible-looking result, and pushes a lockfile that fails only on the Linux CI runner or, worse, only at deploy. That has already happened here more than once, and the recovery is manual: graft the stripped native-binding entries back rather than re-resolve. The open `>=22.0.0` engines range separately means Node 24 or 25 passes the declared check while no CI job or image has ever exercised it.
findings.recommendation: Add `"packageManager": "npm@<the version CI uses>"` to the root package.json and to cli/, extension/ and marketing/, and add `engine-strict=true` to .npmrc. Tighten `engines.node` at package.json:8 to `">=22.0.0 <23.0.0"` so it matches .nvmrc, the CI matrix and the Dockerfile instead of promising a range nothing tests. Corepack then refuses a pnpm or yarn invocation outright rather than letting it half-succeed.

findings.title: Three of the six entries in the overrides block are dead or redundant, including one that replaces the exact postcss version Next.js pins on purpose
findings.description: Checking each entry in the `overrides` block at package.json:137-155 against the resolved tree in package-lock.json: (1) `"brace-expansion@2": "2.1.4"` (package.json:141) matches nothing. The only two brace-expansion copies in the tree are 5.0.9 (dev, via minimatch 10.2.6 which requests `^5.0.8`) and 1.1.18 (dev, via eslint-config-next's minimatch 3.1.5 which requests `^1.1.7`). No package requests a 2.x range, so this override is inert. Its sibling `brace-expansion@1` is live and does pin the 1.x copy. (2) `"postcss": "8.5.26"` (package.json:138) is live and load-bearing in a way worth noticing: `next@15.5.23` declares `postcss: "8.4.31"` as an exact, deliberate pin, and this override replaces it tree-wide with 8.5.26 for Next's own PostCSS pipeline. 8.4.31 is already the version that fixed the last postcss advisory, so the override is not buying a security fix; `npm audit` reports zero vulnerabilities either way. It also duplicates the direct devDependency pin at package.json:132. (3) `"@typescript-eslint/eslint-plugin"`, `"parser"`, `"visitor-keys"` and `"types"` are pinned to 8.67.0 (package.json:142-145) but the typescript-eslint packages ship in lockstep as a set of nine, and the other five are not pinned. The result in the lockfile is a split tree: `node_modules/@typescript-eslint/scope-manager` resolves to 8.66.0 (hoisted, via the `typescript-eslint` 8.66.0 that eslint-config-next depends on) while three nested copies under eslint-plugin, parser and type-utils are 8.67.0. The same split exists for typescript-estree, utils, project-service and tsconfig-utils.
findings.impact: Small but real on each count. The dead brace-expansion@2 entry is a permanent false signal that a 2.x copy needs pinning. The postcss override silently overrides a framework's exact pin with no comment explaining why, which is the kind of thing that is impossible to safely remove later because nobody remembers what it was for. The typescript-eslint split installs two full copies of five packages and means the version a rule actually runs under depends on which config block loaded it, so pinning 8.67.0 does not actually put the whole lint run on 8.67.0.
findings.recommendation: Delete `"brace-expansion@2"` at package.json:141. Delete the `"postcss"` override at :138 (the direct devDependency at :132 already controls the version the build uses, and Next's 8.4.31 is patched) or add a one-line comment saying what advisory or bug it exists for. Replace the four `@typescript-eslint/*` entries at :142-145 with a single `"typescript-eslint": "8.67.0"` override, which pins the meta-package and lets its own exact internal pins carry all nine packages to the same version.

findings.title: The sharp override forces a major version past what Next.js declares, on a package the app never loads because images are unoptimized
findings.category: override on an unused optional dependency
findings.description: package.json:139 has `"sharp": "^0.35.0"` in `overrides`. The only consumer of sharp in the whole tree is `next@15.5.23`, which declares it as an optional dependency at `^0.34.3`. The override therefore does one thing: it pushes Next's image optimizer onto a sharp major it does not declare support for, resolving to 0.35.3 in the lockfile along with the @img/sharp-* prebuilt binaries (@img/sharp-linux-x64, @img/sharp-linuxmusl-x64, @img/sharp-libvips-linux-x64 are all present and installed by `npm ci` on the CI and Docker Linux runners). It is currently inert, because next.config.mjs:26 sets `images: { unoptimized: true }`, so Next never requires sharp at runtime and the mismatch cannot be exercised. That inertness is the problem, because AUDIT-012 recommends turning the optimizer on and explicitly cites this override as the reason it would be safe to do so ('sharp is already pinned in the package.json overrides, so enabling the optimizer with remotePatterns for the three provider CDNs would fix the existing stored URLs too').
findings.impact: Nothing today. But the moment `unoptimized: true` is removed, Next 15.5's image optimizer starts calling a sharp major it was not tested against, and it does so on the avatar-rendering path for every signed-in user, with the failure surfacing only at request time rather than at build. The override also silently installs the sharp native stack into every image for a feature that is switched off.
findings.recommendation: Decide the direction rather than leaving the override floating. If image optimization stays off, delete the `sharp` override at package.json:139 and let Next's own `^0.34.3` govern. If AUDIT-012's recommendation to enable the optimizer is taken, keep the override but move to a Next version whose declared sharp range includes 0.35, and verify the avatar path against the three provider CDNs before shipping.

findings.title: tailwindcss-animate, last published in August 2023, is loaded as a plugin by every production CSS build and is a Tailwind v3 plugin in a Tailwind v4 project
findings.category: unmaintained dependency on the build path
findings.description: Checking `npm view <pkg> time.modified` for all 86 direct dependencies, exactly two have not been published in over two years: `server-only` 0.0.1 (2022-09-03), which is a deliberately frozen one-line marker package maintained by the Next.js team and is not a concern, and `tailwindcss-animate` 1.0.7 (package.json:114), last published 2023-08-28, three years ago. Unlike the twenty-five packages in deps-01 this one is genuinely wired in: tailwind.config.mjs:1 imports it and its last line registers it as `plugins: [tailwindcssAnimate]`, and app/globals.css:3 bridges that config into the v4 pipeline with `@config '../tailwind.config.mjs'`. Sixty-two call sites across components/ and app/ use utilities it provides (`animate-in`, `fade-in-*`, `zoom-in-*`, `slide-in-from-*`), for example components/ai-chat/chat-widget.tsx and components/billing/checkout-skeleton.tsx. The version mismatch is the sharper half: this is a plugin written for Tailwind v3's JS plugin API, while the project runs Tailwind v4 (`tailwindcss` and `@tailwindcss/postcss` both `^4.3.3`, package.json:121 and :134) and reaches it only through the v4 `@config` compatibility shim, which is the migration bridge rather than a supported long-term path.
findings.impact: The animation utilities on 62 call sites depend on an abandoned package reached through a compatibility shim. When Tailwind drops `@config` support, or when the plugin's v3 API assumptions stop holding, the failure is silent CSS: the classes still parse, no build error is raised, and the animations simply stop, which is the kind of regression a test suite does not catch and a reviewer does not see in a diff.
findings.recommendation: Replace `tailwindcss-animate` with `tw-animate-css`, the actively maintained v4-native successor that shadcn/ui itself moved to and that keeps the same `animate-in` / `fade-in-*` / `slide-in-from-*` class names, so the 62 call sites do not change. Swap the import and the `plugins` entry in tailwind.config.mjs, or import it directly from app/globals.css with `@plugin` and drop that part of the `@config` bridge.

findings.title: dependabot.yml groups list three packages that are not dependencies and its security group watches three that are unused
findings.description: .github/dependabot.yml's `scanning` group matches `dompurify` (line 40), which is not a declared dependency at all: it exists in the tree only transitively under jspdf, which deps-01 shows has zero imports. The `build` group matches `autoprefixer` (line 68), which is nowhere in package.json or the lockfile (this project uses Tailwind v4's own pipeline via @tailwindcss/postcss, per postcss.config.mjs). The `security` group is the one worth fixing rather than trimming: it watches `jsonwebtoken` (line 59), `@neondatabase/serverless` (line 61) and `@hookform/resolvers` (line 64), all three of which have zero imports (deps-01). The `scanning` group similarly covers jspdf, jspdf-autotable, cmdk, embla-carousel-react, vaul, sonner, react-day-picker, react-hook-form, react-resizable-panels, input-otp and date-fns, every one of them unused.
findings.impact: Dependabot opens grouped PRs, labelled `security`, for packages no line of code can reach. Reviewers spend attention on them and, more corrosively, learn that a `security`-labelled dependency PR in this repo is usually noise. The group names also encode a wrong mental model of the dependency set for anyone reading the file to understand what the app depends on.
findings.recommendation: After removing the unused packages per deps-01, delete the now-empty group patterns: `dompurify` (line 40) and `autoprefixer` (line 68) can go immediately since neither is a dependency in any form, and the `scanning` group loses most of its members. Keep the `security` group scoped to what actually is on the auth and data paths: bcryptjs, jose, nodemailer, pg and zod.

findings.title: react-icons installs 85 MB to serve sixty brand glyphs across nine files
findings.description: `react-icons` 5.7.0 (package.json:104) is 85 MB on disk, the second-largest package in node_modules after next (149 MB) and ahead of lucide-react (39 MB). It ships every icon set it wraps as generated JS modules. Actual use is nine files and sixty distinct glyphs: components/scanner/tech-icon.tsx:1-60 imports one `IconType`, `GrHeroku`, `FaMagento` and fifty-five `Si*` brand icons for the software-inventory panel, and the remaining eight files (components/auth/oauth-buttons.tsx:3-4, components/admin/users/user-detail-panel.tsx:47-48, components/profile/tabs/profile-social-tab.tsx:6-7, components/profile/tabs/profile-billing-tab.tsx:27, components/scanner/footer.tsx:5, components/modals/github-profile-modal.tsx:9, components/landing/landing-open-source.tsx:2, app/docs/developers/page.tsx:8) between them use exactly three: `FaGithub`, `FaDiscord`, `FcGoogle`. This is an install-size and cold-build cost, not a bundle-size one: the per-icon module layout tree-shakes cleanly, so AUDIT-012#fe-01 and #fe-02's client-bundle findings are not what this is about. The cost lands on the CI npm cache, the Docker builder layer and `npm ci` wall time on every one of the five CI jobs.
findings.impact: 85 MB of the 789 MB node_modules, restored and re-cached on every CI job and every image build, for sixty SVG paths. It also inflates the `npm ci` step that runs five times per push across the lint, typecheck, test, extension and build jobs.
findings.recommendation: This one is worth doing only if the CI or image time actually matters, since it is a mechanical but broad change. The lighter path for the fifty-five brand glyphs in components/scanner/tech-icon.tsx is `@icons-pack/react-simple-icons`, which wraps the same Simple Icons set at a fraction of the install size, or inlining the sixty SVG path strings into a local map in that file (they are static paths, a few KB total). The three OAuth glyphs used across the other eight files are the same three every time and are the obvious first candidates to inline, which alone removes react-icons from eight of the nine importers.

findings.title: eslint-config-next is on major 16 while next is on major 15, so the lint rule set targets a framework major the app is not running
findings.description: package.json:95 pins `next: 15.5.23`; package.json:131 pins `eslint-config-next: 16.3.2`, which in turn hard-depends on `@next/eslint-plugin-next: 16.3.2` (per the lockfile entry for eslint-config-next). The jump was deliberate and is explained at eslint.config.mjs:3-6: eslint-config-next 16 is the first release with native flat config, so moving to it let the repo drop the `@eslint/eslintrc` FlatCompat shim, and eslint.config.mjs:13 imports `eslint-config-next/core-web-vitals` directly. The side effect is that the Next-specific rules being enforced are the Next 16 set: rules added or changed for Next 16 conventions run against a Next 15 codebase, and rules removed in 16 for patterns Next 15 still has are not enforced at all. This also puts the two out of dependabot's `next-stack` group's reach as a unit, since .github/dependabot.yml:75-77 ignores `next` majors while `eslint-config-next` has already taken one.
findings.impact: Bounded and mostly latent: the lint job either flags a Next 16 idiom the app cannot adopt yet, or stops flagging a Next 15 anti-pattern because the rule was dropped in 16. Neither breaks the build, but it means the `lint` gate's Next coverage is not the coverage the running framework needs, and there is no signal anywhere that says so.
findings.recommendation: Add a comment at package.json:131 (or in eslint.config.mjs beside the import at line 13) recording that eslint-config-next is intentionally one major ahead of next and why, so the next person to read the manifest does not treat it as a mistake or 'fix' it downward. Revisit when the Next 16 upgrade lands and the two realign.

findings.title: The four manifests disagree about Node: cli declares >=18 (EOL since April 2025) while root and extension declare >=22, marketing declares nothing, and CI only ever runs the CLI on Node 22
findings.description: `cli/package.json:16` declares `"node": ">=18"`, `package.json:8` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, `extension/package.json:9` declares `"node": ">=22.0.0"`, and `marketing/package.json` declares no `engines` field at all. The Node 18 claim is repeated to users in three places: `cli/README.md:5` ("no dependencies (Node 18+ for global fetch)"), `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4` ("No dependencies: Node 18+ (global fetch) is all it needs"), and the docs page at `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95` ("It needs Node 18 or newer"). Node 18 reached end of life on 2025-04-30 and receives no security updates. It is also never exercised: the only place the CLI runs in CI is `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110`, `node --test` with `working-directory: cli`, inside the `test` job whose `setup-node` step pins `node-version: "22"` (line 47). So the supported-floor claim is asserted in three user-facing places and validated in none. Node's own `--test` runner also behaved differently in 18 (experimental, narrower default file-glob) than in 22, so `node --test` with no path argument is not guaranteed to discover `cli/vulnradar.test.mjs` there.
findings.impact: A user or a CI pipeline pinned to Node 18 follows the documented floor, runs the CLI on a runtime that has had no security patches for over a year, and hits any regression alone because nothing tests that version. Meanwhile a contributor who reads the root manifest reasonably assumes Node 22 is the repo-wide floor and may use a Node 20-or-22-only API in cli/lib.mjs without any check catching it.
findings.recommendation: Raise `cli/package.json:16` to `">=20"` (the oldest Node still in maintenance) or to `">=22"` to match the other three manifests, and update the three copy sites: `cli/README.md:5`, the header comment at `cli/vulnradar.mjs:4`, and `app/docs/cli/page.tsx:95`. If Node 18 support is genuinely wanted, add a matrix entry to the CLI test step in `.github/workflows/ci.yml:110` that runs `node --test` on 18 as well. Also add `"engines": { "node": ">=22.0.0" }` to `marketing/package.json` so all four agree.

findings.title: The root is on TypeScript 6.0.3 and the extension on 5.9.3, so extension source is type-checked by 5.9 in CI while a root-level editor and root eslint analyze the same files with 6.0
findings.description: `package.json:135` pins the root to `"typescript": "6.0.3"`; `extension/package.json:36` declares `"typescript": "^5.7.2"`, resolved to 5.9.3; `marketing/package.json:22` pins 5.9.3. `extension/package.json:20` runs `tsc --noEmit` from the extension's own node_modules, so CI's extension typecheck (`.github/workflows/ci.yml:141`) uses 5.9.3. But the extension's source is also analyzed by the root toolchain: `eslint.config.mjs:22` lists ignores for `scripts/**`, `cli/**`, `dist/**` and others but not `extension/**`, and I verified the effect directly, `npx eslint --print-config extension/src/lib/api.ts` returns a full config while `npx eslint --print-config cli/lib.mjs` returns `undefined` (the marker for an ignored path). So `npm run lint` at the root parses extension TypeScript with @typescript-eslint 8.67.0 while CI type-checks it with tsc 5.9.3, and any editor opened at the repo root resolves the root's typescript 6.0.3 for those same files. The root's Dependabot config already acknowledges this class of problem at `.github/dependabot.yml`, where the ignore list holds TypeScript majors because "@typescript-eslint ... peer range caps at <6.1.0", but that reasoning was applied only to the root manifest.
findings.impact: A developer editing extension/src sees diagnostics from TypeScript 6.0.3 in their editor that CI (5.9.3) does not produce, and vice versa. A syntax or type feature added in 6.0 compiles in the editor and fails the extension CI job, or a 5.9-only behaviour passes CI and shows as an editor error, in both cases with no obvious explanation because the version difference is invisible from the file being edited. Running eslint over the extension's build output is harmless today (I ran `npx eslint extension/dist-chrome/popup.js` and it reports nothing) but it is unintended coverage.
findings.recommendation: Align `extension/package.json:36` and `marketing/package.json:22` to the root's TypeScript major, or, if the extension must stay on 5.x, add a comment in `extension/package.json` saying why and add `"extension/dist-chrome/**"`, `"extension/dist-firefox/**"` to the `ignores` array in `eslint.config.mjs:22` so root lint never walks generated bundles.

findings.title: The packaged extension carries no license text and no third-party attribution, although it bundles the MPL-2.0 webextension-polyfill and BSD-3-Clause lit-html verbatim into background.js and content.js
findings.category: missing license and attribution in a distributed artifact
findings.description: `extension/package.json:5` declares `"license": "GPL-3.0"`, but there is no LICENSE file anywhere under `extension/` and none in the built output: `dist-chrome/` contains only assets, chunks, background.js, content.js, the three page bundles, their .map files, favicon.svg, icons/ and manifest.json. `extension/scripts/package.mjs:66` zips exactly that directory for store upload, so the Chrome Web Store and AMO packages ship with no license text. The two runtime dependencies are inlined into those bundles by the IIFE build at `extension/scripts/build.mjs:59`: `webextension-polyfill@0.12.0` is MPL-2.0 (verified from its package.json) and `lit-html@3.3.3` is BSD-3-Clause, and both appear as sources in the emitted map (`dist-chrome/content.js.map` lists `../node_modules/webextension-polyfill/dist/browser-polyfill.js` and `../node_modules/lit-html/lit-html.js` first in its `sources` array). MPL-2.0 section 3.2 requires that recipients of the binary be informed of the license and be able to obtain the source of the covered files. The source zip built by `extension/scripts/package-source.mjs` is submitted to AMO only, so Chrome Web Store users get neither a license notice nor a source pointer. That same script also has no LICENSE to include: it archives every top-level entry in `extension/` except node_modules, the dist dirs, out/, zips and tsbuildinfo, and there is no license file among them.
findings.impact: Every Chrome Web Store install of a GPL-3.0 project receives a binary with no copy of the GPL and no notice for the MPL-2.0 code compiled into it. It is a compliance gap rather than a user-facing break, but it is an avoidable one for a project whose whole pitch is open source.
findings.recommendation: Add a `LICENSE` file to `extension/` (a copy of the root GPL-3.0 text) plus a short `THIRD-PARTY.md` listing webextension-polyfill (MPL-2.0, link to its source) and lit-html (BSD-3-Clause). Copy both into the build output from `extension/scripts/build.mjs` in the same loop that copies icons (around line 103) so they land in `dist-chrome/` and `dist-firefox/` and therefore in the store zip.

findings.title: cli/package.json is publishable but incomplete: no `private` flag, a `name` that collides with the root manifest, no `repository`, and a `files` list that omits the license it declares
findings.description: `cli/package.json` declares `"name": "vulnradar"` (line 2), `"license": "GPL-3.0"` (line 5), a `bin` entry (line 7), and `"files": ["vulnradar.mjs", "lib.mjs", "README.md"]` (line 10). It has no `"private": true`, so `npm publish` from that directory would succeed. Three things are missing or wrong for that path. The `name` is identical to the root manifest's `"name": "vulnradar"` at `package.json:2`, which is only harmless because the root sets `"private": true` at line 6; the CLI does not. There is no `repository` field, so the published page would carry no source link and no npm provenance attestation. And `files` omits any license file (there is none in `cli/` to include), so a GPL-3.0 tarball would ship without its license text. On the positive side the package is genuinely dependency-free: `cli/vulnradar.mjs` imports only `./lib.mjs`, `cli/lib.mjs` imports nothing, and both use only global `fetch`, `process` and `console`, so there is no accidental dependency on the app's runtime and no lockfile is needed. This finding is the mechanical half of subdeps-01: fixing that one means publishing this manifest, and it is not ready.
findings.impact: A publish today produces a package with no repo link, no provenance, and no license file, under a name that shadows the root manifest. Minor on its own, but subdeps-01 argues the name should be claimed soon, and this is what has to be corrected first.
findings.recommendation: Before publishing, add `"repository": { "type": "git", "url": "git+https://github.com/VulnRadar/vulnradar.dev.git", "directory": "cli" }` to `cli/package.json`, add a `LICENSE` file in `cli/` and list it in `files` at line 10, and publish with `npm publish --provenance` from CI so the tarball carries a signed attestation.

findings.title: The github_review_usage year_month backfill gives every existing row the same window_start and then adds a UNIQUE constraint on it, aborting the whole migration on any table with two rows for one user
findings.category: unique constraint added over a backfilled duplicate
findings.description: The dataUpdates chain runs `ALTER TABLE github_review_usage ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS window_start TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT NOW()` (line 1123), then drops year_month (line 1134), then `ADD CONSTRAINT github_review_usage_user_window_key UNIQUE (user_id, window_start)` (line 1151). NOW() is transaction-start time and is evaluated once, so every pre-existing row receives the identical window_start. The old shape was keyed by calendar month, so a user with rows for two different months collapses to two rows with the same (user_id, window_start) and the UNIQUE add fails with `could not create unique index ... Key is duplicated`. Because runPlan holds one transaction for the entire plan (_runner.mjs:95), that error rolls back the whole v2.0.0 to v3.0.0 upgrade, not just this step. instrumentation.ts:2015-2032 runs the identical statements at boot but inside a `.catch` that logs non-fatally, so there the table is left with no unique constraint at all and every subsequent `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (user_id, window_start)` in lib/billing/github-review-usage.ts:168 fails with "there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification".
findings.impact: This is the one place in the migration where a statement fails purely because of existing row values. Production has never had the year_month shape (production is on v2.3.x per the file header), so the blast radius today is developer and self-host databases that booted an intermediate build. On those, db:migrate aborts entirely with a duplicate-key error on a table nobody would think to look at, and app boot silently leaves GitHub AI review quota tracking broken.
findings.recommendation: Replace the DEFAULT NOW() backfill with a deterministic per-row value derived from the old key, for example `ADD COLUMN window_start TIMESTAMPTZ` then `UPDATE github_review_usage SET window_start = to_timestamp(year_month || '-01', 'YYYY-MM-DD') WHERE window_start IS NULL`, then `SET NOT NULL`, so rows for different months stay distinct. Failing that, collapse duplicates first with a `DELETE ... USING` keeping MAX(tokens_used) per user before the ADD CONSTRAINT. Apply the same change to instrumentation.ts:2015 so the two paths agree.

findings.title: The downgrade's red warning box never mentions that it deletes user accounts, and no documentation anywhere describes what to do when a migration fails
findings.category: undisclosed destructive step and missing recovery procedure
findings.description: showDowngradeWarning builds its "This will PERMANENTLY DELETE" list from `destructiveSteps.filter(s => s.kind === "dropTable")` and `... === "dropColumn"` (lines 227-228). Steps of kind "dataUpdate" are excluded from both filters and their dataLoss is always null (scripts/migrate/_planner.mjs:179-188), so the 3.0.0 to 2.0.0 downgrade's `DELETE FROM users WHERE password_hash IS NULL` (2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs:1293, destructive: true) never appears in the box the operator types yes-delete-data into. It also never appears in renderPlan's per-step "rows will be lost" detail (scripts/migrate/_planner.mjs:228-240), which likewise only handles kind table and column, so the only place the account deletion is stated is the `description` string in the source file, which is never printed. The same applies to the other silent losses that description names: pre_staff_plan and users.ai_credit_balance are dropped without being restored or refunded. Separately, grepping app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx, app/docs/setup/page.tsx and README.md for a failed-migration recovery procedure returns nothing: db:restore is mentioned only in README.md, and the pre-migration dump path (databases/v{major}/{version}/) is documented in no user-facing page at all.
findings.impact: An operator running a downgrade sees a warning that names tables and columns and confirms with an exact phrase, believing that is the full extent of the data loss, while every OAuth-only account is deleted and every purchased AI credit balance is zeroed without either being named. And when a migration does fail, nothing tells the operator that a plaintext dump was just written to databases/, how to restore it, or that db:restore exists.
findings.recommendation: In scripts/migrate/migrate.mjs's showDowngradeWarning, add a third section listing every step where `destructive === true && kind === "dataUpdate"`, printed with its label. Give the dataUpdates step shape an optional dataLoss field so 2.0.0-to-3.0.0.mjs can declare what the DELETE removes, and render it in _planner.mjs's renderPlan. Add a "Recovering from a failed migration" section to app/docs/self-hosting/page.tsx naming the databases/ dump location, npm run db:restore, and the fact that re-running db:migrate is safe.

findings.title: The v1 to v2 downgrade definition is duplicated verbatim in two files and only one copy is ever loaded
findings.description: Both scripts/migrate/versions/1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs:136-174 and scripts/migrate/versions/2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs:21-59 export a `downgrade` object containing the same 15 dropTables and the same 13 dropColumns, character for character. findVersionFile (scripts/migrate/_registry.mjs:612-615) tries `${from}-to-${to}.mjs` first, so a downgrade step of {from: "2.0.0", to: "1.0.0"} always resolves to 2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs and 1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs's downgrade export is never loaded by anything. 2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs's `upgrade` export (line 15-19) is symmetrically dead, since an upgrade step of {from: "1.0.0", to: "2.0.0"} resolves to the other file first. The brief for this audit is correct that a 2.0.0-to-1.0.0 downgrade file is deliberate; the duplication of its contents into the other file is the issue, not its existence.
findings.impact: Someone fixing the v1 drop list has a 50 percent chance of editing the copy that never runs, and the two lists can silently diverge with the runtime behavior determined by filename ordering rather than by intent. They are identical today, so this is a latent hazard rather than a live bug.
findings.recommendation: Pick one file as the home for the v1 to v2 pair. Either delete the dead `downgrade` from 1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs and keep 2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs as the down half, or delete 2.0.0-to-1.0.0.mjs entirely and rely on findVersionFile's documented reversed-name fallback, which already resolves 2.0.0 to 1.0.0 to 1.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs's downgrade export. The second option matches how the 3.0.0 to 2.0.0 downgrade already works, since no 3.0.0-to-2.0.0.mjs exists.

findings.title: db:restore feeds GCM plaintext into psql before the auth tag is verified, so a corrupted or tampered backup is partially applied before the integrity check fails
findings.description: For an .enc backup, runRestore builds `pipeline(source, decipher, decrypted)` at line 84 and immediately assigns the PassThrough to `source` (line 88), then at line 106 pipes it through gunzip into psql's stdin. AES-256-GCM emits plaintext as it decrypts and only validates the auth tag set at line 82 when the final block is processed, so by the time an authentication failure surfaces, every preceding block has already been gunzipped and executed by psql. The failure handler (line 85) prints "Decryption failed" and calls process.exit(1), leaving the already-executed statements committed, since psql is running without --single-transaction (see migrate-04).
findings.impact: The whole point of authenticating the backup is to guarantee that a modified or truncated dump is never applied. As written, an attacker who can modify a backup file, or plain bit rot in cold storage, results in a partially applied dump plus an error message, rather than a clean refusal. Low severity because it requires an already-compromised or corrupted backup artifact, and because the operator does see a failure message.
findings.recommendation: Decrypt and verify to a temporary file first, and only start psql once the decipher stream has ended without error, deleting the temp file in a finally. Alternatively keep the streaming path but combine it with `--single-transaction` on psql (already recommended in migrate-04) so a late decryption failure rolls back everything that was streamed.

findings.title: Twenty-seven of the ninety-seven indexes are redundant: sixteen duplicate a UNIQUE constraint outright and eleven are strict prefixes of a wider index, and a code comment records the reasoning that created most of them
findings.description: New relative to AUDIT-012#perf-15 and #perf-16, which covered missing and unusable indexes; this is the opposite direction. A UNIQUE constraint is implemented as a unique b-tree index, so a separate CREATE INDEX on the same column is a pure duplicate. Sixteen exist: idx_users_email (:323 vs :284), idx_users_stripe_customer (:326 vs :296), idx_api_keys_key_hash (:373 vs :362), idx_scan_history_share_token (:432 vs :425), idx_badges_name (:499 vs :490), idx_discord_user (:724 vs :711), idx_discord_id (:725 vs :712), idx_notif_prefs_user_id (:830 vs :802), idx_team_invites_token (:916 vs :910), idx_admin_notifications_cookie (:991 vs :966), idx_ai_conversations_session_id (:1192 vs :1184), idx_user_ai_configs_user_id (:1219 vs :1210), idx_github_connections_user (:1932 vs :1924), idx_github_review_usage_user_window (:2047 vs the UNIQUE added at :2034), idx_promoted_auto_tag_rules_tag (:2951 vs :2939), and idx_staff_invites_token (lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:45 vs :37). Eleven more are strict prefixes of a wider index or key, which a b-tree already serves: idx_scan_history_user_id (:430) under idx_scan_history_user_scanned (:1587), idx_api_usage_key_id (:408) under idx_api_usage_key_used (:1589), idx_admin_audit_admin_id (:577) under idx_admin_audit_admin_created (:1591), idx_scan_tags_scan_id (:446) under UNIQUE(scan_id, tag) (:444), idx_user_badges_user (:513) under PRIMARY KEY (user_id, badge_id) (:511), idx_rate_limits_key (:844) under UNIQUE(key, window_start) (:842), idx_device_trust_user_id (:863) under UNIQUE(user_id, device_fingerprint) (:861), idx_team_members_team (:902) under UNIQUE(team_id, user_id) (:900), idx_domains_user_id (:3187) under UNIQUE(user_id, domain) (:3185), idx_api_keys_key_locator_backfill (:376), a partial index whose rows are a subset of idx_api_keys_key_locator (:374), and idx_staff_activity_user_heartbeat (:743), a composite on (user_id, last_heartbeat) on a table with UNIQUE(user_id) (:741), which caps the table at one row per user so the second column can never narrow anything. The comment at :1571-1578 states the reasoning that produced the first three of the prefix cases: "The single-column indexes created above each table are left in place; these are additive, not replacements, so unrelated query shapes that only filter on one of the columns keep working the same way." A composite index leading with the same column already serves a filter on that column alone, so the premise is wrong. Separately, six indexes cover low-cardinality columns on tables that are tiny in this deployment (about 50 users) and will never be chosen by the planner over a sequential scan: idx_users_role (:324), idx_users_plan (:325), idx_admin_notifications_type (:990), idx_access_rules_type (:1023), idx_security_alerts_severity (:1108) and idx_broadcast_messages_status (:1143).
findings.impact: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE on these tables maintains a second copy of an index that can never be chosen, which is pure write amplification on the hottest tables in the schema: rate_limits (written on every rate-limited request), api_usage, scan_history and sessions. It also inflates the working set that has to stay in shared_buffers and doubles the vacuum work on those relations. The false comment at :1574 is a maintenance hazard on its own, because it will produce more duplicates the next time someone adds a composite index alongside an existing single-column one.
findings.recommendation: Drop the 27 listed indexes with `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS`. Keep every UNIQUE constraint, they are the constraints doing the work. Fix the comment at instrumentation.ts:1571-1578 to say that a composite index leading with column A replaces a single-column index on A, and delete the three single-column indexes it was written to justify (:430, :408, :577). Verify against a live database with `SELECT indexrelid::regclass, indrelid::regclass, indkey FROM pg_index ORDER BY indrelid;` before dropping, since a self-hosted install created by an older path may have a slightly different set.

findings.title: REQUIRED_TABLES lists 8 of the 66 tables the app creates and omits sessions, so a boot that fails to create the session table reports a healthy schema while every login 500s
findings.description: REQUIRED_TABLES is `[users, scan_history, api_keys, host_reputation, host_badges, webhooks, scan_finding_feedback, system_error_logs]`. It is consumed by the boot-time verification at instrumentation.ts:3515-3543 (which fires a critical admin alert on a miss) and by GET /api/v3/health at app/api/v3/health/route.ts:110-116 (which reports missing_tables). Cross-checking it against the 64 CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statements in instrumentation.ts plus the two lazy ones from schema-02: every name in the list is genuinely created, so there is no phantom entry. The gap is the other direction. The file's own docstring says the list covers "auth, scanning, API keys, billing", and `sessions` is absent, even though lib/auth/auth.ts:99 reads it on every authenticated request and losing it takes down login, logout, and every dashboard route. Also absent and load-bearing: `rate_limits` (lib/rate-limiting/rate-limit.ts:148, every rate-limited endpoint), `notification_preferences` (inserted on every signup at app/api/v3/auth/signup/route.ts:200 and on every OAuth signup at oauth/[provider]/callback/route.ts:239), `processed_stripe_events` (the Stripe webhook idempotency guard at app/api/v3/webhooks/stripe/route.ts:168, whose own instrumentation.ts comment at :536-543 documents what happened the last time it was missing: every Stripe retry reprocessed as a new event), and the three payment idempotency ledgers ai_credit_purchases, github_credit_purchases and browserbase_credit_purchases, each of which is the sole guard against double-crediting a purchase (lib/billing/ai-usage.ts:160-172). Every one of those tables is created inside a `.catch()` that only console.errors, exactly the failure mode this list exists to catch.
findings.impact: The health endpoint is the operator's only signal that the boot-time schema sequence half-completed. Today it can report schema_ok with no missing tables while sessions, rate_limits or processed_stripe_events do not exist, which means a monitor watching /api/v3/health stays green through an outage that makes login impossible or through a state where every Stripe webhook replay re-grants a plan.
findings.recommendation: Add sessions, rate_limits, notification_preferences, processed_stripe_events, ai_credit_purchases, github_credit_purchases and browserbase_credit_purchases to REQUIRED_TABLES, plus staff_invites and admin_audit_log_archive once schema-02 is fixed. The docstring's argument against exhaustiveness (drift with instrumentation.ts) holds for a full 66-name list but not for the seven tables whose absence takes down auth, rate limiting, signup or billing idempotency.

findings.title: The five most load-bearing enum columns (users.role, users.plan, team_members.role, domains.status, gifted_subscriptions.plan) have no CHECK constraint, while a dozen cosmetic ones do
findings.description: CHECK coverage on enum-like text columns is inverted relative to importance. Constrained: admin_notifications.type/variant/audience (:969-971), access_rules.rule_type/value_type (:1007-1008), security_alerts.severity (:1097), broadcast_messages.message_type/status (:1135, :1141), broadcast_recipients.status (:1157), scan_finding_feedback.verdict (:1463), finding_remediation.status (:1506), scan_history.status (:1623), scan_tags.source (:2449), promoted_auto_tag_rules.min_severity (:2944), host_badges.scope (:3411), support_tickets.category/status (:3435-3437). Unconstrained: users.role (:292, values user/beta_tester/support/moderator/admin/super_admin plus the billing, security_analyst, content_manager and ops roles in STAFF_ROLES at lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:22), users.plan (:295), gifted_subscriptions.plan (:949), team_members.role (:898) and team_invites.role (:909), domains.status (:3178, whose 'verified' value is the gate that authorizes intrusive active probing, see lib/domains/scope.ts), scheduled_scans.frequency (:458), webhooks.type (:477), data_requests.status (:873), billing_history.status (:527), user_notifications.type (:1662), email_logs.status (:675), scan_history.source (:424) and .scan_type (:2076), users.auth_provider (:1878), .two_factor_method (:315), .subscription_status (:298) and .billing_interval (:2683). The concrete consequence is in lib/database/cleanup.ts:152-195: the per-plan scan retention runs four DELETEs whose WHERE clauses match the literals 'free' (or NULL), 'core_supporter', 'pro_supporter' and 'elite_supporter'. A users.plan value outside that set matches none of them, so those scans are retained forever with no error and no log line. lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 compounds it by casting an arbitrary column value straight to the enum type (`return effectivePlan as PlanType`) with no membership check, after which lib/billing/plan-limits.ts indexes PLAN_LIMIT_KEYS with it. Every current write path does validate (app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1869-1880 for update_plan, :1652-1657 for gift_subscription, and the billing routes write literals or the output of getPlanFromProductId), so this is a latent constraint gap rather than a live bug: the paths that can introduce a bad value are the SQL repair scripts, scripts/restore-db.mjs, and hand-run SQL, all of which the self-hosting docs point operators at.
findings.impact: The database does not enforce the value sets that authorization and money decisions are made from. A users.plan value outside the four known literals silently exempts that account's scan history from every retention rule in lib/database/cleanup.ts, so their data is kept forever with no error, and lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 hands the same unchecked string to the plan-limits resolver. A users.role value outside the known set fails closed for staff checks but is invisible in the admin panel, and a domains.status other than 'verified' or 'pending' is treated as unverified with no signal that the row is malformed. Every one of these is reachable through the documented self-hosted repair and restore scripts, which is precisely the situation a CHECK exists for.
findings.recommendation: Add CHECK constraints for the five that carry real authorization or money semantics: users.role against the union of STAFF_ROLES plus user, beta_tester and super_admin; users.plan and gifted_subscriptions.plan against the four PlanId values in lib/billing/catalog.ts:12; team_members.role and team_invites.role against the team role set; domains.status against pending/verified/reverify_failed. Use the drop-and-recreate pattern already used for scan_tags_source_check at instrumentation.ts:2469-2475 so widening one later stays possible. Separately, make lib/rate-limiting/daily-limits.ts:96 validate membership before the cast and fall back to 'free' instead of casting blind, and make the cleanup retention in lib/database/cleanup.ts cover the else case rather than silently skipping it.

findings.title: broadcast_recipients has no UNIQUE(message_id, user_id), so the mass-email send loop uses a read-then-insert guard that two concurrent sends both pass
findings.description: broadcast_recipients (instrumentation.ts:1151-1162) has a surrogate `id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` and two separate single-column indexes on message_id and user_id, and no uniqueness on the pair. The send handler and the resend handler each compensate in the application, with a comment that says so verbatim: "broadcast_recipients has no unique key, so this is an app-level guard rather than ON CONFLICT" (app/api/v3/admin/features/route.ts:555-557 and the duplicated copy at :717-719). The guard is `SELECT 1 FROM broadcast_recipients WHERE message_id = $1 AND user_id = $2 AND status = 'sent' LIMIT 1` followed, if the select returned nothing, by sendEmail and then a plain INSERT (:559-573 and :721-735). Nothing serialises the two steps, and the same recipient is only marked after the SMTP round trip completes, so the window between the SELECT and the INSERT is the full duration of one email send. Two admins hitting send and resend for the same message, or one admin double-clicking, or the resend path racing a still-running first send, both pass the SELECT for the same recipient and both send.
findings.impact: The whole verified user base can receive the same broadcast twice, from a feature whose stated design goal in that comment is that it must not. AUDIT-012#perf-07 already established that this loop iterates every verified user with no LIMIT and does one SELECT plus one INSERT plus one sequential SMTP call per recipient, so the race window per recipient is large and the number of recipients is unbounded. Duplicate mass email is the fastest way to get a sending domain reputation-flagged.
findings.recommendation: Add `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_broadcast_recipients_message_user ON broadcast_recipients(message_id, user_id);` in instrumentation.ts and replace both read-then-insert blocks with an insert-first claim: INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (message_id, user_id) DO NOTHING RETURNING id, send the email only when a row came back, then UPDATE the status. That also satisfies AUDIT-012#perf-15's item (8), which asked for a plain composite index on the same two columns for the read side, so one unique index covers both findings.

findings.title: users.unsubscribe_token is the sole lookup key of a public unauthenticated endpoint and has neither an index nor a UNIQUE constraint
findings.description: unsubscribe_token is added at instrumentation.ts:1248-1250 as `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS unsubscribe_token UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()` with no NOT NULL, no UNIQUE, and no CREATE INDEX anywhere in the file (grep for the column name in instrumentation.ts returns only that one line). It is the only credential the unsubscribe flow has: app/api/v3/account/unsubscribe/route.ts:33 runs `SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE unsubscribe_token = $1` for the GET and :68 runs `SELECT id FROM users WHERE unsubscribe_token = $1` for the POST, both unauthenticated, and the token is embedded in every outbound notification email by lib/notifications/notifications.ts:98-105. Every other token column in the schema that identifies a row is declared UNIQUE (scan_history.share_token :425, team_invites.token :910, host_badges.badge_token :3362, staff_invites.token in lib/admin/staff-invites.ts:37) and most also carry an index. Collision is not realistic given the UUID default (the volatile default makes ADD COLUMN rewrite the table and evaluate gen_random_uuid per existing row, so every row gets a distinct value), but the database does not guarantee it and nothing prevents an out-of-band UPDATE or a restore from creating a duplicate, in which case `rows[0]` picks an arbitrary one of the two accounts and unsubscribes the wrong user.
findings.impact: Both unsubscribe lookups sequentially scan the entire users table on every click of an unsubscribe link in any notification email, which is the one link in the product that must work reliably for CAN-SPAM and GDPR compliance. The uniqueness the code depends on to identify an account is a convention, not a constraint, on the one column the app trusts to authenticate an unauthenticated caller.
findings.recommendation: In instrumentation.ts, next to the ALTER at :1248, add `UPDATE users SET unsubscribe_token = gen_random_uuid() WHERE unsubscribe_token IS NULL;` then `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_users_unsubscribe_token ON users(unsubscribe_token);`, following the same backfill-then-unique-index pattern already used for scan_history.public_id at :2609-2619. That fixes the sequential scan and the missing guarantee in one statement.

findings.title: users.updated_at is exported as the account's last-modified timestamp in both GDPR data exports while roughly two dozen UPDATE paths never bump it
findings.description: users.updated_at is `TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT NOW()` (instrumentation.ts:321) with no NOT NULL and no trigger; no table in the schema has an updated_at trigger, so the column is only correct where a hand-written `updated_at = NOW()` appears in the UPDATE. Eight sites do that (app/actions/stripe.ts:110, app/api/v3/admin/route.ts:1884, lib/billing/staff-plan.ts:94, :110, :149, instrumentation.ts:2725, and the two role-change paths).
